Growth and yield of oat as influenced by different 
fertilizer levels
S. S. Kakon, M.Z.Ali, S.S.Nasreen and M. A. K. 
Mian
A field experiment was conducted at Agronomy 
Research Field, Gazipur of Bangladesh Agricultural 
Research Institute during rabi season of 2024-25 to 
assess the growth and yield of oat crop under nutrient 
management.Treatment included in the experiment 
were: T 1= 90-25-20 kg/ha of NPK (BARI),T 2 = 
T1 + 25% NPK (112-31.25-25 kg/ha of NPK) ,T 3 
= T1 + 50% NPK (135-37.5-30 kg/ha of NPK) ,T 4 
= T1 -25% NPK (68-18.5-15 kg/ha of NPK) ,T 5 = 
T1 -50% NPK (45-7.5-10 kg/ha of NPK) and T 6 = 
Control (Native fertility). The soil of the research 
area belongs to the Chhihata series under AEZ-28.
The meteorological data of the experimental site 
revealed that the highest temperature prevails in 
March-April and the lowest in December to January. 
Maximum rainfall was received during the months 
of April .The crop received 105 mm rain showers 
from November to April in 2024-25 years. The 
average maximum (32.08 °C) was found in the 
month of March during the crop growing season and 
minimum (12.77 °C) temperature in the month of 
January during the crop growing season. Soils of the 
experimental plots were collected and analyzed. The 
physical and chemical properties of initial soil of the 
experimental plot has been taken. The soil was clay 
loam with pH 6.42, OC 1.09% (very low), total N 
0.094% (very low), exchangeable K 0.097meq/100g 
soil (very low), available P 17.31 μg/mg (optimum), 
available S 17.57 μg/g (optimum), available Zn 
0.629 μg/g (low) and available B 0.166 μg/g (very 
low). Organic carbon, N, K and B were under 
critical level in the soil. The experiment was laid out 
in a randomized complete block design with three 
replications and the unit plot size was 3m × 3m. Oat 
line was used in the experiment. Seeds were sown 
on 25 November, 2024 and harvested on 25 April, 
2025.Fertilizers were applied as per treatment. Half 
N and all other fertilizer was applied as basal during 
final land preparation and rest N was applied at 
25DAS. Data on growth parameters like leaf area 
and dry matter accumulation were measured at 
different dates with 15 days interval. For recording 
dry matter weight and leaf area, five plants from 
each replication were sampled at 30, 45, 60, 75, 
90 DAS and at harvest. Different plant parts of the 
collected samples were separated and then oven 
dried at 800C for 72 hours. Leaf area was measured 
by an automatic leaf area meter (L13100 c, L1COR, 
USA).At harvest, the yield data was recorded plot 
wise. The collected data were analyzed statistically 
and means were adjudged by LSD test at 5% level 
of significance using Statistics 10 package. Different 
fertilizers level differed in leaf area index (LAI), 
total dry matter production (TDM), yield and yield 
components of oat. Results revealed that, fertilizer 
levels showed great influence on leaf area index 
(LAI), dry matter production and yield of oat. The 
highest LAI was recorded inT 3 (N135P370K30kg/ha) 
treatment. Significantly the highest oat yield (1.15 
t/ha) was observed inT 1 (90-25-20 kg/ha of NPK) 
treatment. Cost and return analysis revealed that the 
highest gross return (Tk.69000/ha) wasfoundinT 1 
(90-25-20 kg/ha of NPK) treatment. But the highest 
benefit cost ratio (BCR) of 2.19-2.21 was obtained 
from T 1 and T4 treatment. The results revealed that 
among the different fertility levels,T 1 (N90P25K20 kg/
ha) and T 4 (68-18.5-15 kg/ha of NPK)were found 
better in respect of yield due to economic returns 
which saving 10% NPKS for oat cultivation. 
N68P18K15kg/ha andN 90P25K20 kg/ha were found the 
most suitable dose for obtaining higher yield and 
economic benefit in oat cultivation.
Productivity and quality of fodder oat as 
influenced by seed rate and cutting time
S. S. Kakon, J.A. Chowdhury, M. Z. Ali, S.T.Zannat, 
M.A H. Khan and M.A.K.Mian
The experiment was conducted during November 
2023 to March 2024 at Grey Terrace Soils of 
Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute 
farm, Gazipur. The objective of the study was to 
determine the optimum seed rate and cutting time 
for oat to produce maximum fodder yield and its 
effect on the quality of the fodder. The soil of the

Agronomy I 161
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
experimental field was silty clay loam in texture 
with pH 5.8 belonging to Chhiata series under AEZ 
28. There were two cutting time viz. C 1= 60 days 
after sowing (DAS) and C 2=70 days after sowing 
(DAS) and five seed rate viz. S 1= 70 kg/ha, S 2= 
80 kg/ha, S 3=90 kg/ha, S 4=100 kg/ha, S 5= 120 kg/
ha included the experiment. The experiment was 
laid out in randomized complete block design with 
three replications. The unit plot size was 3.6 m × 
3 m. Fertilizers were applied @ 90-25-20-27-2-2 
kg/ha N-P-K-S-Zn-B (Rahman et al., 2021). Half 
N and full dose of other fertilizer should be applied 
as basal dose during land preparation. Remaining 
N fertilizer will be top dressed at 55-60 DAS (days 
after sowing) after irrigation in two equal splits and 
mixed thoroughly with the soil as soon as possible 
for better utilization. Seed of fodder oat were sown 
on 28 November 2024 with 20 cm x continuous 
sowing. Cutting of green fodder was done as per 
treatment leaving 6 cm at the bottom. The fodder was 
harvested as per cutting treatment and fodder yield 
was taken from whole plot. Five plant samples were 
collected from each plot, partitioned into different 
components and oven dried for calculating dry 
matter followed by chemical component analysis. 
Chemical component estimation for fodder quality 
was done at Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute 
(BLRI) Laboratory. Data on green fodder yields 
were analyzed statistically with the help of Statistics 
10 Programme and the means were adjudged by 
using LSD at 5% level of significance. Economic 
analysis was also done. Fodder yield of oat was 
significantly affected by different seeding rate and 
cutting time. Fodder yield increased with increasing 
cutting time. Fodder yield and production efficiency 
were significantly influenced by cutting time and 
seed rate. It was found that 120 kg/ha produced the 
highest fodder yield (38.78 t/ha) when cutting was 
done at 70 DAS. Though the highest gross return (Tk. 
154880 /ha) was obtained from T10 (120 kg seed rate 
/ha and cutting at 70 DAS) treatment but the highest 
benefit cost ratio (3.24) was found in T 9 (100 kg 
seed rate /ha and cutting at 70 DAS) treatment. The 
result revealed that the concentration (g/100g dry 
matter) of organic matter (OM) and ash% increased 
significantly with the decrease in crude protein (CP) 
content through advancing the cutting time. The 
result also revealed that cutting at 70 DAS and 120 
kg seed rate /ha recorded significantly higher green 
fodder yield but cut at 60 DAS proved significantly 
better in terms of green (564.27kg/ ha/day) fodder 
production efficiency as well as quality parameters 
viz. crude protein (12.3%) and ADF content. From 
the result it might be concluded that higher fodder 
yield of oat could be obtained by using 100-120 kg 
seeds/ha when cutting was done 60 DAS with better 
profitability at Gazipur region (AEZ 28). 
Growth and yield of barley as influenced by 
fertilizer and weed management
M. Z. Ali, J. A. Chowdhury, A. A. Begum, M. I. 
Hossain and M. A. K. Mian
The experiment was conducted at the research field 
of Agronomy Division BARI, Gazipur during rabi 
season of 2024-25. The soil of the research area 
belongs to AEZ-28. The soil was clay loam with pH

Effect of nutrient management on growth, yield 
and nutrient uptake in sorghum
S.S. Nasreen, A. A. Begum, M. A. H. Khan, J.A. 
Chowdhury, M. Z. Ali and M. A. K. Mian
A two-year field study was conducted at Agronomy 
Research Field, BARI, Gazipur, during rabi season 
of 2023-24 and 2024-25 to evaluate the impact

Agronomy I 163
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
of different nutrient management levels on the 
growth, yield and nutrient uptake of sorghum. 
The experiment was conducted in RCBD with 3 
replications consisting five treatments viz., T 1: 150-
75-62.5-33.75-2.8-1.4 kg/ha of N-P-K-S-Zn-B; T 2: 
120-60-50-27-2.8-1.4 kg/ha of N-P-K-S-Zn-B; T 3: 
90-45-37.5-20.25-2.8-1.4 kg/ha of N-P-K-S-Zn-B; 
T4: 60-30-25-13.5-2.8-1.4 kg/ha of N-P-K-S-Zn-B; 
T5: Control (Native fertility). The unit plot size 
was 3m × 3m. BARI sorghum-1 seeds were sown 
on 29 November 2023 and 01 December 2024, 
respectively maintaining 60 cm line spacing and 10 
cm plant to plant distance. One third N and all other 
fertilizer were applied as basal during final land 
preparation and rest N will be applied at 25 and 50 
DAS in equal split. Data for growth analysis were 
taken at 35 DAS, 55 DAS, 75 DAS, 95 DAS, and 115 
DAS in the year 2023-24. Chlorophyll content was 
measured using a SPAD meter (Model SPAD-502, 
Minolta crop, Ramsey, NJ). The yield component 
data was taken from 10 randomly selected plants 
prior to harvest from each plot. At harvest, the yield 
data was recorded plot wise. The collected data were 
analyzed statistically and means were adjudged by 
LSD test at 5% level of significance using Statistics 
10.The highest SPAD value was observed at 60 DAS 
which declined progressively reaching the lowest at 
90 DAS in all treatments. The highest values (from 
28.1 at 35 DAS to -45.8 at 115 DAS) were observed 
in T 1 treatment all through the growing season. 
The TDM accumulation rate was slower up to 55 
DAS then increased rapidly up to 95 DAS and then 
increased slowly up to harvest. TDM accumulation 
was less with native fertility and higher in higher 
dose of fertilizer (T1) applied (1316 g/m2) at harvest. 
Grain yield was significantly influenced by nutrient 
levels. A general decline in seed weight and yield was 
observed across all treatments in 2024-25, possibly 
due to environmental factors. Thousand seed weight 
showed a clear nutrient response, with the highest 
values in T 1 and T 2 in both years. Thousand seed 
weight declined sharply in lower nutrient levels, 
particularly in T 5. Among the treatments, T 1(150-
75-62.5-33.75-2.8-1.4 kg/ha of N-P-K-S-Zn-B) 
treatment produced the tallest plant (137 cm) and 
the highest yield (4.5 t/ha in 2023-24 and 3.6 t/ha 
in 2024-25) and T 2 (120-60-50-27-2.8-1.4 kg/ha 
of N-P-K-S-Zn-B) treatment also performed well, 
particularly in plant height (138 cm) and seed weight 
(39.5 g in 2023-24), although its yield was slightly 
lower than T 1 treatment. On the other hand T 3, T4 
and T5 treatments showed a gradual decline across 
all parameters. Treatment T5(Control) recording the 
lowest values in plant height, seed weight and yield 
in both years. Nutrient uptake (N-P-K and S) over 
two cropping years highlighted a positive correlation 
with sorghum grain yield. Sorghum's response to 
nutrient management varied significantly across 
years, with 2023-24 outperforming 2024-25 in yield 
and TSW. In conclusion, balanced and adequate 
nutrient application significantly enhanced sorghum 
growth and yield.
Growth and yield of sorghum as affected by row

S. Akther, A. A. Begum, M.Z.Ali and M. A. K. Mian
The field experiment was conducted at Agronomy 
Research Field, Joydebpur, Gazipur of Bangladesh 
Agricultural Research Institute, Joydebpur, Gazipur 
during Rabi season of 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 
to find out suitable planting geometry for getting

50 cm × 10 cm (20 plants/m 2), T 2= 50 cm × 15 
cm (13 plants/m 2), T3= 60 cm × 10 cm (16 plants/
m2), T4= 60 cm × 15 cm (11 plants/m 2), T5= 70 cm 
× 10 cm (14 plants/m 2) and T 6= 70 cm× 15 cm (9 
plants/m2) were used in the study. The trial was set 
up in randomized complete block design with three 
replications. Unit plot size was 3m × 3m. The crop 
was fertilized with 120-48-75-30-3-1.5 kg/ha N-P-
K-S-Zn-B and 5 t/ha cowdung (BARI). One third 
of N and all other fertilizers were applied as basal. 
Rest N was applied at 25 and 45 DAS in two equal 
splits. A light irrigation was given after sowing of 
seeds for uniform germination. Three irrigations 
were done at 30 and 50 DAS and grain development 
stage. Thinning was done at 20 DAS and weeding 
at 25 and 45 DAS. Data on growth parameters 
like leaf area and dry matter accumulation were 
measured at different dates with 25 days interval. 
For recording dry matter weight and leaf area, three 
plants from each replication were sampled at 30, 
45, 60, 75, 90 DAS and at harvest. Different plant 
parts of the collected samples were separated and 
then oven dried at 800C for 72 hours. Leaf area was 
measured by an automatic leaf area meter (L13100 
c, L1COR, USA). Light interception (LI) by the 
crop was recorded at five times (30, 45, 60, 75, 90 
DAS and at harvest) at around 11:30 am to 13:00 pm

by Sunfleck Ceptometer (Model Decagon, Pulman, 
Washington, USA). Four readings each of PARinc

plot. The proportion of intercepted PAR (PARint)

Light interception {PARint (%)} = × 100 
where, PARinc= Incident PAR, PARt= Transmitted

BARI Sorghum-1 was used in the experiment. Seeds 
were sown on 27 November, 2022 in 1 st year and 
28 November, 2023 in 2nd year and harvested on 17 
April, 2023 in 1st year and 17 April, 2024 in 2nd year. 
At harvest 10 plants were randomly selected for 
collecting data on yield components. Grain yields 
were calculated on whole plot basis and adjusted 
at 14% moisture content. The collected data were 
analyzed statistically with the help of Statistics 10 
program and mean separation was done by LSD 
at 5% level of significance. Results revealed that 
planting geometry has great influence on leaf area 
index (LAI), dry matter production and yield of 
sorghum. Plant spacing 70 cm × 15 cm produced 
higher LAI, which intercepted higher light energy.

highest TDM. Significantly the maximum grain 
yield (4.56 t/ha at 2023-24 and 4.65 t/ha at 2024-25) 
was recorded from T3 (60 cm × 10 cm: 16 plants/ m2) 
treatment due to higher plant population. From the 
two years (2023-2024 and 2024-2025) study it may 
be concluded that plant spacing 60 cm × 10 cm (16 
plants/m2) is suitable for sorghum cultivation.

environment. The soil type is clayey loam. The land

up as the sorjan system. The soil shows a neutral 
reaction in nature, low organic matter content, and 
overall low fertility level The experiment consisted 
of two factor with nine treatments viz., Factor A.

of vermicompost. The time taken for curd maturity 
was highest in treatment C 1T3 (72.00 days) and 
lowest in treatment C3T1 (69.33 days). The heaviest 
individual curd was produced by plants treated with 
C1T3 (1.75 kg), while the lightest curd was obtained

Effect of irrigation on yield of sunflower in 
Barishal region
M. M. Rahman and M. A. Rahman
The field trial was conducted at RARS, BARI, 
Rahmatpur, Barishal during 2024-25 to make an 
effective irrigation regime for getting maximum 
yield of sunflower. The location represents the 
Ganges Tidal Floodplain (AEZ-13), characterized 
with a subtropical monsoon climate and a humid 
environment. The soil type is clayey loam. The 
land of the experiment is medium low land. The 
treatments included various irrigation schedules: 
I0 = No irrigation, I 1 = Irrigation at 35days after 
emergence (before flowering), I 2 = Irrigation at 
55 days after emergence (during heading), I 3 = 
Irrigation at 75days after emergence (during grain 
filling), I4 = Irrigation at 35 DAE + 55 DAE, I 5 = 
Irrigation at 35 DAE + 75 DAE, I 6 = Irrigation at 
55 DAE + 75 DAE, I 7 = Irrigation at 35 DAE + 55 
DAE + 75 DAE. The experiment was laid out in 
RCB design with three replications. The unit plot 
size was 6m×5m.The seeds are sown in line sowing 
method with row to row distance 50 cm and plant 
to plant distance 25 cm. The crop received N-P-K-
S-Mg-Zn-B @ 105-36-84-24-6-2-1.6+2 kg/ha. Half 
of urea and full amount of other fertilizers will be 
broadcasted during final land preparation. The rest 
amount of urea was top dressed at 20-25 and 40-
45 days after emergence of seedling. Weeding, plant 
protection and other intercultural operations were 
done as and when necessary as per the recommended 
production technologies of the crops. Data were 
collected and analysed statistically using windows 
based computer software of Statistix 10 version 
and then the mean differences were adjudged with 
Duncan's Multiple Range Test (DMRT). 
Irrigation scheduling had significant impact on the 
growth characteristics of sunflower. The longest 
plant was obtained from treatment T 3 (110.96 cm) 
which was irrigated at 75 DAE and statistically 
similar with treatment T 6, T4, T5 and T2 at 65 DAE. 
The shortest plant was found from T0 (70.6 cm) with 
no additional irrigation. At harvest stage, the largest 
plant was obtained from treatment T 7 (120.36 cm), 
which was irrigated at 35, 55 and 75 DAE due to 
sufficient irrigation and statistically similar with 
treatment T 6 (115.74 cm), T 3 (111.05 cm) and T5 
(110.77 cm) and the shortest plant was found from 
T0 (80.91 cm), which was controlled. The highest 
leaf area (8033.52 cm 2 at 65 DAE and 9275.88 cm 2 
at 75 DAE) was obtained from T 7 treatment and the 
lowest (4729.74 cm 2 at 65 DAE and 5635.50 cm 2 
at 75 DAE, respectively) was observed from T 0 
treatment. Highest (40.57 g at 65 DAE and 48.87 
g at 75 DAE, respectively) dry weight per plant 
was found from treatment T7(irrigation at 35 DAE 
+ 55 DAE + 75 DAE) treatment . The lowest dry 
weight was found from treatment T 0 (26.25 g at 65 
DAE and 28.52 g at 75 DAE). Irrigation interval 
significantly influenced thousand seed weight 
and yield. The increase in irrigation intervals 
affected sunflower yield. The highest yield (1967 
kg /ha) was obtained from T 7 (irrigation at 35 
DAE + 55 DAE + 75 DAE) treatment which was 
statistically similar to treatments T6 and T5 while the 
lowest seed yield was obtained from treatment T 0 
(848 kg). The highest gross return (Tk. 165860/
ha), gross margin (Tk. 81260/ha) and benefit 
cost ratio (1.96) was found from T7 (irrigation at 
35 DAE + 55 DAE + 75 DAE) treatment which was 
followed by T 6 and T 5 treatments. Application of 
irrigation water at 35 DAE + 55 DAE + 75 DAE 
might be optimum for getting higher yield of 
sunflower in Barishal. 
Effect of seasonal variation on growth and yield 
of foxtail millet (Kaon)
S.S. Nasreen, S. S. Kakon, J.A. Chowdhury, A. A. 
Begum, M. Z. Ali, M. A. H. Khan and M. A. K. Mian
A two-year field experiment was conducted during 
the rabi and kharif-1 seasons of 2023-24 and 2024-
25 at the Agronomy Research Field, BARI, Gazipur, 
to evaluate the optimum sowing time for foxtail 
millet in the region. It was consisted 8 treatments 
(sowing dates): T1: November 15, T2: November 30, 
T3: December 15, T 4: December 30, T 5: February 
15, T6: February 29 /March 01, T 7: March 15, T 8: 
March 30. It was done in randomized complete 
block design with 3 replications. The unit plot size 
was 3.0 m × 3.0 m. BARI Kaon-2 seeds were sown 
as respective dates as treatments. Fertilizer doses

166 I Agronomy
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
for foxtail millet was followed by FRG, 2018 (50-
20-35-8-1.5 kg/ha N-P-K-S-Zn respectively). Half 
of N and all other fertilizers were applied as basal 
during final land preparation of each sowing date 
and remaining N was top-dressed in two equal splits 
at 25 DAS (Days after sowing) and 60 DAS. The 
yield component data was taken from 10 randomly 
selected plants prior to harvest from each plot. At 
harvest, the yield data was recorded plot wise. The 
collected data were analyzed statistically using 
Statistics 10. March 30 (T8) sowing was unsuccessful 
due to poor germination. Early sowing dates like 
T1 (November 15) and T 2 (November 30) resulted 
in relatively good yields, particularly in 2024. In 
contrast, late sowing, especially T7 (March 15), led to 
significantly lower yields, highlighting the negative 
impact of delayed planting. While some treatments 
showed strong performance in individual traits, T 6 
demonstrated the most balanced and stable results 
across all measured parameters. In 2023-24, plant 
height varied widely, with the tallest plants observed 
in T6 (93.2 cm) and T4 (89.4 cm), while the shortest

and T6 and shortest in T 1 and T 7. Seed weight was

lowest seed weight was recorded in T 3. Yield was 
significantly higher in T 1, T2, and T6, and lowest in 
T7 (0.50 t/ha), suggesting poor productivity with 
delayed sowing. In 2024-25, although plant height 
differences were not statistically significant, T 5, T3, 
and T6 maintained taller plant stature. Panicle length 
remained highest in T 3 and T 6, and shortest in T 4. 
Seed weight was again highest in T 4 and T 6, and 
lowest in T5 and T3. Yield followed a similar pattern 
as the previous year, with T 1 and T 6 showing the 
highest values, while T3 and T7 had the lowest. Early 
sowing dates (T 1: November 15 and T 2: November 
30) in the rabi season, and February sowing (T 5 and 
T6) in the kharif season, are suitable for maximizing 
the yield of foxtail millet in Gazipur. March sowing 
(T7 and T8) should be avoided due to low productivity 
and risk of crop failure.

Effect of herbicides for controlling weeds in onion 
field
A. A. Begum, M.R. Islam, S. Akther and M. A. K. 
Mian
The experiment was conducted at Agronomy 
Research Field, Gazipur and the Regional 
Agricultural Research Station, Ishurdi, Pabna of 
BARI during 2024-2025 to find out the appropriate 
herbicide for controlling weed in onion field. 
Six treatments were included viz; T 1=Beenash 
(Oxidiazon 38%) @ 700 ml/ha, T 2 = Bounce30 WP 
(Bensulfuron methyl 12% + Bispyribac sodium 
18%) @ 75g/ha, T 3 =Agristar 25 EC (Oxidiazon 
25%) @ 1 L/ha, T 4= Dictate 46 SL (Bentazone 
Sodium 40%+MCPA potassium salt 6%) @ 2 L/
ha, T5 = Two hand weeding (HW) at 25 and 45 days 
after transplant (DAT), T 6= Control (No weeding). 
The experiment was laid out in a Randomized 
Complete Block design with three replications. The 
unit plot size was 3 m × 3 m. The crop was planted 
on 31 December 2024 and harvested on 28 March 
2025 in both locations. Fertilizer was applied @ 
105-45-90-30-3-1.4 kg/ ha of N-P-K-S-Zn-B (FRG, 
2018), respectively. All amount of P, S, Zn, B and 1⁄2 
of N and K were applied as basal during final land 
preparation. Remaining N and K were applied in 
two equal splits at 25 and 50 DAT. No weeding was 
done in case of herbicide applied plots. All herbicide 
were spraying at 2-3 leaf stage of weed. The data 
were analyzed by partitioning the total variance 
with the help of a computer using the R software 
program in Ishurdi and statistix-10 in Gazipur. The 
mean values were adjudged by LSD at 0.05 levels of 
probability in both locations. The highest WCE (81 
and 82% in Gazipur; 81and 81% in Ishurdi) were

168 I Agronomy
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
found in T5 treatment at 30 and 50 DAT, respectively. 
The highest bulb yield (14.71 t/ha in Gazipur and 
14.92 t/ha in Ishurdi), gross return (Tk. 588400/
ha and Tk. 596800/ha in Gazipur and Ishurdi, 
respectively) and cost of cultivation (Tk. 286900/ha 
in both locations) were observed in T 5 followed by 
T1. But the highest BCR (2.90 and 2.64 in Gazipur 
and Ishurdi, respectively) was observed in T 1 
treatment followed by T3 (2.65 and 2.59 in Gazipur 
and Ishurdi, respectively). The result revealed that 
two hand weeding at 25 and 45 days after transplant 
was found suitable weed management practice for 
controlling weeds in onion to get higher bulb yield. 
But post emergence herbicide Beenash (Oxidiazon 
38%) @ 700 ml/ha and Agristar 25 EC (Oxidiazon 
25%) @1 L/ha would be remunerative and effective 
herbicide for controlling weeds with higher bulb 
yield of onion during rabi season in Gazipur (AEZ 
28) and Ishurdi (AEZ 11) regions.

controling weeds in onion field
M. Z. Ali, Sabikunnahar, A. A. Begum, S. S. Kakon

A field experiment was conducted at Agronomy 
research field of Bangladesh Agricultural Research 
Institute, Gazipur and Regional Agricultural 
Research Station, Cumilla, during the period from 
December 2024 to March 2025. Seven treatments 
viz., T 1 = Fair 33 EC (Pendimethalin 33%) @ 
800 ml/ha spraying at 2-4 leaf stage of weeds, T 2 
=Victor 33 EC (Pendimethalin 33%)@ 1000 ml/
ha spraying on soil 1-2 days before transplanting, 
T3= Super Clean 23.5 EC (Oxyfluorfen 23.5% EC) 
@750 ml/ha spraying at 3-4 days before onion 
seedling transplanting, T 4=Two hand weeding at 
25 & 50 DAT and T 5 = Control (No weeding and 
no herbicide). The trial was set up in randomized 
complete block design with three replications. The 
unit plot size was 3 m × 3 m. The crop was fertilized 
with cowdung 10 t/ha and 140-60-120-40-4.5-2.1 
kg/ha of N-P-K-S-Zn-B (FRG 2024) respectively. 
Cowdung was applied at the time of land preparation. 
All of P, S, Zn, B and 1⁄2 of N and K were applied 
as basal during final land preparation. Remaining N 
and K were applied in two equal splits at 25 and 50 
days after transplanting followed by irrigation and 
mixed thoroughly with soil as soon as possible for 
better utilization followed by irrigation. Seedlings 
of onion variety (BARI Piaj-4) were transplanted 
at Gazipur on 23 December 2024 and 26 December 
2024 at Cumilla maintaining the spacing of 15 cm × 
5 cm. A light irrigation was given after transplanting. 
Weed samples were collected using 50 cm × 50 cm 
quadrate, from randomly selected four places from 
each plot as per treatment. Number and dry weight 
of weeds were recorded carefully. The weed control 
Efficiency (WEC) was calculated by the following 
formula.
WCE (%) =

BA

Where, A = Dry weight of weeds in no weeding plots 
and B = Dry weight of weeds in treated plots. The 
crop was harvested on 12 April 2025 at Gazipur 19 
April, 2025 at Cumilla. Yield and yield contributing 
characters were recorded and analyzed statistically 
and mean separations were done by LSD test at 5% 
level of significance. The maximum weed dry weight 
at 25 DAT (15.41 g/m 2 at Gazipur and 16.13/m 2 at 
Cumilla) and at 50 DAT (32.31 g/m2 at Gazipur and 
30.15 g/m2 at Cumilla) was obtained in T5 treatment 
(control plot), whereas, the minimum weed dry 
weight at 25 DAT (2.49 g/m2 at Gazipur and 2.34 g/
m2 at Cumilla) and at 50 DAT (5.12 g/m2 at Gazipur 
and 4.75 g/m2 at Cumilla) was found in T2 treatment 
followed by T 1, T4 and T 3 treatments (Table 2). The 
variation in WCE was observed among different 
herbicides in both locations. The highest WCE at 
Gazipur (83.84% and 84.15%) was found at 25 and 
50 DAT in T 2 treatment followed by T 4, T1 and T 3 
treatments (Table 2). Similar trend also observed 
in case of Cumilla. The highest WCE at Cumilla 
(85.49% at 25 DAT and 84.25% at 50 DAT) was 
found in the same treatment (T 2) followed by T4, T1 
and T3 treatments (Table 2). The target weeds of all 
herbicides were controlled 81-87% at 25-50 DAT in 
both the locations. The height of pseudo stem, single 
bulb weight and yield of onion were significantly 
influenced at both locations by applying different 
type of herbicides (Table 3). The tallest pseudo stem 
(56.61 cm at Gazipur and 53.86 cm at Cumilla), the 
highest single bulb weight (70.26 g at Gazipur and 
69.22 g at Cumilla) and bulb yield (18.64 t/ha at 
Gazipur and 18.71 t/ha at Cumilla) were observed in 
T4 treatment (Two hand weeding at 25 and 50 DAT). 
Among the herbicides treated plots the tallest pseudo 
stem (55.77 cm at Gazipur and 53.86 cm at Cumilla), 
the highest single bulb weight (65.02 g at Gazipur 
and 63.98g at Cumilla) and bulb yield (17.50 t/ha

at Gazipur and 18.02 t/ha at Cumilla) were obtained 
from T 2 treatment which was statistically similar

the smallest pseudo stem (31.30 cm at Gazipur

weight (20.87 g at Gazipur and 19.84 g at Cumilla) 
and bulb yield (10.33 t/ha at Gazipur and 10 .45t/

there by reducing availability of moisture, light and

Weed control in brinjal through intercropping
A. A. Begum, J.A. Chowdhury, S. S. Kakon, M. Z. 
Ali, S. Shanjida and M. A. K. Mian
A field experiment was undertaken at Agronomy 
Research Field of BARI during rabi season of 
2024-2025 to find out the suitable intercrop with 
brinjal for weed control and higher productivity 
with monetary advantage. Treatments included in 
the experiment were: T 1= Brinjal (80 cm × 60 cm) 
+ Spinach intercrop, T 2= Brinjal (80 cm × 60 cm) 
+ Red amaranth intercrop, T 3= Brinjal (80 cm × 
60 cm) + Coriander intercrop, T 4= Brinjal (80 cm 
× 60 cm) + Grasspea intercrop (twig used as leafy 
vegetables), T5= Brinjal (80 cm × 60 cm) + Garden 
pea intercrop, T6= Sole brinjal (80 cm × 60 cm) + 3 
hand weeding at 20, 40 and 60 days after transplant 
(DAT) and T7= Sole brinjal (80 cm × 60 cm) + No 
weeding/no intercrop (Control).The experiment was 
laid out in randomized complete block design with 
four replications and the unit plot size was 4m × 3m. 
The variety of brinjal was BARI Begun-8 and that of 
spinach was BARI Palongshak-1, red amaranth was 
BARI Lalshak-1, coriander was BARI Dhonia-1, 
grass pea was BARI Kheshari-6 and garden pea was 
BARI Motorshuti-3 were used in the experiment. 
Brinjal (35 days old seedlings) was transplanted 
on 1 December, 2024 and seeds of all vegetables 
were sown (broadcast) on 12 December, 2024 after 
establishment of brinjal seedlings. Three vegetables 
(spinach, red amaranth and coriander) were sown 
two times. Seeds of spinach and red amaranth were 
second time sown on 20 January, 2025 (after harvest 
of first time). Second time coriander seeds were sown 
on 22 February 2025 (after harvest of first time). The 
seeds of all vegetables were treated with provex at 
the rate of 3 g per one kg of seed. Fertilizers were 
applied at the rate of 140-48-140-20-3-1.5-4000 kg/
ha of N- P- K-S- Zn- B, OF (FRG, 2018) as urea, 
triple super phosphate (TSP), muriate of potash 
(MoP), gypsum, zinc sulphate and boric acid for both 
sole brinjal and intercrop. Half of organic fertilizer 
and all of P, S, Zn and B were applied as basal during 
final land preparation. Remaining organic fertilizer 
were applied in pits before planting of seedlings. N 
and K were applied in three equal splits at 20, 40 and 
60 DAT as ring method under moist soil condition 
and mixed thoroughly with the soil as soon as 
possible for better utilization. Besides this, 20 kg/
ha of urea was top dressed in second time sowing 
of spinach, red amaranth and coriander at 15 DAS 
and at 30 DAS of gardenpea. Weed samples were 
taken at 40 and 70 DAT of brinjal from 1 m2 area in 
each plot using quadrate and weed population and 
dry weight were recorded. Weed control efficiency

170 I Agronomy
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
(WCE %) was calculated following Kundu et al. 
(2009) as:
WCE (%) = 

 −
A
BA
100 where, A = Dry weight of 
weeds in control plots and B = Dry weight of weeds 
in treated plots. Data on yield contributing characters 
of brinjal were taken from randomly selected 5 plants 
from each plot. Yield of all crops were taken from 
whole plot area. Brinjal was harvested 4 times on 3 
March, 10 March, 17 March and 6 April 2025. On the 
other hand, spinach and red amaranth were harvested 
2 times on 17 January and 25 February 2025 (Every 
time 35 DAS of vegetable). Coriander and grass pea 
(twig as leafy vegetable) were harvested 2 times 
on 22 January and 5 March 2025 (Every time 40 
DAS of vegetable). Garden pea was harvested on 
17 February (65 DAS). Brinjal equivalent yield was 
computed by converting yield of intercrops on the 
basis of prevailing market price of individual crop 
following the formula of Bandyopadhyay (1984) as 
given below: 
Brinjal equivalent yield = Yib + (Yix × Px)/ Pb
Where, Yib = Yield of intercrop brinjal, Yix = 
Yield of intercrop vegetable (spinach/red amaranth/
coriander/grass pea/garden pea), Pb = Market 
price of brinjal and Px = Market price of vegetable 
(spinach/red amaranth/coriander/grass pea/garden 
pea).
Collected data of all the crops were analyzed 
statistically with Statistix 10 and the means were 
adjudged by LSD test at 5% level of significance. 
Economic analysis was also done considering local 
market price of harvested crops. Weed management 
practice through intercropping with vegetables 
showed influence on weed population, weed dry 
matter, weed control efficiency (WCE), yield 
components and yield of brinjal. The highest weed 
population 95 and 146/m 2 were recorded in control 
plot at 40 and 70 DAT, respectively. The lowest 
weed population 11 and 12/m 2 were recorded in T 2 
treatment at 30 and 70 DAT, respectively. Similar 
trend was observed in weed dry matter. Intercropping 
treatments showed 82-90% WCE and the highest 
WCE (90% both at 30 and 70 DAT) was recorded 
in T 2 treatment. All intercropping treatments 
showed better performance than sole brinjal (with 
and without weeding). Intercropping treatments 
showed 28.98-39.64 t/ha brinjal equivalent yield 
(BEY) which were 15-57% higher than sole brinjal 
(T6). The highest BEY (39.64 t/ ha), gross return 
(Tk. 1189288/ ha), gross margin (Tk. 899558/ 
ha) and benefit cost ratio (4.10) were observed in 
Brinjal (80 cm × 60 cm) + Red amaranth intercrop. 
The results revealed that weed control in brinjal 
through intercropping might be higher productive 
and economically viable for brinjal production. 
Moreover, spinach and red amaranth intercrop with 
brinjal might be agronomically more feasible and 
economically more profitable at Gazipur region 
(AEZ- 28).
Effect of integrated weed management on yield 
of sesame
S.S. Nasreen, J.A. Chowdhury, A. A. Begum, S. S. 
Kakon, M. A. H. Khan and M. A. K. Mian
A field experiment was conducted at Agronomy 
Research Field of BARI, Gazipur during Kharif-1, 
2025 to find out suitable weed management practice 
for controlling weeds in sesame for getting higher 
yield and economic return. The treatments were 
as follows: T 1= Pendimethalin 33% EC @ 2.5 L/
ha as pre-emergence, T 2= Pendimethalin 33% EC 
@ 2.5 L/ha as pre-emergence + one hand weeding 
at 25 DAS, T 3= Quizalofo-p-ethyl 5% EC @ 1 L/
ha as post- emergence (2-3 leaf stage of weed), T4= 
Intercropping black gram (broadcast sowing) with 
sesame simultaneously, T 5= Two hand weeding at 
25 DAS and at 45 DAS, T6= No weeding (control).
The experiment was set up in randomized complete 
block design with three replications. The unit 
plot size was 3.6 m × 3.6 m. Seeds of sesame 
(BARI Til-4) were sown @ 25 kg/ ha on 10March 
2025maintained30 cm row to row distance. 
Fertilizers were applied at the rate of 75-30-60-21-
2.6-2 of N-P-K-S-Zn-B Kg/ha as urea, triple super 
phosphate, muriate of potash, gypsum, zinc sulphate 
and boric acid (FRG, 2018). Half of N and all other 
fertilizer was applied as basal during final land 
preparation and rest N was applied at 25 -35 DAS. 
Two irrigations were applied, one at immediately 
after seed sowing and another at flowering stage 
(35 DAS) of crop. Intercultural operations such as 
thinning, applying insecticides were done as and 
when necessary. Weed samples were taken at 25 and 
45 DAS from 1 m2 area in each plot using quadrate 
and weed population and dry weight were recorded. 
Weed control efficiency measures the efficiency 
of any weed control treatment in reducing the 
weed biomass production in comparison to weedy

Agronomy I 171
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
treatment (Mani 1968). Mathematically, it could be 
expressed as below. 
WCE (%) = 

 −
A
BA
100 where, A = Dry weight of 
weeds in control plots and B = Dry weight of weeds 
in treated plots. 
Sesame was harvested on 01June 2025.Atharvest 
yield and yield contributing characters were 
recorded and analyzed statistically following 
Statistix-10 software package. Mean was adjudged 
by LSD test at 5% level of significance. Economic 
analysis was also done considering local market 
price of harvested crop. 
Weed management practice showed influence on 
weed population, weed dry matter, weed control 
efficiency (WCE) and yield of sesame. Number 
of weeds, weed dry weight, WCE and intensity of 
weed infestation have been affected by different 
weed control method. The common and dominant 
weeds during the period of experimentation were 
grasses like , Shyama (Echinochloa crusgalli), 
Chapra (Eleusine indica) and Anguli (Digitaria 
Spp.), sedges like Mutha (Cyperus rotundus) 
and broad-leaved weeds like Helencha (Enhydra 
fluctuans), Malancho (Alternanthera philoxeroides), 
Kanai banshi (Commelina benghalensis), kanainala 
(Cyanoties axillaries) and Shaknote (Amaranthus 
viridis). The highest WCE (94% at 45 DAS) and 
the lowest intensity of weed infestation (18. at 45 
DAS) were found in T 2(Pendimethalin 33% EC 
@ 2.5 L/ha as pre-emergence + one hand weeding 
at 25 DAS) treatment. The highest seed yield 
(0.98 t/ha), gross return (Tk.98000/ha) and cost 
of cultivation (Tk.56500/ha) was observed in T 5 
followed by T 2. But the highest BCR (1.90) was 
observed in T 2(Pendimethalin 33% EC @ 2.5 L/ha 
as pre-emergence + one hand weeding at 25 DAS) 
treatment followed by T 1 (1.88). From the result 
it may be concluded that among all treatments T 2 
(Pendimethalin + one hand weeding) treatment 
provided the best combination of weed suppression 
and yield enhancement. Highest weed control 
efficiency was recorded in T 2 treatment which was 
followed by T 1 correlating with improved yield.T 4 
and T6 exhibited poor weed suppression, especially 
T6 with no control measures.T 5 also achieved good 
WCE, validating the efficacy of manual weeding. 
Highest yield was observed in T 5 (0.98 t/ha) 
followed closely by T2 (0.97 t/ha), demonstrating the 
effectiveness of two hand weeding and integration of 
chemical + manual control. Lowest yield occurred 
in T6 (0.62 t/ha) where no weed management was 
implemented. Despite higher plant height in T 6 and 
T3, yield was compromised due to increased weed 
competition, especially with higher dry matter 
accumulation in weeds.

one hand weeding at 45 DAS, T4 = Quizalofop-p-
ethyle @ 2-3 L/ha spraying as post sowing + one 
hand weeding at 45 DAS, T5 = Mulching with straw 
(5-6 cm) after sowing, T6 = Two Hand weeding at 
25 and 45 DAT and T 7 = Control (No weeding). 
The trial was set up in randomized complete block 
design with three replications. Sowing was done 
on 14 January, 2025 at Gazipur whereas at RARS, 
Barishal sowing was done on 19 December 2024 
due prevailing weather and temperature. The unit 
plot size was 3 m × 3 m. Test crop was BARI 
hybrid soybean-7. The crop was fertilized with 
cow dung (3 t/ha), 32-40-80-20-3.0-1.5 kg/ha 
of N-P-K-S-Zn-B respectively (FRG' 18) in the 
form of urea-TSP-MoP-gypsum-zinc sulphate 
and boric acid. All Fertilizers should be applied 
as basal dose during final land preparation and 
mixed thoroughly with soil as soon as possible for 
better utilization. A light irrigation was given after 
sowing for uniform emergence of seeds. Weed 
samples were collected from randomly selected 
four places from each plot at 25 and 45 days after 
planting. Harvesting was done on 6 May, 2025 at 
Gazipur and on 7 April, 2015 at Barishal. Yield 
and yield contributing characters were recorded 
and analyzed statistically using "STAR" software 
package and means were separated by LSD at 
5% level of significance. Economic analysis was 
performed considering the prevailing market price 
of applied inputs and output of soybean. Results 
showed that the highest number of weeds/m 2 (94/
m2at 25 DAS and 174/m 2 at 45 DAS in Gazipur 
and 67/m2 at 25 DAS and 168/m 2 at 45 DAS in 
Barishal) recorded in T7 (No Weeding) treatment. 
Maximum Weed dry weight (144.51 g/m 2 at 25 
DAS and 284.98 g/m 2 at 45 DAS in Gazipur and 
40.18 g/m2 at 25 DAS and 231.75 g/m2 at 45 DAS 
in Barishal) found in controlled plots. Whereas, 
highest weed control efficiency (88.05% at 25 DAS 
and 89.10% at 45 DAS at Gazipur and 90.06% 
at 25 DAS and 93.44% at 45 DAS in Barishal) 
found in T1 (Pendamethylene @ 1.5 L/ha spraying 
as post sowing + one hand weeding at 45 DAS) 
treatment. Significantly, the highest yield (2.09 at 
Gazipur and 2.14 t/ha at Barishal) was observed 
in T 1 (Pendamethylene @ 1.5 L/ha spraying as 
post sowing + one hand weeding at 45 DAS) 
treatment. The highest gross margin (34728 Tk/ha 
at Gazipur and 38280 Tk/ha at Barishal) and BCR 
(1.71 at Gazipur and 1.81 at Barishal) showed in 
T1 (Pendamethylene @ 1.5 L/ha spraying as post

Agronomy I 173
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
sowing + one hand weeding at 45 DAS) treatment. 
From the result it may be concluded that, spraying 
Pendamethylene @ 1.5 L/ha as post emergence 
followed by one hand weeding at 45 DAS would 
be cost effective and economically profitable and 
effective for controlling weed in soybean field. 
Multiple Cropping 
Improvement of cropping pattern through chilli-
vegetable intercropping system
J.A. Chowdhury, S.S.Kakon, M. Z. Ali and M. A. 
K. Mian
The experiment was conducted at the Research Field 
of Agronomy Division BARI, Joydebpur, Gazipur 
(AEZ 28), during rabi season of 2024-25 to find out 
suitable inter crop based cropping pattern for higher 
productivity. Six treatments of cropping sequence 
were: CP 1=Chilli (100%) + gardenpea (40%) - T. 
aman - T. aman, CP 2=Chilli (100%) + bushbean 
(40%) - T. aus - T. aman, CP3=Chilli (100%) +red 
amaranth (66%) -T. aus -T. aman CP4=Chilli (100%) 
+ spinach (66%) - T. Aus - T. aman, CP5= Chilli- 
T. aus - T. aman, CP 6= Potato- T. aus (15 cm×15 
cm)- T. aman (25cm×20 cm) (Farmers' practice). 
The experiment was laid out in a RCB design with 
3 replications. The unit plot size was 4 m × 4.8 m. 
Different dates of operation and durations followed 
are described. A pre-sowing irrigation was given 
for proper emergence of the crops. Vegetable yield 
was taken from whole plot Chilli was transplanted 
with 2 seedlings per hill and later maintained one 
seedling per hill. The inter row spacing was 60 cm 
and intra row spacing was 50 cm. Intercrops were 
sown between the rows. Five tons of cowdung/
ha was applied to the crop before transplanting. 
Before chilli seedling transplanting, the land was 
fertilized with 96-45-75-15-1.5-1.4 kg/ha N-P-K-S-
Zn-B (FRG, 2018). Half of N and full amount of all 
other fertilizers were applied as basal during final 
land preparation. Remaining N was applied in three 
equal splits at 25, 50 and 70 days after transplanting 
(DAT).Transplanted aus (var. BRRI dhan 82) rice 
was transplanted (twenty five days aged seedling) 
with 15cm × 15 cm spacing. One third urea and 
full amount of TSP and MoP @ 135-55-85 kg/
ha, respectively, were applied as basal during final 
land preparation. Rest of the urea was applied in 
two equal splits at 15 and 45 DAT. Intercultural 
operations were done when necessary. Grain yield 
was taken from whole plot. Transplanted aman (var. 
BRRI dhan 56) rice (twenty five days aged seedling) 
was transplanted during kharif II season. One third 
urea and full amount of TSP, MoP and gypsum @ 
150-55-85-60 kg/ha, respectively, were applied as 
basal during final land preparation. Rest of the urea 
was applied in two equal splits at 15 and 40 days 
after transplanting (DAT). Intercultural operations 
were done when necessary. Grain yield was taken 
from whole plot. The higher rice equivalent yield 
(16.88 t/ ha), highest gross return (Tk. 590800/ha) 
and highest benefit cost ratio (2.95) were found in 
CP4 cropping pattern. Productivity and economic 
returns were lower in farmers' existing pattern. In 
terms of rice equivalent yield was increased by 
43.42% in CP4 followed by 37.13 % in CP1, 28.72 % 
in CP2 and 7.05 % in CP3 cropping pattern compared 
to farmers' practice (FP). In case of gross margin, the 
income was increased by 125.63 % in CP4 followed 
by 108.39 % in CP1, 88.44 % in CP2 and 39.46 % in 
CP3 cropping pattern compared to Farmers' practice 
(FP). Considering crop productivity, CP 4 (Chilli 
(100%) +spinach (66%) - T. aus -T. aman) was 
found the most suitable pattern for sustainable crop 
production.

Feasibility study of different component crops 
intercropping with chickpea
M. R. Islam 
A field experiment was conducted at the Regional 
Agricultural Research Station, Ishurdi, Pabna 
during 2024-2025 to find out the suitable intercrop 
combination with chickpea for higher productivity 
and economic return. Nine treatments combination 
viz; T 1=One row of chia in between two rows of 
chickpea; T2= One row of coriander in between two 
rows of chickpea; T 3 = One row of black cumin in 
between two rows of chickpea; T 4 = Two row black 
cumin in between two rows of chickpea; T 5 = One 
row of linseed in between two rows of chickpea; T6 = 
One row of barley in between two rows of chickpea; 
T7= One row of wheat in between two rows of 
chickpea; T8= One row of foxtail millet in between 
two rows of chickpea and T 9 = Sole chickpea were 
evaluated in this study. The main crop (chickpea) 
and component crops were sown simultaneously 
maintaining 40cm line with continuous sowing at 20 
November 2024. The experiment was conducted in 
a randomized block design with three replications. 
The unit plot size was 4m × 4m. Chickpea var. BARI 
chola-9, Chia var. BARI Chia-1, Coriander var. 
BARI Dhania-1, Black cumin var. BARI Kalogira-1, 
Linseed var. Nila, Barley var. BARI Barley-8, Wheat 
var. BARI Gom-33, Foxtail Millet var. BARI Kaon-
2 were used as a test variety in the experiment. The 
sole crop of chickpea and intercrops were fertilized 
with 27-18-24-12-2-1.2 kg /ha of N-P-K-S-Zn-B 
in the form of urea, triple super phosphate, murate 
of potash, gypsum, zinc sulphate and boric acid, 
respectively (FRG, 2018). The entire dose of N-P- 
K- S- Zn and B were applied at the time of final land 
preparation. The field were kept weed free for whole 
growing period. A post sowing irrigation was applied 
for proper germination and seedling establishment. 
Subsequently, irrigation was applied at 60 DAS. 
Other intercultural operations were done as and 
when required. Chickpea, chia, coriander, black 
cumin, linseed, barley, wheat and foxtail millet were 
harvested on 130 DAS, 112 DAS, 115 DAS, 125 
DAS, 115 DAS, 110 DAS, 110 DAS and 121 DAS, 
respectively. Data were analyzed statistically with 
the help of 'R' program and mean separation was 
done by LSD at 5% level of significance. The result 
revealed that the highest chickpea equivalent yield 
(2.39 t/ha) was obtained from T6 (One row of barley 
in between two rows of chickpea). The highest 
gross return (Tk.227043.95/ha), gross margin 
(Tk.152113.95/ha) and benefit cost ratio (3.03) were 
obtained from same treatment and the lowest (1.01 
t/ha) chickpea equivalent yield (CEY), gross margin 
(96016.80 kg/ha) and BCR (1.37) were recorded in 
T8 (One row of foxtail millet in between two rows of 
chickpea) treatment. Considering the produce higher 
chickpea yield barley and wheat intercropping with 
chickpea might be better combination.

software package. Economic analysis was also done

considering local market price of harvested crops.

Enhancement productivity and economic return 
of pigionpea through inclusion of turmeric
M. R. Islam and J. Hossain
A field experiment was conducted at the Regional 
Agricultural Research Station, Ishurdi, Pabna, 
BARI, during 2024-2025 to find out the suitable 
planting geometry of turmeric with pigeonpea in 
relation to higher system productivity and economic 
returns. Six treatments combination viz; T 1= Four 
rows of turmeric in between two rows of pigeon pea; 
T2=Three rows of turmeric in between two rows of 
pigeon pea; T 3=Two rows of turmeric in between 
two rows of pigeon pea; T 4= One row of turmeric 
in between two rows of pigeon pea; T 5=Sole 
turmeric; T 6=Sole pigeon pea were evaluated in 
the experiment. The design of the experiment was 
RCB and replicated thrice. The crops (Pigeonpea 
and turmeric) were sown/planted maintaining 2m × 
2m and 60cm × 25m plant spacing. The pigionpea 
var. BARI Arhar-1 and turmeric var. BARI Holud-5 
were used as a test. The sole crop of pigionpea and 
intercrops were fertilized with 20-60-40-20 kg ha-1 of 
N-P-K-S in the form of urea, triple super phosphate, 
murate of potash and gypsum, respectively (Ray et 
al., 2015; Jadhav, 2020). Half of the nitrogenous 
fertilizer and entire dose of P, K and S were applied 
at the time of land preparation and the rest half of 
nitrogen were top dressed at 50 days after sowing 
(DAS). Furthermore, additional 10 kg N was applied 
at 80 days after sowing/planting of component crops. 
For sole crop of turmeric, 140-40-120-20-5-2 kg ha-1 
of N-P-K-S-Zn-B was applied (FRG, 2018). Half K 
and full amount of P, S and Zn were incorporated 
as basal. Half N was top dressed at 50 days after 
planting (DAP). Rest 1⁄2 N and K were applied in two 
equal installments, at 80 and 110 DAP of turmeric. 
Plots were kept weed free for whole growing period. 
Irrigation and other intercultural operation were 
done as and when required. Pigeonpea seed were 
sown in line keeping seed rate of 15 kg/ ha on 21 
April 2024 maintaining 2 m× 2 m plant spacing, 
and harvested on 24 February 2025. Turmeric was 
planted on same date maintaining plant densities/
according to the treatments. Earthing up was done 
at 80 days after planting of turmeric. Turmeric 
was harvested at 8 January 2025. Collected data 
were analyzed statistically with the help of 'R' 
program and mean separation was done by LSD at 
5% level of significance. Significantly the highest 
pigeonpea yield (3.22 t/ha) was obtained from their 
respective sole crops. While considerably turmeric 
yield (21.49 t/ha) was obtained where four rows of 
turmeric intercrop in between two rows of pigeon 
pea (T1). Pigeonpea yield was reduced (2-18%) due 
to intercropping which was compensated by the 
turmeric yield. Results reveled that T1 (Four rows of 
turmeric in between two rows of pigeon pea) and 
T2 (Three rows of turmeric in between two rows 
of pigeon pea) intercropping system gave higher 
economic return as compared to sole crop. Four rows 
of turmeric in between two rows of pigeon pea (T 1) 
was found as the best intercrop combination in terms 
of higher gross margin (Tk. 566450/ha) along with 
pigeon pea equivalent yield (17.69 t/ ha) fallowed 
by three rows of turmeric in between two rows of 
pigeon pea (T 2). However, the highest benefit cost 
ratio (2. 89 and 2.78, respectively) was observed 
when three rows / four rows of turmeric intercrop in 
between two rows of pigeon pea (T2 and T1). Farmers 
could be benefited by adoption this technology.

Sunflower- legume strip cropping for resource 
conservation
A. A. Begum, M. Z. Ali, J.A. Chowdhury, S. Akther, 
M. R. Karim and M. A. K. Mian
The field experiment was conducted at the research 
field of Agronomy Division BARI, Gazipur during 
rabi season of 2024-25 to find out the effect of strip 
cropping on maintaining soil health and sustainable 
productivity. Four treatments viz., T 1= Sunflower 
four rows alternate with eight rows lentil, T 2= 
Sunflower four rows alternate with eight rows garden 
pea, T3= Sunflower 100% Brinjal (80 cm × 60 cm) 
rows alternate with five rows grass pea, T 4= Sole 
sunflower 16 rows were tested. The experiment was 
laid out in a RCB design with three replications. The 
unit plot size was 8.0 m × 15.0 m. Seeds of sunflower 
(var. BARI Surjomukhi-3), lentil (var. BARI 
Masur-8), garden pea (var. BARI Motorshuti-3) and 
grass pea (var. BARI Kheshari-3) were sown on 18 
November 2024 maintaining with each spacing. All 
crops were fertilized with recommended dose of 
fertilizer (FRG, 2018). For sunflower, one third of N 
and all of other fertilizers were applied during final 
land preparation and rest N was applied in two equal 
splits at 30 and 50 days after sowing. Other three 
crops were fertilized with all fertilizers during final 
land preparation. All intercultural operation and 
plant protection were done as and when required. 
Sunflower was harvested on 5 March 2025, lentil on 
11 March 2025, garden pea on 22 and 28 January 
2025 and grass pea on 6 March 2025. Sunflower 
equivalent yield (SEY) was computed by converting 
yield of intercrops on the basis of prevailing market 
price of individual crop following the formula of 
Bandyopadhyay (1984) as given below: 
Sunflower equivalent yield (SEY) = Yis + (Yil × Pl)/ 
Ps
Where, Yis = Yield of intercrop sunflower, Yil = 
Yield of intercrop legume crop (Lentil/garden pea/
grass pea), Ps = Market price of sunflower and Pl 
= Market price of legume crop (Lentil/garden pea/
grass pea),
At harvest the yield data was recorded whole plot 
wise. Collected data of all crops were analyzed 
statistically following Statistix-10 software package 
and the means were adjudged using LSD (0.05) test. 
Economic analysis was also done considering local 
market price of harvested crops. Strip cropping 
increased the accumulation of all investigated 
nutrient in sunflower grain and in soil. The inclusion

The experiment was conducted at the research field

Where, Yis = Yield of intercropped sorghum, Yicp

Barley- legume strip cropping for higher 
productivity and soil health
J.A. Chowdhury, M. Z. Ali, S. S. Kakon, 
M.A.H.Khan, M. R. Karim and M. A. K. Mian
A field experiment was conducted during rabi 
season, 2024-2025 at the Agronomy Research Field 
of Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute, 
Gazipur to maintain sustainable productivity and to 
conserve soil health. The experiment consisted of 
four treatments viz., T 1= Barley (12 row) alternate 
with garden pea (8 row), T 2= Barley (12 row) 
alternate with lentil (8 row), T 3= Barley (12 row) 
alternate with grass pea (6 row) and T4= Sole Barley 
(48 row). Experiment was laid out in a RCB design 
with three replications and each gross plot was 
9.6 m×8 m. Barley (BARI Barley-9), gardenpea 
(BARI Motorsuti-3), lentil (BARI Masur-6) and 
grasspea (BARI Khasari-1) were used as test 
crop. All crops were sown on 21 November 2024 
and harvested from 20 January to 12 March 2025 
(gardenpea: 20 January; lentil: 3 March; grasspea: 
12 March and barley: 2 March). 5 t/ha of cowdung 
and recommended dose of fertilizer was applied to 
all crops (for barley: 225-60-120-45-4-1.6kg/ha N- 
P- K- S- Zn- B; for lentil: 21-18-21-9-2-1.2 kg/ha 
N- P- K- S- Zn- B; for pea 45-24-30-12-1.4 kg/ha 
N- P- K- S- Zn and for grass pea 15-15-18-9 kg/
ha N- P- K- S) (FRG, 2018) in the form of urea, 
triple super phosphate (TSP), muriate of potash 
(MoP), gypsum, zinc sulphate and boric acid. For 
barley half of N and all other fertilizer was applied 
during final land preparation and rest N was applied 
in two equal splits at 30 days after sowing and 55 
days after sowing. For other three crops all fertilizer 
was applied during final land preparation. Cultural 
and plant protection measures were taken up as and 
when required. Observations were made on the 10 
randomly selected plants in each plot in respect to 
plant height and yield contributing characters. Yield 
data was taken whole plot basis. For economic 
analysis, gross return, total operational cost, gross 
margin and BCR were used. Strip cropping increased 
the accumulation of all investigated macronutrient in 
soil. The inclusion of pea as strip crop (T1 treatment) 
resulted in higher content of all investigated nutrients 
among the legume crops. The grain yield of barley 
(2.42 t/ha) was higher in sole barley plot than all 
strip cropping plot. But barley equivalent yield 
(BEY), gross return, gross margin and benefit cost 
ratio (BCR) were higher in all strip plot than sole 
barley plot. The highest barley equivalent yield (3.99 
t/ha), gross return (Tk. 199500/ha), gross margin 
(Tk.132500/ha) and BCR (2.98) were observed in 
T1 treatment. The result revealed that the farmers can 
be benefited by cultivating any one barley legume 
strip cropping with higher productivity. But among 
the three strip- cropping, barley + pea strip cropping 
was more profitable.

hat,8022271) to the traditional Potato-Boro-T.

The objective was to assess crop scheduling 
efficiency, yield performance, and economic

four cropping patterns e.g. CP 1: Potato-Boro rice-
T-aman (Check), CP 2: Gladiolus-Sesame-T. aman 
(early), CP3: Gladiolus-Sesame-T. aman (optimum),

180 I Agronomy
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
CP4: Gladiolus-T. Aus-T. aman (late). The 
experiment was laid out in Randomized Complete 
Block Design (RCBD) with three replications. 
Uniform agronomic practices were applied to all 
four patterns. Unit plot size was 4 m × 4 m with 
the recommended plant spacing of the respective 
crops. Fertilizer used for potato: 90-20-90-10-5-2-1 
N-P-K-S-Mg-Zn-B (kg/ha)-3 OF(t/ha), Gladioluus: 
120-44-90-16-2-1 N-P-K-S-Zn-B (kg/ha)- 5 OF(t/
ha), Sesame: 50-30-60-21-2-2 N-P-K-S-Zn-B 
(g/ha) and Rice: 60-10-50-8-1NPKSZn (Kg/ha) 
Source: FRG, BARC-2018. For Gladiolus, all OF 
(Organic fertilizer) and chemical fertilizers except N 
was applied as basal during final land preparation. 
In case of potato, all OF (Organic fertilizer), P-K- 
S- Zn, B and half of N & K was applied as basal 
during final land preparation and remaining half N 
& K was applied at 30-35 DAP during earthing up 
operation. For sesame, half of the N and all of P- K- 
S- Zn and B were applied as basal during final land 
preparation. Remaining half N was top dress at 25-30 
DAS. In case of Rice, all OF (Organic fertilizer) and

in both the year targeting production for the happy

record the yield and yield contributing characters.

out to analysis of variance (ANOV A) using the R 
studio. Further statistical validity of the differences 
among treatment means was estimated using the 
least significant difference (LSD) comparison 
method. Results revealed that Gladiolus-based 
patterns could be effectively incorporated within a

with a total cycle of 361 days and shorter idle

1,80,000 to 1,90,000 spikes or corms per hectare. 
Economic evaluation highlighted the superiority 
of Gladiolus-based systems, where the optimum

highest gross return (Tk.20,85,000/ha), net return 
(Tk.8,55,000/ha), and MBCR (1.70), significantly 
outperforming the traditional cropping system. The 
findings suggest that integrating high-value flower 
crops like Gladiolus into conventional cropping 
patterns can improve profitability, promote crop 
diversification, and enhance sustainability.

Intercropping of garden pea with brinjal under 
different plant population
M. Rahman and M. A. Siddiky 
An experiment was conducted at the research field 
of Regional Agricultural Research Station (RARS), 
Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI), 
Cumilla during rabi season 2024-2025 to find out 
the suitable crop combination for increasing total 
productivity, return and maximize land utilization 
under climatic conditions of Cumilla. The experiment 
was set up in a randomized complete block design 
with three replications and four treatments (T 1 = 
Sole brinjal (100%), T 2 = 100% brinjal + two rows 
of garden pea (46%), T3 = 100% brinjal + three rows 
of garden pea (70%), T 4 = 100% brinjal + garden 
pea broadcast (80%). The experiment was set up 
in a randomized complete block design with three 
replications. The sole crop of brinjal and intercropped 
treatments were fertilized with cow-dung at the rate 
of 5 t/ ha and 180-50-140-20-3-2 kg/ha of N-P-K-
S-Zn-B, respectively. One third of N, half of K and 
full amount of cowdung, P, S, B, Zn were applied 
during final land preparation. Remaining N and 
K were applied in three equal installments at 20, 
40 and 60 days after transplants (DAT) as ring 
method around the brinjal plant. Brinjal (var. BARI 
Begun-10) as base crop and garden pea (var. BARI 
motorshuti-3) were used as intercrops in this study. 
The unit plot size was 3.2 m × 3.6. The sole crop of 
brinjal was planted at a spacing of 80 cm x 60 cm. In 
intercropping systems, 46%, 70%, and 80% garden 
pea were intercropped in between brinjal rows 
maintaining 25 cm x 15 cm plant spacing. Seedling 
of brinjal (thirty-five days old) and seeds of garden 
pea were planted/sown on 23 and 24 November 
2024 respectively. Harvesting of brinjal was started 
from 20 February 2025 and it was continued up to 
28 April 2025. Five irrigations were applied in the 
experimental field and the first was applied at just 
after transplanting (brinjal) and sowing of the crops. 
Second to fourth irrigation was applied at 30, 60, 90 
and 120 days after transplanting/sowing (DAT/ DAS) 
of brinjal and garden pea, respectively. Weeding 
was done as per requirement. The yield component 
data of brinjal and garden pea was taken from 10 
randomly selected plants prior to harvest from each 
plot. Data on yield and yield contributing characters 
were taken and analyzed statistically using statistix 
10 package and means were adjudged by LSD at 
5%level of probability. Among treatment T2= 100% 
brinjal + two rows of garden pea (46%) was the most 
feasible intercropping system in respect of brinjal 
equivalent yield (38.73 t ha -1), gross return (Tk. 
5,80,950), gross margin (Tk. 3,83,550) and benefit 
cost ratio (2.94).

Estimation of temperature co-efficient of lentil 
for adjusting proper sowing time
M. Z. Ali, M. R. Islam, J. A. Chowdhury A. A. 
Begum and M. A. K. Mian
The experiment was conducted at the research 
field, Gazipur, BARI during rabi of 2024 - 2025. 
The soil was silty clay in texture at experimental 
sight (AEZ-28). The treatments were four sowing 
date: D1 = 15 November, D2 =25 November, D3=05 
December and D 4=15 December. The experiment 
was laid out in a RCB design with three replications 
and the unit plot size was 4.5 m × 5 m. Lentil seeds 
(var. BARI Mosur-8) were sown as per treatment 
in line with maintaining 30 cm row to row distance 
with continuous sowing. Fertilizers were applied 
@ 25-22-25-11-2.5-1.5 kg/ ha of N-P-K-S-Zn-B 
respectively (FRG, 2018), in the form of urea, 
TSP, MoP, gypsum, zinc sulphate and boric acid. 
All fertilizers were applied as basal during the 
final land preparation. A light irrigation was given 
after sowing of seeds for uniform germination. In 
addition, 5 t/ha of cow dung were applied before 
land preparation. Intercultural operation was done as 
and when required. Data on growth parameters like 
dry matter accumulation were measured at different 
dates with 15 days interval. To record dry matter 
weight, one linear meter was sampled at 15, 30, 45, 
60, 75 DAE and at harvest. Collected samples were 
separated in to different plant parts like leaf, stem 
and grain and then oven dried at 80 °C for 72 hours. 
Daily air temperatures were recorded for computing 
the growing degree days (GDD). The GDD was 
calculated using the following formula: 
GDD = ∑ Tmax+ Tmin - Tbase2
Where, T max and T min were daily maximum and 
minimum air temperatures, respectively. T base 
indicated base temperature of lentil (5°C). The GDD 
can be summed over days to indicate the amount of 
heat for growth that the crop has received over the 
period of the growing season (Kumar et al., 2023). 
For estimation of physiological maturity and grain 
growth study fifteen lentil plant were harvested from 
each plot at fifteen days interval. It was continued up 
to 33 to 48 days after anthesis (DAA). The harvested 
grain was oven dried at 70°C for 72 hours. Fifteen 
grains were separated from the middle of each plant 
and then weight was taken. The crop was harvested 
at physiological maturity 01 March, 19 March, 20 
March and 20 March, 2025 respectively. The yield 
component data was taken from one linear meter 
prior to harvest from each plot. At harvest, the yield 
data was recorded plot wise excluding border. Yield 
and yield contributing characters were recorded and 
data analyzed statistically and mean separations 
were done by LSD test at 5% level of significance. 
TDM of 25 November sowing was higher which 
was more or less similar with 15 November. Low 
temperatures might favor the growth of early sowing 
(15 November and 25 November) that caused higher 
TDM production. Among the different sowing 
dates, 25 November sowing exhibited higher grain 
growth in all over the grain filling period. It might 
be due to prevailing optimum air temperature on 25 
November sowing. 25 November sowing took the 
maximum duration 115 days and minimum mean 
air temperature (20.80 °C) to reach physiological 
maturity with maximum GDD (1896) followed 
by 15 November (GDD: 1747) and 05 December 
sowing (GDD: 1634). 15 December sowing took the 
minimum duration 94 days to reach physiological 
maturity with minimum GDD (1538) and it might be 
due to comparatively higher temperature prevailed 
at the earlier and later sowing than 25 November 
to 05 December sowing. The longest duration 115 
days due to prevailing lowest temperature (20.80°C) 
with highest GDD (1896) produced the highest 
grain yield and the shortest duration (94 days) due 
to prevailing highest mean air temperature (22.11°C) 
with lowest GDD (1538) produced the lowest grain 
yield of lentil. The higher number of pods/plant 
(65.00), number of seeds/pod (1.87) and 1000-seed 
weight (22.00 g) was obtained from 25 November 
sowing and it was higher than all sowing time of 
lentil. 15 November sowing time of lentil gave the 
number of pods/plant (61.33), number of seeds/pod 
(1.67) and 1000-seed weight (19.33 g) followed 
by 05 December, number of pods/plant (54.33),

184 I Agronomy
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
number of seeds/pod (1.37) and 1000-seed weight 
(18.00 g). The lowest number of pods/plant (51.33), 
number of seeds/pod (1.10) and 1000-seed weight 
(16.00g) was recorded in 15 December sowing. The 
highest seed yield (2.49 t/ha) was obtained from 25 
November sowing which was statistically identical 
with with 15 November sowing (2.28 t/ha) due to 
cumulative effect of better yield components and 
the lowest seed yield (1.65 t/ha) was observed in 15 
December sowing followed by 05 December sowing 
(1.74 t/ha) due to cumulative effect of poor yield 
components. It was observed that 25 November 
sowing received lower temperature during growing 
period that caused longer crop growth duration and 
ultimately produced higher TDM and translocation 
of higher TDM to grain. It might be 25 November 
sowing probably received favorable environment 
mainly optimum temperature resulting better 
vegetative growth of the plants which ultimately 
led to the better anthesis, grain filling and finally 
increased seed yield and the lowest seed yield might 
be received high temperature at early growth stage 
which shorten the vegetative and reproductive stage 
as a result that forced maturity and reduced TDM 
production and translocation of less dry matter to the 
reproductive organ (grain). Yield decreases over 25 
November sowing (early or late sown) caused about 
8.57-33.73% yield reduction over 25 November 
sowing. The result of the present study was also 
supported by Bhandari et. al., (2016). There was a 
negative linear correlation between grain yield (t/ha) 
of lentil and mean air temperature has been shown in 
Fig. 5. The regression line (Y= -0.4034x + 10.727, 
R2= 0.7646) that means the correlation of coefficient 
(x) was -0.4034 stated that seed yield decreases at 
the rate of 0.4034 t/ha for per unit change (1 °C) 
of air temperature at harvest. The contribution of 
regression (R 2= 0.7646) value indicated that 76% 
seed yield of lentil was attributed due to mean air 
temperature. Thus result showed that increasing air 
temperature decreasing the seed yield of lentil. The 
results revealed that physiological maturity period 
as well as crop duration of lentil was reduced as 
influenced by higher temperature. The 25 November 
sowing would be the optimum sowing date for lentil 
in relation to mean air temperature and early or late 
sown caused about 8.57-33.73% yield reduction 
over 25 November sowing. The temperature co-
efficient of lentil was estimated at -0.4034 t/ha 
indicated that grain yield would reduce @ 0.4034 
t/ha per unit (1°C) change of air temperature that 
means increasing air temperature decreasing the 
seed yield of lentil and the effect of temperature on 
grain yield of wheat was estimated at 76%.
Salinity
Effect of sowing date on yield of sorghum in 
saline soil
M. A. H. Khan, J. A. Chowdhury, S. S. Kakon, M. R. 
Karim, M. S. U. Khan and S. Mondal
An experiment was conducted at the Agricultural 
Research Station, Benerpota, Satkhira during rabi 
season of 2024-2025 to find out the optimum sowing 
time for sorghum in saline area. The treatments 
of the experiment were five sowing date: T 1 =1 
December, T2 =10 December, T 3 = 20 December, 
T4= 30 December and T 5= 10 January. The 
experiment was laid out in a RCB design with three 
replications and the unit plot size was 4.8m × 4m. 
Sorghum seeds (var. BARI Sorghum-1) were sown 
as per treatment with maintaining 60 cm row to row 
and10 cm plant to plant distance. Fertilizers were 
applied @ 120-60-50-27-2.8-1.4 kg/ha of N-P-K-S-
Zn and B in the form of urea, TSP, MoP, gypsum, 
zinc sulphate and boric acid. One third urea and all 
other fertilizers were applied as basal during final 
land preparation and rest N was applied at 25 and 
50 DAS in equal split following irrigation. Salinity 
level was taken at different time. Weeding was done 
at 25 and 50 DAS. Irrigation and other intercultural 
operation were done properly. Yield contributing 
characters were recorded from randomly selected 10 
plants from each plot at the time of harvest. Yield 
data was recorded by harvesting nine square meter 
area excluding border. Collected data was analyzed 
statistically following statistix-10 software package 
and means were compared using LSD test at 5% 
level of significance. The result indicated that, the 
highest hill/m2 (19), and the highest panicle length 
(19.3 cm) was observed in T 3 (20 December) and 
the highest grains/panicle (1013), and 1000 grain 
weight (26.24) and the highest grain yield (1675 
kg/ha) was found in T 4 (30 December) sowing date 
which were identical to (1595) T 3 (20 December). 
So, the optimum date of sowing in saline area for 
sorghum might be 20 December to 30 December for 
getting higher yield and avoiding salinity.

Effect of integrated nutrient management on 
yield of murikata Peaj at charland of Jamalpur 
under AEZ-9
M. R. Ali, J. Rahman and M. M. Kadir
An experiment was carried out at the farmer's field 
at Naovanga char under Jamalpur district during 
November 2024 to March 2025 to find out the 
effect of integrated nutrient management on yield 
of murikata peaj at charland of Jamalpur under 
AEZ-9. The treatments were T 1= Recommended 
fertilizer dose (FRG' 2023) 115-55-75-20-20-1.5 
kg/ha N-P-K-S-Zn-B, T 2= 125% recommended 
fertilizer dose, T 3= IPNS with vermicompost (3 t/
ha), T 4= IPNS with 3t/ha FYM, T 5= Farmers' 
practice. BARI Peaj-4 was used in the study. The 
treatments were tested in randomized complete 
block design with 3 dispersed replications. The unit 
plot size was 3.0 m × 2.0 m and spacing was 15 cm 
× 10 cm. BARI Peaj-4 was used as test material. 
Murikata piaj was sown on 12 December 2024 and 
harvested on 6 February 2025. Fertilizer was used as 
per treatment. Fifty percent N was applied as basal 
at the time of planting and remaining 50% N was 
applied in two equal splits during 30 and 45 days 
after sowing; full dose of P and K were applied at 
the time of planting and full dose of S was given 
fifty days before planting per treatments. Weeding, 
irrigation and other intercultural operations were 
done as and when necessary. The yield of murikata 
piaj was calculated in tons per hectare considering 
the whole plot as harvest area. Ten plants of onion 
from each plot were selected randomly to collect 
data on yield components. Collected data were 
analyzed statistically with the help of a computer 
package program STAR and the means were 
adjusted by Least Significance Difference (LSD) test 
at 5% level of significance. The result indicated that 
onion yield was increased due to integrated nutrient 
management. The highest onion yield (19.73 t/ha) 
was found from IPNS+ vermicompost (3.0 t/ha) 
and the lowest yield (11.31 t/ha) was found from 
recommended fertilizer dose (95-35-25-3-3 kg/ha 
N-P-K-S-Zn-B) treatment.
Performance of sweet gourd varieties at charland 
area of rangpur region
M.M. Sheikh, A.I. Sarker and K. Islam
The experiment was carried out in charland of 
Mohipur, Gangachara, Rangpur during rabi season 
2024-25 to find out suitable sweet gourd varieties 
for the charland areas of Rangpur region. The 
location of the experimental site was at AEZ-3, the 
Tista Meander Floodplain (25.86884°N latitude and 
89.25521°E longitudes).The soil was sandy heavy 
5.6 P H and 0.5% organic matter. In this research 
work five varieties were used, namely BARI Misti 
kumra-2, BARI Hybrid Misti kumra-2, company 
hybrid Sweety (Laltir), Block Stone (Indian) and 
a local one. The seeds of local, Indian varieties 
was collected from the farmers of the area, BARI 
Misti kumra-2 from RARS office, BARI, Burirhat, 
Rangpur BARI Hybrid Misti kumra-2 from 
Vegetable division, HRC, Bangladesh Agricultural 
Research Institute, Gazipur and the company (Laltir)

186 I Agronomy
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
hybrid sweety from the market of Rangpur. The 
experiment was laid out in a Randomized Complete 
Block Design (RCBD) with 3 replications. Pits of 
60 x 60 x 60 cm were drug and dried in the sun and 
decomposed cowdung was mixed with the soil. A 
basal dose of urea, triple super phosphate (TSP), 
muriate of potash (MP) and molybdenum were used 
as the source of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium 
and molybdenum applied at the rate of @ 250, 210, 
120, 100 and 1kg/ha, respectively. Urea was applied 
as top dressing in 2 equal splits at 30 and 50 days 
after sowing. The entire amount of cowdung, TSP, 
MOP and molybdenum were applied at the time 
of final land preparation. Seeds were treated by 
autostin @ 2 g/kg seed. Treated seeds were sown 
in the pits on 20 November 2024. Mulching was 
done to keep the soil moist. Irrigation was given 
at regular intervals during the growing season was 
applied through the plastic pipe. The parameters 
such as number of leaves/vine, number of vines/
plant, number of fruit/plant, individual fruit weight 
(g), fruit yield (t/ha) were measured to interpret the 
results. BARI Misti kumra-2 exhibited attractive 
golden yellow skin and deep orange flesh. It also 
showed superior performance in yield-related traits, 
producing the highest number of vines (11.30), fruits 
per plant (10.8), and yield (41.89 t/ha). The Sweety 
hybrid (Laltir) also demonstrated good performance, 
whereas Black Stone (Indian) produced the heaviest 
fruits but had a lower overall yield. The local 
variety showed the poorest performance across all 
parameters. BARI Hybrid Misti kumra-2 emerged 
as the most promising variety for commercial 
cultivation in charland areas. Farmers are interested 
with BARI Hybrid Misti kumra-2 as it had attractive 
shape, skin and pulp color and produced highest 
yield than other varieties. Therefore, efforts should 
be directed towards increased seed production and 
distribution of these promising varieties to enhance 
production and profitability in the region.

the BARI released mustard varieties gave higher 
yield than the farmers used local variety. BARI 
Sarisha-18 produced the highest seed yield (1.97 t/
ha), followed by BARI Sarisha-11 (1.74 t/ha) and 
BARI Sarisha-20 (1.53 t/ha). BARI Sarisha-14 
noticed as the early maturing variety among the 
farmers in charland area of Rangpur region. Farmers 
are interested to cultivate BARI varieties e.g. BARI 
Sarisha-18, Sarisha-20 and BARI Sarisha-11 if seeds 
are available. They preferred those varieties because 
of their high yield potentials and economic benefits. 
Therefore, efforts should be directed towards 
increased seed production and distribution of these 
promising varieties to enhance mustard production 
and profitability in the region.

established guava orchard (BARI Peyara-2)

The guava seedlings were produced through grafting 
method where BARI developed guava variety (BARI 
Peyara-2) was used as scion and local Swarupkati

method on sorjan bed maintaining recommended 
plant spacing with row to row distance 3m and 
plant to plant distance 2m. Staking was also given
