respectively. Treatment GICST-5 (Guava + Sweet 
gourd-Bitter gourd) showed the lowest GEY (40.51 
t/ha).The orchard of the grafted BARI Peyara-2 
variety is dwarf type and the canopy structure is 
comparatively lower than that of Swarupkati guava 
variety. Intercropping of creeper vegetable crops 
(like bottle gourd, bitter gourd, sweet gourd, ridge 
gourd etc.) can be practiced on sorjan trellis with 
newly established dwarf type of guava orchard (like 
BARI Peyara-2 variety) for increasing the total yield 
and economic return of the sorjan system. However, 
non-creeper vegetable crops can be cultivated 
on sorjan bed only in the first year of orchard 
establishment and thereafter it cannot be done due to 
shading effect of plant leaf canopy. Farmers showed 
their interest to cultivate creeper vegetable crops 
(like bottle gourd, bitter gourd, sweet gourd, ridge 
gourd etc.) on sorjan trellis as intercrop with newly 
established dwarf type guava orchard (like BARI 
Peyara-2) under sorjan system.
Intercropping of pineapple with existing fruit 
orchard on sorjan system
M.A.Rahman
The intercropping initiative has been implemented in 
Gava village, located within the Banaripara upazila 
of the Barishal district, under the supervision of 
farmer Sajal Mondal and Atghar, nesarabad upazilal 
of the Pirojpur district, under the supervision of 
farmer Md.Nazrul Chowdhuri. This program aims 
to assess the productivity and profitability of the 
indigenous Swarupkati variety of guava cultivated 
within a sorjan system in the Barishal region. The 
experimental site is positioned at the coordinates 
N 22°45'29.912" and E 90°10'18.818" and N 
22°44'13.93742" E 90°10'49.47348". In this setup, 
pineapple plants (Giant Kew) were interspersed 
between two rows of guava trees, with four rows 
of pineapple established between the guava lines, 
utilizing a Randomized Complete Block Design 
(RCBD). There were four treatments, viz. i. Sole 
guava ii. Guava+ pineapple intercropping, iii. 
Sole golden apple iv. Golden apple+ pineapple 
intercropping. The treatments were applied to a 
nine-year-old guava orchard of the local Swarupkati 
variety and a twelve year old local golden apple 
orchard. The experimental plot consisted of four 
guava trees, with a unit plot size of 24 m2 and incase 
of golden apple trees, experimental plot consisted 
of two trees, with unit plot size of 36 m 2, while the 
pineapple plot actually calculated as 18m2. Each 
guava tree received an annual application of 12 kg 
of cow dung, 500 g of urea, 416 g of TSP, 416 g 
of MoP, 14 g of zinc sulfate, and 60 g of gypsum 
(FRG, 2018). Fertilizers were administered in 
two equal splits: the first application occurred in 
October post-harvest, and the second in April, 
just prior to the onset of flowering. The fertilizers 
were distributed around the tree within a canopy 
spread of 1.0-1.5 meters from the base and were 
incorporated into the soil through gentle ploughing

190 I Agronomy
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
with a hand spade, followed by irrigation. During 
the dry season, irrigation was conducted as needed 
(BARI, 2020). Weeds were meticulously removed 
from the base of the trees, and the soil around the 
tree base was regularly tilled to achieve a fine 
tilth. Pruning of diseased, dead, and unwanted 
branches was performed in October. Instances of 
anthracnose disease were noted, prompting the 
application of Tilt 250 EC (Propiconazole) at a rate 
of 1.5 ml per liter, administered twice at fifteen-
day intervals, commencing when the guava fruits 
reached marble size. Harvesting occurred when the 
fruits attained physiological maturity, indicated by 
a color transition from green to yellow. The total 
soluble solids (TSS) percentage was determined 
using a Digital Refractometer (Atago Pocket 
Refractometer, Model: PAL-1, Japan), and fresh 
samples were subsequently dried using a drying. 
The fruit yields from the sole and intercropped 
systems in guava cultivation were recorded at 28.13 
t/ha and 24.29 t/ha, respectively. The sole cropping 
system yielded fruits that were both larger and 
heavier, with an average weight of 98.55 grams, 
compared to the intercropped system, which had an 
average weight of 96.25 grams for golden apples. 
Furthermore, the total fruit weight per tree in the 
golden apple orchard was noted to be 33.80 kg for 
sole cultivation and 27.62 kg for the intercropped 
system. The fruit yields for the sole and intercropped 
systems in golden apple cultivation were 18.78 t/
ha and 15.34 t/ha, respectively, translating to 
guava equivalent yields of 28.17 and 23.01 t/ha. 
Pineapple production was measured at 19.60 t/ha 
in the guava intercropping system and 19.76 t/ha 
in the golden apple intercropping system, leading 
to guava equivalent yields of 49.00 and 49.40 t/
ha, respectively. In summary, the guava equivalent 
yield was higher in the intercropped plots, with 
measurements of 73.29 t/ha in one system and 
72.41 t/ha in the other, while the sole cropped 
plots yielded guava equivalent yields of 28.13 and 
28.17 t/ha. This indicates that farmers can achieve 
nearly three times the yield and income through the 
intercropping system, leading to a strong interest in 
its adoption among farmers. Farmers showed their 
high interest to cultivate pineapple as an intercrop 
in their existing Swarupkati guava and local golden 
apple orchard on sorjan bed for getting higher yield 
and economic return.

M.A.Rahman
An experiment was conducted during 2023-24 at 
Gava village (farmer's field) in Barishal district 
of Bangladesh to determine the appropriate

harvested during they became physiological maturity

M. A. Rahman
The field experiment was conducted at Gava village 
in Banaripara, Barishal during 2023-24 all the year

showed that treatment T 5 resulted the highest yield 
of fruit (23.97 t/ha). Treatments T2, T3 and T 4 gave

respectively. On the other hand, farmers' practice 
(control treatment) (T1) gave the lowest yield (16.72 
t/ha). Treatment T 5 increased the yield of 43.36% 
over the control. The same treatment (T 5) also 
contributed the highest amount of marketable yield 
(22.93 t/ha) and exhibited the highest shelf life (9.25 
days). Therefore, golden apple cultivated on sorjan 
bed with improved agronomic practices (Earthing

gypsum, and 15 g boric acid/tree/year) enhanced the

fruit yield as compared to that of farmers' practice.

apple by applying improved agronomic practices.
Pilot production programme of grafted BARI 
Peyara-2 replacing local Swarupkati guava 
variety on sorjan bed
M. A. Rahman
The pilot production programme has been conducting 
at Gava village under Banaripara upazila of Barishal 
district (Farmer's name: Md. Rashedul Islam) for 
all the year round to examine the performance 
of grafted BARI Peyara-2 over the existing local 
Swarupkati variety under sorjan system in Barishal 
region. The experimental site is situated in the 
latitudes and longitudes of N 22°45 /52.57796// and 
E 90°10 /36.06172//, respectively. BARI developed 
guava variety (BARI Peyara-2) was used as grafted 
planting material. The whole plot size was 0.26 ha 
(64 decimal). Previously, scion of BARI Peyara-2 
was placed on the root stock of Swarupkati variety 
for seedlings production. Seedlings were planted on 
sorjan bed with row to row distance 3m and plant 
to plant distance 2m through zigzag method on 22 
February 2022. Recommended doses and application 
method of fertilizers were applied for new guava 
orchard (BARI Peyara-2). Before planting of guava 
seedling, pits of about 60 cm x 60 cm x 45 cm 
were dug in zigzag system. The pits were exposed 
for 15 days before it is filled with soil, manure and 
fertilizer. The pits were filled with 15 kg well rotten 
cowdung or compost, 250 g TSP, 250 g MP, 100 g 
gypsum and 25 g zinc sulphate (FRG, 2018). At the 
planting time a small hole was made at the centre of 
the refilled pit and the seedlings were planted. Water 
was applied immediately after planting. Staking was 
also given to protect the plant from lodging. Pruning 
of branch was done to encourage new shoots. 
Spraying of fungicide (Tilt 250 EC @ 0.5 ml/L) was 
applied prior to bagging for controlling anthracnose. 
Mulching was done using water hyacinth for 
conserving soil moisture and suppressing weed 
growth. Fruit bagging are being done using small 
transparent polythene bag for protecting the fruit 
from the infestation and insect-pest and diseases 
(BARI, 2020). Guava was harvested when attain 
full physiological maturity. Data regarding yield 
components and yield was collected after attaining 
the fruit at ripening stage. Number of fruit/plant 
were 114 and 239 in BARI Peyara-2 and Swarupkati 
variety, respectively. Single fruit weight of BARI 
Peyara-2 was 271.15 g, while it was 83.50 g in 
Swarupkati variety. Fruit weight of a single tree 
was 30.91 kg in BARI Peyara-2 and 19.96 kg in 
Swarupkati variety. Fruit yields obtained from 
BARI Peyara-2 and Swarupkati variety were 36.26 
and 28.59 t/ha, respectively. It can be noted that age 
of BARI Peyara-2 was lower as compared to that 
of existing local Swarupkati variety (3 and 9 years, 
respectively). Fruit yield of BARI Peyara-2 might be 
increased with the increasing of age of the tree. The 
shelf life of BARI Peyara-2 fruit was range from 12 
to 13 days and shelf life for Swarupkati variety was 
range from 5 to 7 days. Brix value BARI Peyara-2 
and Swarupkati guava were 8.50% and 10.18%, 
respectively. Market prices of BARI Peyara-2 and 
Swarupkati guava were Tk. 40.00 and 8.00/kg. It can 
be mentioned that farmers sold the guava fruits at 
the local market. The consumers' demand for BARI 
Peyara-2 was high but the demand for Swarupkati 
variety was medium. The findings from the pilot 
production suggest that the grafted BARI Peyara-2 
is potentially well-suited for cultivation on sorjan 
beds in the tidal flood-prone areas of the Barishal 
region. Furthermore, the yield performance and 
economic returns of BARI Peyara-2 are expected 
to surpass those of the current Swarupkati variety 
progressively over time. Farmers showed their high 
interest to cultivate grafted BARI peyara-2 with 
replacing their existing Swarupkati variety on sorjan 
bed for getting higher yield and economic return.

Survey on crops and cropping in drought prone 
areas of bangladesh
M. A. K. Mian, J. A. Chowdhury, A. A. Begum, S. S. 
Kakon, M. Z. Ali, S.S. Nareen, M. A. H. Khan and 
M. R. Karim
Drought is a serious crop production constraint 
in Bangladesh. Every year 3-4 million ha of land 
are affected by drought with different magnitude 
in Bangladesh. A survey by BARC shows 4.2 
million hectares of land are prone to droughts with

Agronomy I 193
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
different intensities. High Barind Tract (HBT) is a 
typical drought prone area. High Barind Tract (AEZ 
26) comprises parts of Rajshahi, Nawabganj and 
Naogoan districts, characterized by grey terrace 
soil, low organic matter, low rainfall and high 
temperature. The main constraint to crop production 
is drought due to erratic and low rainfall from 
October. The long term mean annual rainfall is 1200 
± 300 mm. The maximum temperature reaches as 
high as 450C in May and the minimum falls as low 
as to 60C in January. More than 90% of the rainfall 
occurs from June to September. Moisture depletion 
starts from October and in December, no residual 
moisture is normally available for crop emergence, 
a situation that continues up to April (Idris and Huq, 
1987). There is a very short period after harvest of 
rice, then low soil moisture conditions are conducive 
for sowing of rabi crops. Moisture holding capacity 
of HBT soil is poor due to critical organic matter 
content and low infiltration water (Ali, 2000). 
The study was conducted at selected locations of 
Naogaon, Natore, Rajshahi, Nawabganj, Bogra and 
Joypurhat region during 2022-2025. Data collection 
was done by face to face interviewing with FGD at 
farmers' field using a pretested interview schedule. 
About 3-7 numbers farmers were involved in 
each FGD group. Total 150 original farmers were 
interviewed at different locations. Some relevant 
data were collected from local DAE office and 
BMDC office. Data on major crops and cropping, 
and other relevant information were recoded and 
analyzed in MS Excel. About 16 major crops are 
grown in the drought prone areas. Among them, 
Wheat, Boro rice, Mustard, Aus rice, T.aman, Mango 
and Vegetables are dominant at Naogaon region 
but Wheat, Maize, Boro rice, Potato, Mustard, Aus 
rice, Onion, Garlic, Sugarcane, Mango, Litchi and 
Jute are found dominant at Natore, Rajshahi and 
Nawabganj regions. On the other hand, Boro rice, 
Potato, Mustard, Maize, Wheat, Aus rice, Banana, 
Chilli, Aroids are major crops observed at farmers' 
field of Bogra and Joypurhat region. There are three 
most dominant cropping practiced by the farmers. 
They are Wheat-T.aman, Boro rice-T.aman and 
Potato-Boro rice - T.aman. Besides these cropping 
patterns, there are 18 major cropping patterns at 
three study region practiced by the farmers. Farmers 
of this area already general crop cultivation shifted to 
mango cultivation. Mango is grown as intercropping 
with blackgram, wheat, rice and other crops in 
early stages of mango. Early tomato cultivation 
practiced in Barind area. Deep Tube well is used for 
irrigation. Major cropping patterns cover more than 
60-80% area of the study locations. The patterns are 
changing from year to year due to market demand/
farmers' choice or govt. policy. Minor cropping 
patterns are not listed in the report. Aroid Latiraj 
exported to different countries of Europe including 
Kuwait, Malaysia, Singapore, Saudi Arabia and 
other countries.

Background
Irrigation and Water Management Division (IWM) 
is one of the16 research divisions of Bangladesh 
Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) that conducts 
research on advanced irrigation methods, irrigation 
scheduling, and on-farm water management of 
BARI mandated crops. It also conducts research on 
water quality, agricultural meteorology, drainage, 
salinity management, groundwater and surface 
water management through field observations, and 
applying simulation models and machine learning 
tools. Till date, IWM Division already developed 53 
irrigation and water management technologies and 
most of them are being used at the farm level. The 
titles and abstracts of the research conducted during 
2024-25 are provided below.
Changes in crop water requirements and future 
irrigation water demand with climate change in 
the southwest coastal area
R. P. Rannu, K. K. Sarker, S. K. Biswas, M. A. 
Hossain
Fresh water is limited for agricultural purposes in 
Bangladesh, especially in coastal areas. For the 
judicial use of this limited water, this study intended 
to estimate the irrigation water requirements 
through crop water requirements. The CROPWAT 
model was employed to estimate reference crop 
evapotranspiration, crop water need and irrigation 
requirement for the Boro rice in Khulna district. 
Results revealed that there is almost no increasing 
or decreasing trend annually for the long-term 
historical data period. Monthly variation of net 
irrigation requirement was also observed, and that 
could be due to ETo or rainfall variability. However, 
this is a partial study with one crop and for a 
historical period. The conclusion will be done once 
the full study is completed. 
Response of proso millet to different levels of 
irrigation
C. R. Paul, T. H. Munmun, K. K. Sarker, S. H. Anik
Proso millet is a short-duration, drought-tolerant 
cereal with potential for cultivation in water-limited 
environments of Bangladesh. A field study was 
conducted during 2024-2025 at the IWM Division, 
BARI, Gazipur, and RARS, BARI, Jamalpur to 
evaluate the effect of irrigation at different growth 
stages on growth, yield, and water productivity 
of proso millet. Six irrigation treatments at 
different growth stages were considered with three 
replications. The results showed that irrigation during 
the vegetative and flowering stages, treatment T 2, 
produced the highest yields, at 2.72 t/ha and 2.92 t/
ha in Gazipur and Jamalpur, respectively. In contrast, 
no irrigation (T0) resulted in the lowest yields at both 
locations. Yield and plant growth traits followed 
similar trends, with higher performance at Jamalpur 
compared to Gazipur, likely due to reduced stress 
conditions (biotic and abiotic). Although treatment 
T5, three irrigations at vegetative, flowering and 
grain filling stages, enhanced vegetative growth, it 
did not result in higher grain yield, indicating that 
excessive irrigation promotes biomass production 
but lower grain yield. This study will be continued 
in the next year at both locations for the validation 
of these results.
Effect of irrigation on yield and water productivity 
of foxtail millet
T. H. Munmun, C. R. Paul, K. K. Sarker, S. H. Anik
Foxtail millet is an important crop for both 
cereal production and animal feed, but its water 
requirements have not yet been thoroughly studied. 
Therefore, this study aimed to examine the effect of 
irrigation at different growth stages on the yield and 
water productivity of foxtail millet. The research was 
conducted at the research field of the IWM Division,

Irrigation and Water Management I 195
BARI Annual Report 2024-25

IRRIGATION AND
WATER MANAGEMENT
BARI, Gazipur, and RARS, BARI, Jamalpur. Six 
irrigation treatments with three replications were 
considered. The results showed that irrigation 
during the vegetative and flowering stages produced 
the highest yields, at 2.81 t/ha and 2.71 t/ha in 
Gazipur and Jamalpur, respectively. Conversely, a 
single irrigation at the vegetative stage resulted in 
the highest water productivity, at 2.28 kg/m3 and 
1.88 kg/m3 in the two locations. Although maximum 
irrigation improved both growth and yield attributes, 
the overall findings indicated that the vegetative and 
flowering stages are the most critical for irrigation. 
However, for water-scarce areas, a single irrigation 
at the vegetative stage is preferable.
Yield and water productivity of chia to different 
levels of irrigation
F. Akter, S. K. Biswas, M. A. Hossain, K. K. Sarker, 
R. P. Rannu
This study investigated the impact of different 
irrigation treatments on BARI chia-1 for the year 
2023-24 and 2024-25. Five treatments: T1= irrigation 
at vegetative stage, T 2=irrigation at vegetative + 
flowering stage, T3= irrigation at vegetative + grain 
filling stage, T 4= irrigation at flowering + grain 
filling stage, and T 5= irrigation at vegetative + 
flowering + grain filling stage. The study indicated 
that irrigation during the flowering stage and grain 
filling stage led to the highest seed yield and water 
productivity, followed by irrigation at the vegetative 
and grain filling stage. Overall results as well as 
water use of the treatments indicated that irrigation 
at the flowering stage and grain filling stage is the 
critical stage for irrigation. 
Temperature forecasting using bayesian 
optimization tuned machine learning algorithms
C. R. Paul, T. H. Munmun, D. K. Roy
Accurate temperature predictions are crucial for 
agricultural planning and weather forecasting. 
This study explored soft computing techniques 
for predicting average daily temperatures using 
a dataset over 44 years (1980-2023) across two 
meteorological stations (Dhaka, and Ishurdi). The 
study developed and compared Artificial Neural 
Network (ANN), Extreme Learning Machine 
(ELM), Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), and 
Support Vector Regression (SVR) models. The 
optimal hyperparameters of these models were 
selected using Bayesian optimization to ensure their 
best performance. Results showed that prediction 
accuracy was influenced not only by the choice 
of algorithm but also by the characteristics of 
the training and testing datasets. In Dhaka, ELM 
consistently outperformed all models across all 
forecast horizons. In Ishurdi, SVR demonstrated 
superior performance for one-day-ahead and ELM 
for two, and three-day-ahead average temperature 
predictions (RMSE = 0.0495 °C and 0.0697 °C, 
respectively), as indicated by Shannon's Entropy-
based decision theory. Therefore, ELM emerged 
as the most effective method in nearly all cases, 
except for the one-day-ahead prediction at Ishurdi, 
highlighting both its robustness and the importance 
of dataset-specific characteristics in predictive 
modelling.
Estimation of crop water requirement using 
an optimization algorithm-tuned fuzzy tree 
approach 
T. H. Munmun, C. R. Paul, M. P. Haque, D. K. Roy
Crop evapotranspiration (ETc) plays a vital role 
in making informed decisions for both real-time 
and future irrigation scheduling of major crops. 
Therefore, accurately predicting ETc is essential 
in the field of water resources management. This 
study investigates the effectiveness of a fuzzy tree 
(FT) approach, optimized using various algorithms, 
for predicting ETc during the initial, development, 
mid-season, and late-season growth stages of onion 
and potato crops in Gazipur. A total of 16 FT models 
were developed, and model performance was ranked 
using Shannon's Entropy (SE) method. For onion, 
the results showed that the FIS, GA-PSO, PSO-
PSO, and FIS performed best during the initial, 
development, mid-season, and late-season stages, 
respectively. In contrast, for potato, the FIS model 
consistently outperformed other models across all 
growth stages. However, since the FT models were 
developed by optimizing tunable parameters, they 
are expected to outperform standalone FIS models 
when applied to unseen data. Overall, the study 
concluded that the FT model is highly effective for 
predicting seasonal ETc values for both onion and 
potato crops.

BARI Annual Report 2024-25
Projection of medium-term weather parameters 
using deep learning models
D. K. Roy, M. P. Haque, C. R. Paul, M. A. Hossain
Accurate forecasting of weather parameters and 
reference evapotranspiration (ET0) is vital for 
effective irrigation planning and climate-resilient 
agriculture. This study evaluated the performance of 
three deep learning models-LSTM, Bi-LSTM, and 
Pro-LSTM-for projecting daily weather variables 
and ET0 up to 730 days ahead at three stations in 
Bangladesh. Bi-LSTM showed the best performance 
on short-term predictions (R ≈ 0.999-1.000; low 
NRMSE), but its accuracy declined over extended 
forecasts, likely due to its bidirectional structure. 
Pro-LSTM, by contrast, outperformed others in 
long-range projections, aided by its projected-layer 
design. Results highlight Pro-LSTM's robustness 
for medium-term forecasting, supporting data-
driven agricultural water management. 
Automation of drip irrigation using advanced soil

D. K. Roy, M. P. Haque, C. R. Paul, M. A. Hossain
Efficient irrigation management is critical for 
optimizing water use and maximizing crop yield, 
particularly for water-sensitive crops like tomato. 
This study evaluated the performance of different 
soil sensor-based automation systems for drip 
irrigation in the cultivation of BARI Tomato-21. The

production.

Water management of dwarf sunflower at various 
time of sowing 
A. J. Mila, R. W. Bell, S. K. Biswas, M. A. Hossain 
Proper sowing along with appropriate use of 
irrigation at actual crop growth stages can minimise 
misuse of these costly inputs and can increase water 
productivity. Dwarf sunflower (BARI Surjamukhi 3) 
was grown at three sowing dates (Factor A) using 
four irrigation combinations with full and 50% 
of full irrigation at 3 crop growth stages (Factor 
B). Due to seasonal rainfall variability, sowing

24, mid-December sowing gave the significantly 
highest seed yield and in the following year, 1st 
week of December sowing gave the significantly 
highest seed yield. Three irrigations at vegetative, 
pre-flowering, and flowering produced the highest 
yield. Higher irrigation water productivity (IWP) 
was found by mid-Nov sowing, and 50% of 
irrigation at vegetative, pre-flowering, and flowering 
which sacrificed 15% of yield. However, to meet our 
SDG goal we need to increase IWP just sacrificing 
5% yield in situations of meeting demand of 17.12 
crore people by focusing on limited water resources. 
Therefore, it can be difficult to conclude in case of 
sowing date because of rainfall variability. However, 
the dwarf sunflower can be irrigated at 50% of full 
irrigation at three growth stages to get higher IWP 
with 15% yield reduction compared to FI at the same 
crop growth stages in central Bangladesh.

Design and development of a low-cost sprinkler 
system
M. P. Haque, D. K. Roy, K. K. Sarker, M. A. Hossain
Efficient water management is crucial for 
agricultural productivity, especially in regions 
facing water scarcity and climate variability. This 
study developed a low-cost sprinkler system using 
locally available materials in Bangladesh to provide 
small-scale farmers with an economical irrigation 
alternative. The system was constructed with 
UPVC-thread pipes (3/4 inch diameter), G.I. screws 
(1-1/2 inch), end plugs (3/4 inch), G.I. sockets 
(3/4 inch), and Teflon tape (1/2 inch). Tested on a 
28 ft by 16 ft area (448 ft2) with a domestic water 
supply (5-6 psi), the system achieved a Coefficient 
of Uniformity (CU) of 88% ( above the acceptable 
limit of 80%).The discharge rates varied from a 
maximum of 0.15 cm/min to a minimum of 0.09 
cm/min, with peak at 360 cm from the sprinkler. 
The sprinkler system, equipped with a submersible 
0.75 Hp DC solar pump, was also tested, and the 
coefficient of uniformity (CU) was relatively low 
(approximately 60%). This high uniformity and 
efficient water distribution with domestic water 
supply underscore the system's potential to optimize 
water use, conserve water, and enhance crop 
yields by maintaining optimal soil moisture. The 
system's low cost (850 Tk.) and ease of construction 
may make it accessible for smallholder farmers, 
promoting sustainable agricultural practices and 
improved livelihoods. For further confirmation, the 
study should be conducted for the next year.

Projection of groundwater level fluctuations using 
long short term memory networks in a drought 
prone region of northwestern Bangladesh 
D. K. Roy, M. P. Haque, C. R. Paul, M. A. Hossain
This study investigates the capability of Long 
Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to 
forecast groundwater level (GWL) fluctuations 
in northwestern Bangladesh, a region particularly

Irrigation and Water Management I 199
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
susceptible to drought. The performance of LSTM 
was benchmarked against traditional time series 
models, dynamic system response models and 
their hybrid forms. A total of eight models were 
evaluated using historical GWL data from 19 
observation wells: LSTM, ARMA, three state-
space models (n4sid, SSEST, SSREGEST), and 
three corresponding hybrid ARMA-state-space 
models. Model performance was assessed using 
key statistical indicators. Across most locations, the 
LSTM model consistently outperformed the others, 
achieving correlation values between 0.53 and 0.92. 
To identify the top-performing models, an integrated 
Entropy-EDAS decision-making framework was 
applied, further validating the dominance of LSTM. 
The best-performing models provided accurate GWL 
projections for five years beyond the available data, 
offering a practical tool for informed and sustainable 
groundwater management in drought-affected areas. 
Investigation of groundwater level fluctuations in 
relation to rainfall at Kushtia district
M. M. Morshed, R. P. Rannu, M. A. Hossain
This study examines 30 years of rainfall and 
groundwater data from Kushtia District, Bangladesh, 
to evaluate rainfall-groundwater interactions. 
A moderate negative correlation (r = -0.28) was 
found between rainfall and groundwater depth, 
with the strongest effect at a two-month lag (r = 
-0.65), showing delayed recharge. High annual 
rainfall variability (CV > 1.0) was linked to deeper 
groundwater, indicating reduced recharge efficiency 
under irregular rainfall. Regression analysis revealed 
that 61% of fluctuations were explained by current 
and lagged rainfall. These findings underscore the 
role of consistent rainfall in aquifer replenishment 
and emphasize the need for adaptive irrigation and 
sustainable groundwater use.

Impact of a small municipal solid waste dumpsite 
on groundwater quality: A case study in Gazipur 
city 
D. K. Roy, M. P. Haque, M. A. Hossain
This study evaluates the impact of a small municipal 
solid waste dumpsite on groundwater quality in 
Konabari, Gazipur, Bangladesh. Specifically, it 
assesses the travel time and direction of particle 
movement from the dumpsite to a pumping well and 
quantifies leachate migration into the subsurface 
system. The study employs finite difference-based 
numerical models: MODFLOW-MODPATH and 
MODFLOW-MT3DMS. Two pumping wells used 
for beneficial purposes were considered-one 
located near the dumpsite and the other farther away. 
The results show that MODFLOW-MODPATH 
effectively delineates the flow direction of water 
particles from the dumpsite to the pumping well, as 
well as the associated travel time. The average flow 
length and travel time to the nearest well were 429.41 
meters and 5,163.57 days, respectively. Likewise, 
MODFLOW-MT3DMS-based contaminant 
transport modeling successfully simulates leachate 
migration from the dumpsite toward the well as a 
result of pumping. 
Adaptive trials on water-saving irrigation 
technologies in water-scarce regions of 
Bangladesh 
D. K. Roy, M. A. Hossain, K. K. Sarker, A. J. Mila, 
M. P. Haque, C. R. Paul
This study evaluates the performance of various 
water-saving irrigation technologies through 
adaptive field trials conducted in farmers' fields 
across water-scarce regions of Bangladesh during 
the 2024-2025 growing season. A total of 71 
demonstrations were implemented across multiple

200 I Irrigation and Water Management
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
sites, comprising 22 trials of alternate furrow 
irrigation, 8 trials of conjunctive use of fresh and 
saline water, 16 trials of deficit irrigation, 7 trials 
of drip irrigation, 5 trials of solar-powered drip 
irrigation, 7 trials of sprinkler irrigation, and 6 
trials of solar-powered sprinkler irrigation. These 
technologies were applied to diverse crops and soil 
types representative of the region. Key performance 
indicators included water use efficiency, crop yield, 
and water productivity. Results showed that alternate 
furrow irrigation reduced water use by up to 33% 
(e.g., potato: 0.30 m to 0.20 m, water productivity 
9.79 kg/m3; cauliflower: 0.26 m to 0.17 m, water 
productivity 11.83 kg/m3) without compromising 
yield. Deficit irrigation saved 15-20% water while 
improving water productivity (e.g., mustard: 0.15 
m to 0.12 m, water productivity 1.21 kg/m3; maize: 
0.33 m to 0.26 m, water productivity 3.85 kg/m3). 
Conjunctive use maintained stable yields (e.g., 
maize 10.00 t/ha, potato 19.10 t/ha) but showed no 
significant water savings. Drip irrigation achieved 
high yields for high-value crops such as tomato 
(80.00 t/ha) and brinjal (50.00 t/ha), while solar-
powered systems reduced operational costs and 
improved energy sustainability. Sprinkler irrigation 
performed well for moderate water-requirement 
crops like onion (18.00 t/ha) and garlic (8.00 t/ha). 
Farmers perceived these technologies as effective 
strategies for addressing water scarcity, enhancing 
yields, and lowering operational costs, with strong 
interest in continued adoption. The study will extend 
for the next three years, evaluating these irrigation 
methods under varying agro-ecological conditions 
to further validate their long-term benefits.
Water-efficient irrigation management for 
enhancing crop production in char areas of 
northern Bangladesh
M. A. Hossain, D. K. Roy, M. P. Haque
This study investigated the performance and 
economic viability of modern, water-efficient 
irrigation technologies in the water-scarce char

Improvment and evaluation of a new tunnel shed 
design for summer tomato production
M. R. Hasan, M. A. Hoque and M. N. Amin
This study evaluates a new, scientific tunnel shed 
design for cultivating summer tomatoes to overcome 
challenges like heat stress, heavy rainfall, and poor

designs with ridge vents (T 1, T2, and T 3) against a 
traditional farmers' practice (T 4). The sheds were 
constructed using GI pipes, hollow square bars, and

7.05 tons/ha and 4.10 tons/ha, respectively. The 
average fruit weight was similar across all treatments, 
but the new sheds enhanced overall fruit production. 
In conclusion, the study finds that these innovative 
shed designs, particularly T1, offer a practical and 
effective solution for enhancing tomato cultivation 
in challenging summer conditions by improving the 
microclimate and increasing overall yield.

Development of an oat dehulling machine
N. Jahan, M. N. Amin, M. M. Hossain, S. Akter and 
A. H. Akhi 
An oat dehulling machine removes the outer hull, 
enhancing the quality and palatability of oats for 
consumer use. This research explores the design and 
performance evaluation of an oat dehulling machine 
aimed at improving the processing efficiency and 
quality of oats by removing their outer hulls. The 
machine was tested using different pulley sizes to 
determine optimal operational parameters, with 
materials including whole oats and various machine 
configurations. Key performance indicators such 
as broken groats, unhulled grains, and dehulling 
efficiency were measured in this study. A larger 
15.24 cm pulley proved ineffective, generating 
insufficient force and resulting in a low dehulling 
efficiency of only 59.67% with 30.38% of grains 
unhulled. Conversely, a smaller 10.16 cm pulley 
applied excessive force, achieving a high efficiency 
of 83.55% but causing significant damage with 
25-30% broken grains.The optimal performance 
was achieved using a 12.7 cm pulley, which 
struck a balance between effectiveness and grain 
preservation. This configuration provided a high 
dehulling efficiency of 93.33% while minimizing 
damage, with broken grain and unhulled grain 
rates of 13.69% and 10.34%, respectively. When 
compared to imported machines, the developed 
prototype demonstrated better performance by 
effectively balancing high efficiency with acceptable 
levels of grain breakage and unhulled grains.

Development of a vapor heat treatment plant for 
extending shelf life of mangoes and controlling 
pests
M. A. Gulandaz, M. A. Hoque, M. Z. Hossain and 
M. N. Amin
Mango (Mangifera indica L.) is one of the most 
important tropical fruits in Bangladesh, but it is 
highly perishable and faces considerable postharvest 
losses, estimated at 20-30%. These losses are

FMP Engineering I 209
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
mainly due to physiological weight loss, rapid 
decay, color degradation, and fungal infections such 
as anthracnose, which severely reduce marketability 
and export potential. To address these challenges, 
this study developed and evaluated a sensor-based 
Smart Vapor Heat Treatment (SVHT) system for 
postharvest management of the high-yielding 
'BARI-4' mango variety. The SVHT system was 
designed using SOLIDWORKS and fabricated at the 
FMPE Division, BARI. It consisted of a coal-fired 
boiler supplying steam to a stainless-steel treatment 
chamber with a capacity of 150 kg per batch 
(arranged in 3×50 kg rows). An IoT-enabled control 
unit, based on a Raspberry Pi 4 microcomputer, 
regulated temperature and humidity through DHT22 
sensors using closed-loop logic. Data were logged at 
1 Hz, stored in CSV format, and remotely accessible, 
ensuring precise and automated operation. Seven 
treatments were tested: T1 (53 °C for 22 min), T2 (47 
°C for 27 min), T3 (42 °C for 30 min), T4 (37 °C for 
35 min), T5 (hot water treatment [HWT] at 55 °C for 
7 min), T6 (HWT at 60 °C for 5 min), and T7 (control, 
no treatment). Results demonstrated that the higher 
temperature SVHT treatments, particularly T1 and 
T2, significantly reduced physiological weight loss 
(final weight retention of 9.09 kg for T1 and 8.43 kg 
for T2) and delayed decay progression (50% decay 
by day 15 for T1 and day 13 for T2). Moreover, these 
treatments maintained superior fruit color, enhanced 
sweetness (higher TSS values), and completely 
eliminated anthracnose infection. In comparison, 
hot water treatments and untreated controls showed 
faster deterioration, lower sweetness, and higher 
disease incidence. Overall, optimized SVHT, 
especially at higher temperatures, proved superior 
to conventional treatments. It represents a practical, 
eco-friendly, and technologically advanced solution 
for prolonging mango shelf life, ensuring quality 
retention, and improving marketability both locally 
and internationally.

Real-time whitefly detection and control through 
precision sprayer for vegetable crop
M. A. Gulandaz, M. A. Hoque, S. Akter, M. A. 
Rahman and M. N. Amin
Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci ) are among the most 
damaging insect pests in vegetable cultivation, 
particularly in crops like tomato, due to their role as 
vectors of viral and fungal diseases that significantly 
reduce yield. Conventional pest control methods, 
which rely heavily on pesticide spraying, often 
result in excessive chemical use, environmental 
contamination, and poor pest-targeting efficiency. To 
address these limitations, this study aimed to develop 
and evaluate a real-time machine vision system for 
whitefly detection, serving as a foundational step 
toward an autonomous precision spraying solution. 
The experimental setup integrated a Raspberry Pi 
4B microcontroller with an HD webcam for real-
time image acquisition. A dataset of 1,500 annotated 
images was collected, consisting of 900 images for 
training, 300 for validation, and 300 for testing. 
Images were taken under diverse conditions, with 
particular attention to the undersides of leaves where 
whiteflies predominantly occur. Two state-of-the-
art deep learning architectures, Mask R-CNN and 
YOLOv8, were implemented and assessed under 
both image-based analysis and real-time detection 
scenarios. Results demonstrated that both models 
achieved high detection accuracy, highlighting the 
feasibility of automated pest recognition. For real-
time detection, YOLOv8 consistently outperformed 
Mask R-CNN, achieving an accuracy of 96.14% 
compared to 94.99% for Mask R-CNN. In image-
based evaluations, performance levels were slightly 
higher, but YOLOv8 again demonstrated marginal 
superiority. These findings confirm that YOLOv8 
provides robust and reliable results, particularly in 
real-time environments where faster inference speed 
and adaptability are critical. Overall, the study 
establishes the effectiveness of machine vision for 
insect detection, providing a strong foundation 
for future integration into autonomous precision 
sprayers. The ability to accurately identify pests in 
real time will enable targeted spraying, reducing 
chemical input, minimizing environmental impact, 
and supporting sustainable vegetable production.

BARI Annual Report 2024-25

M. Z. Hossain, T. N. Barna, M. A. Hoque, M. M.

A seed storage unit (1030 × 810 × 1150 mm) for 
high-value vegetables and spices was developed 
at the FMPE Division, BARI, Gazipur during 
2024-2025 to improve storage conditions and 
maintain seed quality for smallholder farmers. The 
performance of the FMPE Seed Storage system was 
evaluated in comparison with the SRC Cool Room 
and traditional steel drum storage over a three-month 
period. The FMPE and traditional systems were 
installed in Faridpur (onion true seed grower Ms 
Shahida Begum's home), while the SRC Cool Room 
was tested in Gazipur. Environmental monitoring 
revealed that the FMPE unit consistently maintained 
an average of 11°C and 39% relative humidity, while 
the SRC system sustained 12°C and 45%. In contrast, 
the traditional steel drum reached 29°C with 86% 
humidity, creating unfavorable storage conditions. 
Initial germination tests indicated retention rates 
of 82% in FMPE storage, 86% in SRC, and 87% in 
traditional storage. However, fungal contamination 
was lowest in the FMPE unit (39%), compared with 
42% in both SRC and traditional storage. The final 
germination and contamination data will be taken 
in October 2025, before the seeds are sold. The 
FMPE system was also equipped with integrated 
IoT-based sensors linked to an Android mobile 
application using Firebase, allowing real-time 
monitoring of storage temperature and humidity. 
Unlike conventional systems, the FMPE design 
combines portability, cost-effectiveness, and digital 
monitoring features, making it highly suitable for 
small-scale farmers handling high-value seeds. 
Overall, the FMPE storage unit demonstrated stable 
environmental control, reduced fungal incidence, 
and user-friendly monitoring, offering a practical and 
sustainable solution for enhancing seed preservation 
in resource-limited farming communities.
Development of an automated squirrel repellent
M. Z. Hossain, M. N. Amin, M. S. Alam and A. T. 
M. Hasanuzzaman
Squirrels are a major cause of damage to stored seeds 
and high-value crops, necessitating effective and 
sustainable control technologies. During 2024-2025, 
two automated squirrel repellent systems (Model 1 
and 2) were developed at the Farm Machinery and 
Postharvest Process Engineering (FMPE) Division, 
BARI, and their performance was compared with 
a commercially available Chinese repellent. All 
systems were powered by solar energy to ensure 
eco-friendly operation. Model 1 was designed as 
an AI-based system with rapid image recognition, 
enabling accurate squirrel detection under diverse 
environmental conditions. It demonstrated low 
false trigger rates and consistent all-weather 
performance, though it required moderate levels of 
maintenance to sustain reliability. Model 2 utilized a 
passive infrared (PIR) sensor and showed 90-100% 
detection accuracy within a 5 m range. It achieved 
a medium response time but required minimal 
maintenance, making it more user-friendly for 
farmers in field conditions. In contrast, the Chinese 
repellent was inexpensive and widely available 
but exhibited a limited sensing range and frequent 
false alarms, which reduced its effectiveness for 
long-term crop protection. Comparative evaluation 
indicated that Model 2 offered the most practical 
field solution, balancing accuracy, reliability, and 
ease of use. Meanwhile, Model 1 was identified as 
the most suitable choice for precision environments 
where advanced monitoring and higher control are 
essential, despite higher maintenance needs. Overall, 
both BARI-developed systems demonstrated 
superior performance over the commercial option, 
offering sustainable, solar-powered solutions to 
reduce postharvest losses and safeguard high-value 
agricultural commodities from squirrel damage.

Development and evaluation of two-wheel power 
tiller-operated automated seeder for precise 
seeding 
N. Jahan, M. S. Mia, M. M. Hassan
A precision seeder was developed for two-wheel 
power tillers to plant seeds automatically and more 
accurately for smallholder farmers. Traditional and 
semi-mechanized seeding methods, still prevalent 
among over 60% of Bangladeshi farmers, often 
result in inconsistent seed spacing and missed 
placements, contributing to an estimated 10-15% 
annual yield reduction .The design of the precision 
seeder includes six seed meters, each controlled 
by a stepper motor and monitored in real-time by 
an infrared (IR) sensor to detect missing seeds. 
Its intelligence is centralized in an Arduino Mega 
controller, which synchronizes the seed meter's 
operation with the wheel speed of the power tiller, 
measured by a rotary encoder. This adaptive control 
allows the system to maintain performance despite 
speed variations. Field tests demonstrated effective 
synchronization; as the tiller's speed increased from 
35 to 70 rpm, the seed meter speed correspondingly 
rose from 5 to over 8 rpm. Furthermore, the system's 
programming delay significantly decreased from 
over 14,000 to around 8,400 microseconds as speed 
increased, ensuring precise timing. The seeder 
showed high accuracy during operation, with actual 
seed drops of 45, 48, and 52 in one test and 44 and 
45 in another, closely matching the target of 48 seeds 
over 10 meters of driving distance. In conclusion, 
the automated seeder proves to be a reliable and 
effective solution for precise seeding.

Introduction of solar energy for operation of 
winnower
N. Jahan, M. A. Hoque, M. S. Miah, M. Z. Hossain 
and M. A. Rahman
A winnowing machine separates grain from debris, 
enhancing processing efficiency for farmers. The

212 I FMP Engineering
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
BARI winnower was modified by replacing AC 
motor with a 500W, 48V DC motor to create a solar-
powered system. When winnowing machine powered 
directly by solar panels, the motor failed to function 
if the supplied voltage was too high (e.g., 92.7V , 
93.5V) or became suboptimal at lower voltages. 
Optimal solar performance was achieved when the 
panel's voltage matched near to the motor's rating. 
In contrast, when the winnower was operated using 
batteries charged by solar panels, performance was 
highly stable and efficient. The system functioned 
excellently within a narrow voltage range of 50.1V 
to 51.3V . Within this range, the machine maintained 
varying motor speeds (510-550 rpm), achieved high 
cleaning capacities (530-536 kg/h), and delivered 
consistently high cleaning efficiencies between 
95.6% and 97%. The fill factor of the solar panels, 
an indicator of their efficiency, was also identified as 
a key factor influencing overall system performance 
by ensuring sufficient power conversion. The study 
concludes that while solar power is viable for 
operating agricultural machinery like winnowers, it 
necessitates intense voltage regulation. Future work 
will involve testing the system with inverters.
 Development of a handy solar weeder
N. Jahan, R. Ahmed and M. N. Amin
Weeding significantly hampers crop production

the BARI and tested in field conditions using an

efficiency (92.5%) but with lower energy draw and 
field capacity. The study concludes that the solar

consumption, providing a sustainable solution for 
smallholder farmers. 
Adaptive trial of BARI tomato seed separator 
cum pulper
T. N. Barna, S. Parvin, M. Islam, N. Jahan, M. N. 
Amin and M. A. Hoque
Tomato seed extraction in Bangladesh is largely 
manual, resulting in labor-intensive work and 
reduced seed quality. To address this, BARI 
developed the BARI tomato seed separator cum 
pulper machine. It aims to enhance seed recovery 
and utilize the leftover pulp. In 2024-2025, six 
adaptive field trials were conducted in different 
upazilas, alongside a demonstration at HRC, BARI. 
The machine's field performance was compared 
with lab results using Welch's t-test, while farmer 
feedback was gathered through surveys.The 
machine processed 91 kg/h in the field (vs. 107 kg/h 
in-lab), with seed loss 3.9% and germination at 96%. 
No seed injury occurred. Statistical analysis showed 
no significant performance difference between lab 
and field. User perceptions were mostly positive 
to highly positive, based on Likert-scale scoring of 
operational, pulping, and seed separation features.
Using Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) 
methods like AHP, TOPSIS, and VIKOR, BARI's 
machine outperformed the HRC machine, Millet 
Wet separator and traditional methods. Economic 
analysis revealed a Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) of 1.97 
with a payback period under one year for farmers, 
while a local service provider model showed a 
BCR of 1.43 and payback in 1.6 years. Processed 
tomato pulp from the machine was preserved and 
found acceptable in taste, color, and texture after 4 
months ambient storage. In conclusion, the BARI 
seed separator demonstrated strong technical and 
economic performance, with high user acceptance 
indicating high potential for wider adoption with 
scaling support.

Badhakopi-3. The transplanter demonstrated a

Development of a multiple-capacity insect killer
M.Z. Hossain, M.Y . Mollah, M. Hossain, N. Amin 
and A.K.M.R.H. Ferdous
A multiple-capacity insect killer was developed at 
the FMPE Division, BARI, and its performance 
was evaluated in collaboration with the Entomology 
Division, BARI, Gazipur during 2024-2025. The 
study compared the BARI Multi-Capacity Insect 
Killer with two existing devices: the BRRI Solar 
Light Trap and the BARI Pheromone Trap, tested in 
an eggplant field over nine consecutive days. Results 
indicated that the BRRI Solar Light Trap captured 
the highest average number of insects (41,485), 
but this included a large proportion of beneficial 
species, raising concerns about ecological balance. 
The BARI Multi-Capacity Insect Killer recorded 
a total of 12,124 insects, demonstrating a more 
selective capture efficiency. The BARI Pheromone 
Trap attracted comparatively fewer insects overall 
but proved highly specific, with a 100% moth 
capture rate. In terms of shoot borer (Leucinodes 
orbonalis) captures, averages were 19.2 in the BARI 
Multi-Capacity, 3.1 in the BRRI Solar Trap, and 5.8 
in the Pheromone Trap. Species analysis further 
highlighted that the BRRI Solar Trap primarily 
targeted diverse pest groups, including termites 
(37%) and beetles (15%), whereas the Pheromone 
Trap exclusively targeted moth species. The findings 
suggest that the BRRI Solar Light Trap may be more 
suitable for broad-spectrum pest control, albeit with 
risks to beneficial insect populations. In contrast, the 
BARI Multi-Capacity Insect Killer offers a balanced 
approach, with higher selectivity and effectiveness 
against shoot borers, while the BARI Pheromone 
Trap remains ideal for targeted monitoring of moth 
pests. Together, these tools provide complementary 
options for integrated pest management in vegetable 
production.

Development of a forced air smart onion storage 
system 
M. A. Gulandaz, T. T. Rakin, M. A. Hoque and M. 
N. Amin
Postharvest loss of onion (Allium cepa L.) remains 
a serious challenge in Bangladesh, where traditional 
storage practices are often unable to maintain 
quality over extended periods. In conventional 
onion storage systems, inadequate ventilation, 
uncontrolled temperature, and high relative humidity 
frequently lead to excessive sprouting, rotting, and 
physiological weight loss. These factors collectively 
result in significant economic losses for farmers and 
traders. To address this problem, the present study 
was undertaken to design, develop, and evaluate 
a solar-powered forced-air smart onion storage 
system (SOSS) and compare its performance with 
Traditional Onion Storage Systems (TOSS). The 
SOSS was powered by a 200 W solar panel and 
incorporated DC axial fans for forced air circulation, 
temperature and humidity sensors for continuous 
monitoring, and an IoT-enabled microcontroller for 
automated control and real-time data access. The 
system was tested under a randomized complete 
block design with two treatments (SOSS and TOSS) 
and three replications. During the storage period, 
the smart system successfully maintained relatively 
stable humidity levels ranging between 45% and 
56%, whereas traditional storage exhibited wide 
fluctuations, often dropping below safe thresholds. 
Onion quality indicators demonstrated clear 
differences between the two storage approaches. 
Physiological weight loss in the SOSS ranged from 
only 2.22% to 6.22%, compared to 13.33% to 13.33-
15.56% in TOSS. Similarly, decay percentages were 
substantially lower in the SOSS (4-6%) than in 
the traditional system (17-20%). Color retention 
was also superior in the smart storage, with bulbs 
showing less discoloration and better firmness. 
Statistical analysis confirmed that these differences 
were significant at both p<0.05 and p<0.01 levels. 
The results highlight that the solar-powered smart

216 I FMP Engineering
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
storage system is highly effective in minimizing 
postharvest losses while preserving bulb quality. 
This system demonstrates strong potential as a 
sustainable, cost-effective, and scalable technology 
for improving onion storage management and 
reducing economic losses in Bangladesh.

Development of a smart universal seed cleaning 
and disinfection machine
M. Z. Hossain, M. Hossain, M. H. M. M. Rahman

A seed disinfection machine was developed by 
the Farm Machinery and Postharvest Process 
Engineering (FMPE) Division of BARI and 
evaluated during 2024-2025 at Gazipur to provide an 
effective, chemical-free method for reducing seed-
borne pathogens. The system employs a vibrating 
conveyor mechanism that rotates seeds 360° under 
UVC lamps, ensuring uniform exposure to radiation. 
Machine functions, including conveyor speed, 
blower fan, and sieve shaker intensity, are controlled 
through the "Xavier Air" unit, allowing adjustments 
for different seed types. Initial experiments using 
short light and vibration treatments showed no 
significant reduction in fungal contamination, with 
infection levels ranging between 8-14%. However, 
extending treatment duration from 2 to 4 minutes 
led to a marked improvement, reducing fungal 
infection from 32-48% in untreated controls to 
3-12% in treated seeds. Further laboratory analysis 
demonstrated that UV-C exposure time strongly 
influenced effectiveness: a 20-minute treatment 
reduced fungal colony counts to approximately 8, 
compared to 32 at 10 and 15 minutes. Importantly, 
germination performance was not adversely affected, 
confirming the machine's suitability for preserving 
seed viability. Constructed primarily from locally 
available materials, the unit achieved a throughput 
of 20-30 kg/h, offering portability, affordability, and 
scalability for smallholder applications. Overall, the 
FMPE-developed disinfection machine achieved 
over 90% reduction in seed-borne pathogens without 
reliance on chemical fungicides, making it a safe, 
eco-friendly, and practical solution for on-farm seed 
treatment and sustainable crop production

BARI bee pollen dryer
T. N. Barna, M. N. Amin, N. Jahan and M. A. Hoque 
Bee pollen is a nutritionally rich and commercially 
valuable apicultural product, but its usage in 
Bangladesh remains limited due to lack of affordable 
drying technologies. To address this, a low-cost, 
microcontroller-based pollen dryer was developed 
and improved under the FMD project at BARI. 
Since real pollen was unavailable off-season, soaked 
rice was used as a substitute for drying trials. The 
improved dryer includes features such as glass wool 
insulation, thermistor-based temperature sensing, 
microcontroller-controlled heating, and improved 
airflow systems. It has a 2500-gram capacity, a 
significant upgrade from the original 500-gram 
model. The system automatically maintains a 
drying temperature of 35-40°C, as per adjustable 
settings. with airflow speeds ranging from 2.37 
to 5.76 m/s, ensuring uniform drying. In a 4-hour 
drying trial, final moisture contents across five trays 
ranged from 4.0% to 20.5%, with optimal levels 
(4-10%) achieved in three trays. Drying behavior 
was modeled using Newton, Page, Henderson and 
Pabis, and Logarithmic models. The Page model 
showed the best fit overall (R2 > 0.97 in most trays), 
though tray-specific variations were observed due 
to airflow and temperature distribution differences. 
These results demonstrate the technical feasibility 
of the dryer design, but real pollen trials during 
the harvesting season are needed for validation. 
The system shows promise for scalable, affordable 
pollen drying, enabling better preservation, extended 
shelf life, and enhanced commercial potential in the 
apiculture sector of Bangladesh.
Development and performance evaluation of 
BARI groundnut thresher
T. N. Barna, M. N. Amin and M. A. Hoque 
This study evaluated the performance and economic 
viability of the BARI Groundnut Thresher under real 
field conditions using a Completely Randomized 
Design (CRD). The machine was optimized for 
275 RPM cylinder speed and 264 kg/h feed rate, 
achieving a threshing capacity of (29.2-35) kg/h, 
91.02% efficiency, 3.2% grain breakage, and 2.02% 
unthreshed loss in silty clay loam soil at 25% crop 
moisture. Economic analysis compared two rental 
models. In the first model (Tk. 3,800/day rental), the 
machine had a BCR of 1.17, a 5.18-year payback 
period, and a break-even point of 602 hours/year. 
The alternative model (Tk. 2,400/day rental + 
transport by user) showed the same BCR but with 
a longer 8.16-year payback and higher break-even 
point of 948 hours/year. Despite lower investment, 
this model suits cost-sharing or self-labor systems 
better. Compared to manual threshing (Tk. 2,400/
day, 6 laborers), the machine reduced labor demand 
to 3 operators, saving 28 hours and 5 labor-days for 
threshing 240 kg of groundnut per day. The fodder-
to-pod ratio observed was 8.16:1, lower than high-
yielding varieties, indicating room for agronomic 
improvement. In conclusion, the BARI Groundnut 
Thresher is efficient, labor-saving, and economically 
sustainable. It enhances groundnut post-harvest 
operations and becomes more profitable when used 
seasonally or for multiple crops, offering practical 
benefits for smallholder farmers and local service 
providers in Bangladesh.
Improvement and performance evaluation of a 
heavy-duty groundnut sheller
M. Hasan, M. N. Ali, N. Jahan and M. N. Amin
Groundnut (Arachis hypogaea L.) is an important 
oilseed crop, and efficient shelling is crucial for 
post-harvest processing. This study evaluated a 
heavy-duty groundnut sheller developed under the 
FMDP Project, FMPE Division, BARI, Gazipur. The 
machine, powered by a 3 HP motor and equipped 
with a shelling drum, concave, and vibrating sieve, 
achieved a throughput of 160 kg/hr. Operational 
challenges included improper discharge of kernels 
and straw due to incorrect inclination, unsuita+ ble 
sieve hole size, and insufficient blower fan speed, 
which resulted in incomplete cleaning. Optimizing 
the machine's inclination and fan speed is expected 
to improve shelling efficiency, kernel quality, and 
overall performance.

Cost and return analysis of selected varieties of 
lentil in selected districts of Bangladesh
M. A. Rashid and M. Khatun
The study was conducted to estimate the financial 
and economic returns and competitiveness of lentil 
varieties in Bangladesh. A total of 300 lentil growers 
were randomly selected from Natore, Jashore and 
Faridpur district for the study. Cost and return analysis 
was done on both variable and total cost basis. 
Domestic resource cost (DRC) was also estimated for 
evaluating the comparative advantage of lentil crop. 
The study revealed that the gross margins of producing 
BARI Masur-6, BARI Masur-4, BARI Masur-3 and 
BINA Masur-5 varieties were found positive. BCR 
of producing BARI Masur-6, BARI Masur-4, BARI 
Masur-3 and BINA Masur-5 were 1.65, 1.61, 1.57 
and 1.51, respectively. The estimates of DRC showed 
that Bangladesh had comparative advantage in lentil 
production as these estimates were less than one (0.47) 
implied that the production of lentil would be highly 
efficient for import substitution. Responded farmers 
mentioned that low market price at harvesting time 
and market syndicate were the major constraints for 
lentil production. The constraints were also fertilizer, 
not working properly might be due to adulterations, 
crisis of labour at harvesting time and high wage 
rate in the study areas. Ministry of commerce and 
Department of Agricultural Marketing (DAM) take 
initiatives for reasonable price at harvesting time. 
Mechanization should be introduced to the farmers 
field for minimizing the labour crisis.
Farm level adoption and market status of BARI 
released major fruits varieties in Bangladesh: A 
socio-economic study
M. A. Rashid, Moniruzzaman, M. S. Hoq, M. 
Khatun, M. S. Rahman, N. Nahar, R. Hasan, F. 
Rahman and S. M. A. Shiblee
The study was conducted to identify the adoption 
status and marketing performance of selected fruits 
in major growing areas of Bangladesh. A total of 2565 
respondents were interviewed to collect primary data 
for the study. Purposive random sampling technique 
was used to select the respondent farmers and traders. 
Four important fruits such as mango, dragon, banana, 
malta and guava were selected for the study. This 
study investigated varietal adoption, willingness, 
marketing channels, costs, margins, and efficiency 
of selected fruits production and marketing in 
Bangladesh, with emphasis on both BARI-released 
and local cultivars. Adoption analysis revealed 
that BARI varieties and other improved varieties 
were increasingly preferred due to higher yields 
(76% of responses), profitability (82%), and fair 
price opportunities (71%). However, adoption was 
constrained by lack of own land (75%), insufficient 
cash (56%), and market-related challenges. Despite 
these constraints, a considerable proportion of 
farmers are willing to expand mango cultivation, 
highlighting the profitability and demand potential 
of improved varieties. The adoption of BARI banana 
varieties analysis showed that BARI-4 (Champa) 
is the most widely cultivated improved variety, 
covering 26.32% of the total banana area, with 
particularly high adoption in Chittagong and Barisal. 
In contrast, local and traditional varieties such as 
Sobri and Chapa Sobi remain dominant in Dhaka, 
Khulna, Rangpur, and Mymensingh, indicating 
farmers' continued reliance on familiar cultivars. 
The adoption analysis of dragon fruits shows that 
BARI Dragon-1 occupies 100% of the cultivated 
area, while in Khulna it accounts for 72.4%, with 
the remaining 27.6% under BARI Dragon-2. At 
the national level, BARI Dragon-1 covers 97.5% 
of the total 389.7 hectares, while BARI Dragon-2 
represents only 2.46%. Marketing analysis identified 
four major channels of mango, with product flows 
of 35%, 30%, 20%, and 15%, respectively. On the 
other hand, Dragon and Banana marketing involved 
three major channels contributing 40%, 26%, 36%

Among the intermediaries Bepari incurred highest

Production, handling and consumption of 
selected fruits in Bangladesh: A concern of good 
agricultural practices adoption
M. Khatun, M. S. Hoq, M. A. Rashid, and S. M. A. 
Shiblee
The study assessed the knowledge, attitude and 
practices (KAP) of different stakeholders toward 
production, handling and consumption of fruits and 
the problems associated with not adopting Good 
Agricultural Practices (GAP). The study analyzed 
355 stakeholders data collected from guava and 
mango growers (175), traders (42) and consumers 
(138) from two guava growing districts, namely 
Rajshahi and Chuadanga; and two mango growing 
districts namely Chapainawabganj, and Satkhira. 
Descriptive statistics was used for analyzing the 
data. Farmers had a high degree of knowledge 
regarding GAP standards was held by 53% of guava 
farmers, followed by a medium level by 47% and a 
low level by 1%. Conversely, 58% of mango farmers 
had a high degree of understanding regarding GAP 
standards. Regarding the farmers' attitudes, 55% of 
the guava and 52% of mango farmers had a highly 
positive attitude toward the GAP standards adoption. 
Farmers' degree of experience showed that the 
majority of respondents cultivating guava (57%) 
and 76% mango farmers came into the category 
of intermediate-level practitioners. There were no 
farmers found in having high level experiences 
in this aspect. Decent price is not ensured in local 
market (43%), can't get satisfactory production 
(42%), comparatively small in size (35%), increased 
attack of insects and diseases (30%) were the major 
causes of not adopting GAP standards. Mango 
traders have a slightly higher proportion of highly 
knowledgeable traders (44%), while guava traders 
were more towards the medium knowledge category 
(58%). Traders overall had a positive mindset about 
GAP-based fruit handling, with mango traders 
showing stronger enthusiasm (72% high attitude) 
compared to guava traders, who are split equally 
between medium and high. For mango, a relatively 
large proportion (39%) is still in the low practice 
group. Guava traders perform somewhat better, but 
still, most remain in the medium group rather than 
reaching high compliance. The most frequently 
cited cause of not adopting GAP standards were high 
cost involvement (48%), safe handling may not be 
possible when supply is excessive (33%), and lack of 
awareness about health (32%). Approximately, 83% 
consumers were agree with paying more money. On 
average, the market price for mango was 60 Tk./
kg and for guava it was Tk. 55, but consumers are 
willing to pay more 82 Tk./kg on mango and Tk. 78 
for on guava. For adopting GAP standards in fruits 
production, the first and foremost crucial way is 
motivating farmers ethically and creating the market 
linkage of safe fruits for ensuring better price which 
will encourage the farmers. Improving monitoring 
systems, reducing implementation costs, and raising 
health awareness among traders could encourage 
better adoption of GAP-compliant handling.
Investigating the dynamics and determinants of 
price volatility in the potato and onion markets 
of Bangladesh
M. S. Rahman
Potato and onion are among the most essential crops 
in Bangladesh, playing a crucial role in household 
consumption, market dynamics, and farm-level 
income generation. Despite their significance, the 
production, marketing, and pricing mechanisms of 
these crops are subject to volatility, policy neglect, 
and structural inefficiencies, which adversely affect 
farmers' livelihoods and food security. This study 
investigates the long-term production trends of potato 
and onion in Bangladesh, analyzes stakeholders' 
perspectives on demand and supply, assesses the 
sensitivity of farm-level returns to cost, price, and 
yield fluctuations, and explores the mechanisms 
of farmgate price determination. To address these 
objectives, both primary and secondary data sources 
were utilized. Primary data were collected through a

220 I Agricultural Economics
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
structured questionnaire survey administered to 320 
potato farmers and 320 onion farmers, alongside 80 
market actors in the potato value chain and 60 in 
the onion value chain. The survey was conducted 
in major production hubs: Bagura, Nilphamari, 
Rangpur, Panchagarh, and Munshiganj for potato, 
and Rangpur, Lalmonirhat, Pabna, and Faridpur for 
onion. Multistage stratified random sampling was 
employed, with support from the respective upazila 
agricultural extension offices. Data collection was 
conducted by the researcher, assisted by three 
scientific assistants, and was complemented with 
secondary data sourced from the Bangladesh 
Bureau of Statistics (BBS). The findings reveal 
that potato production has shown steady long-term 
growth, supported by improved technologies and 
storage facilities, whereas onion production remains 
stagnant and highly vulnerable to climatic, input, and 
market uncertainties. Farmers' profitability in both 
crops is highly sensitive to fluctuations in farmgate 
prices, input costs, and yield variations, with onion 
farmers in particular facing greater risks due to 
inadequate storage facilities and exploitative pricing 
structures. The analysis of the onion's farmgate 
pricing mechanism highlights a complex system 
involving post-harvest drying, storage, and market 
intermediaries. Farmers sell their produce either 
in local markets (hatbar) or directly to traders, but 
their bargaining power is limited due to asymmetric 
access to market information, dependency on 
immediate cash needs, and syndicate-like control 
exerted by terminal market aratdars. Evidence 
suggests that farmers often receive lower-than-fair 
prices, with local traders measuring one mon as 45 kg 
instead of the standard 40 kg, further reducing their 
returns. Overall, the study highlights the need for 
institutional reforms, enhanced storage and market 
information systems, and strengthened regulatory 
oversight to ensure fair pricing mechanisms and 
sustainable returns for farmers. The insights 
provide critical implications for policymakers, 
development agencies, and researchers concerned 
with agricultural marketing, rural livelihoods, and 
food security in Bangladesh.
Price volatility of summer green chilli in 
Bangladesh: an economic analysis
M. R. Hasan
This study examined the price volatility patterns of 
summer green chili in Bangladesh over the period 
2010-2024, employing advanced econometric 
techniques including multiple regression analysis 
and ARCH-GARCH models. Green chili is a crucial 
spice crop in Bangladesh, significantly impacting 
both producer incomes and consumer expenditure 
patterns. The research revealed high price volatility 
characterized by seasonal patterns, supply-demand 
imbalances and external shocks. Using daily 
wholesale price data from major markets, the 
study identified key determinants of price volatility 
and provides policy recommendations for market 
stabilization. The findings indicate that weather 
variability, seasonal production cycles and market 
integration significantly influenced price dynamics, 
with GARCH (1,1) model effectively capturing 
volatility clustering in green chili prices.

This study aimed to assess the adoption, input

Joypurhat achieved the highest BCR (2.08) and yield

Alu-90's BCR dropped to 1.15 indicating a decline 
in profitability compared to the previous year, due to 
higher input costs and lower farmgate prices. Local 
varieties like Pakri and Sakila, though grown on 
small scales, achieved higher market prices but had 
lower yields. BADC-1 (Sunshine) covered 2.36% 
of the area and performed moderately (26.53 t/ha).
Farmers faced multiple challenges including high 
seed costs (96%), low-quality seeds (94%), and 
poor market access, especially in terms of unstable 
prices and limited storage. The declining BCR trend 
highlighted the need for better input management, 
stable pricing and enhanced extension services to 
sustain profitability

Comparative study of mustard in adoption 
inclusion and existing pattern
M. Rasheduzzaman, M. I. Nazrul, M. A. Rashid
Increase of cropping intensity in rice based cropping 
system is becoming important for food security and 
poverty alleviation. Therefore, this study evaluates 
the impacts of incorporating mustard into the fallow 
land in Sylhet region of Bangladesh for improving 
cropping intensity. The current cropping pattern, 
Fallow-T. Aus-T. Aman, limits productivity, while 
introducing mustard during the fallow period may 
optimize land use. Data from the farmers revealed 
that the improved Mustard-T. Aus-T. Aman pattern 
significantly enhanced land use efficiency (79.73% 
vs. 61.37%), production efficiency (42.38 vs. 35.50 
kg ha−1 day−1), and rice equivalent yield (12.33 vs. 
7.95 t ha−1). Economically, the mustard-inclusive 
system yielded higher gross returns and benefit-
cost ratio (1.90). Furthermore, the dichotomous 
logistic regression showed that age, education, 
farm size, training received, extension contact, and 
incentive received were significant determinants 
of adoption and incorporating mustard production 
in existing cropping pattern. Results suggest that 
adopting mustard cultivation in fallow periods can 
improve productivity, profitability, and sustainable 
intensification of rice-based farming in Sylhet, 
benefiting local farmers and food security efforts.

acute pedicel attachment, green colour at the 
immature stage, red colour at maturity, and semi-
wrinkled surfaces. Quantitative analysis revealed 
wide variation in plant height, flowering and fruiting 
time, fruit size, and fruit number, with the highest 
variability in fruit number per plant (CV 86.8%). 
These findings highlight the rich genetic diversity in 
chilli germplasm, offering valuable traits for future 
crop improvement and conservation programs. 
Chilli germplasm showed wide variability, 
presenting useful traits for genetic improvement and 
preservation.

Evaluation of hyacinth bean germplasm for 
seasonal variation
Q M Ahmed and I Ahmed
Among 89 hyacinth bean (Lablab purpureus) 
genotypes, most exhibited stem pigmentation; green 
veins and absence of anthocyanin were predominant. 
Leaves varied in size, flowers were largely white, 
and fresh pods were generally green in color, with 
pod shape ranging mostly flat or curved. Fresh seeds 
were typically light green and oval; dry seeds were 
mainly brown or black. Flowering initiation varied 
widely from 45 to 112 days post-transplanting, while 
edible pods emerged between 74 to 145 days (mean 
113), and full maturity occurred at about 143 days. 
Pod size and weight were highly variable (length: 
4.8-11 cm; width: 1.4-4.3 cm; weight: 5.2-19.78 g), 
with pod weight showing the greatest variability 
(about 26% CV) and days to maturity the least 
(about 14% CV).

I Ahmed and M M Ali

226 I Plant Genetic Resources
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
set, six primers were selected based on their

Conservation of germplasm in active and base 
collection
S. Rahman, N. Jahan and M. M. Ali
The Plant Genetic Resources Centre (PGRC) of 
BARI has been conserving germplasm since 1987 
through ex situ methods, including seed and field 
gene banks. Currently, PGRC conserves 13,165 
accessions of 154 crops, comprising cereals, pulses, 
oilseeds, spices, vegetables, fruits, cash crops, 
medicinal, and other minor crops. Of these, 12,998 
accessions are maintained in the seed gene bank and 
167 in the field gene bank. In 2024-25, an additional 
152 new accessions-consisting of oilseeds (52), 
spices (10), vegetables (82), and fruits (8) were 
collected, assigned BD codes, and preserved in both 
active and base collections. These conservation 
efforts ensure the availability of diverse genetic 
resources for future crop improvement, food 
security, and adaptation to environmental changes.
Monitoring of germplasm in active collection
S. Rahman, N. Jahan and M. M. Ali
A total of 3402 accessions of 20 crops viz. ash 
gourd, black gram, bottle gourd, coriander, halim 
shak, hinta, indian spinach, mallow, niger, okra, 
onion, pea, pigeon pea, ridge gourd, roselle, sesame, 
sorghum, sulfa, sword bean, and velvet bean, were 
monitored from the active collection during 2024-
25 through germination testing. Out of these, 1172 
accessions (34.4%) recorded poor germination (0-
40%), 1016 accessions (29.8%) exhibited medium 
germination (41-80%), and 1214 accessions 
(35.7%) maintained high viability (81-100%). The 
crops okra, sorghum, pea, pigeon pea, and ridge 
gourd showed considerable deterioration, while 
bottle gourd, sesame, and pea demonstrated better 
performance in the desirable category (81-100%). 
The accessions having germination below 80% 
and/or limited seed quantity will be prioritized for 
regeneration in the upcoming year to restore their 
viability and ensure long-term conservation.

sustainable yield and economic return of onion

100-30-3-1-1.5 kg ha -1 NPKSZnBMg. On the basis

On the basis of gross return (Tk 825725 ha-1), gross 
margin (Tk 575017 ha-1) and benefit cost ratio 3.34, 
respectively. The soil test based fertilizer plus 2 ton 
Vermicompost ha-1 was found to be profitable in 
Faridpur region.

Effect of different fertilizer doses and application 
methods for potato production under zero tillage 
condition in coastal area
H. M. K. Bashar, M. M. Islam, K. N. Islam and N. 
Sultana
The experiment was conducted using the potato 
variety BARI Alu-72 during the Rabi season 
of 2024-25 at the Multi Location Testing site in 
Kalapara, Patuakhali. RCBD with three replications 
and six treatments was employed. A uniform 
spacing of 25 cm between plants and 60 cm 
between rows was maintained across all treatments, 
resulting in a plot size of 5 × 4 meters per treatment. 
The study evaluated three fertilizer application 
methods-broadcasting, ring placement, and side 
placement-in combination with two fertilizer 
levels: 125-50-100-30-2-1.5 kg h -1 NPKSZnB and 
120-40-80-20-2-1.5 kg h -1 NPKSZnB. Significant 
differences were observed among the fertilizer 
application methods for key parameters such as 
the number of tubers per plant, tuber weight per 
plant (g), and tuber yield per hectare (t ha -1). The 
analysis of variance also revealed significant 
interaction effects for all traits studied. Similarly, 
fertilizer levels showed highly significant effects 
on these parameters. The highest performance was 
recorded with side placement, which resulted in 
an average of 5.49 tubers per plant, 522 g of tuber 
weight per plant, and a tuber yield of 21.69 tons per 
hectare. The best interaction outcome was achieved

230 I On-Farm Studies
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
when 120-50-100-30-2-1.5 kg h -1 NPKSZnB was 
applied through side placement. These findings 
suggested that side placement is the most effective 
and economical method of fertilizer application for 
potato under zero tillage conditions at Kalapara, 
Patuakhali. Furthermore, the 120-50-100-30-2-1.5 
kg h-1 NPKSZnB fertilizer rate appears to be the most 
promising for maximizing yield and productivity in 
this context.
Response of vermicompost on growth, yield and 
fruit quality of watermelon in coastal saline soil
H. M. K. Bashar, M. M. Islam, K. N. Islam and N. 
Sultana
An experiment was conducted at the Multi Location 
Testing (MLT) site in Kuakata, Patuakhali, during 
the rabi season of 2024-25 to evaluate the impact 
of varying vermicompost application rates on the 
yield and fruit quality of watermelon under farmers' 
field conditions. The study incorporated different 
doses of vermicompost alongside the recommended 
levels of inorganic fertilizers as per the Fertilizer 
Recommendation Guide (FRG' 2018). The 
treatment combinations were 1 ton Vermicompost 
ha-1 + N 150P50K125S40Zn5B4 T1, 2 ton Vermicompost 
ha-1 + N 150P50K125S40Zn5B4 T 2, 3 ton Vermicompost 
ha-1 + N 150P50K125S40Zn5B4 T 3 and Farmers practice 
(N175P70K120S30Zn10B5) T 4. Sprouted seeds of the 
popular hybrid watermelon variety 'Big Family' 
were sown in plots assigned to each treatment. 
The combined application of vermicompost and 
inorganic fertilizers significantly influenced yield 
and yield contributing parameters in watermelon 
cultivation in the coastal region. The highest yield 
(31.69 t ha-1) was achieved with the application of 3 
t vermicompost ha -1 in combination with inorganic 
fertilizers. The maximum amount of Total Soluble 
Solid (TSS) indicated improved fruit quality 
with higher doses of vermicompost application. 
Conversely, the lowest TSS was observed in T 4, 
where no vermicompost was applied. Economic 
analysis revealed that T3 resulted in the highest gross 
return (Tk 633800 ha-1), gross margin (Tk 444900 ha-
1), and benefit cost ratio (BCR) of 3.36. In contrast, 
the control plot i.e. the farmers practice yielded the 
lowest economic return (Tk 535800 ha-1) and a BCR 
of 3.18. These findings suggested that integrating 3 
ton vermicompost ha-1 plus recommended inorganic 
fertilizers can enhance both the yield and quality of 
watermelon, offering a viable strategy for sustainable 
and profitable watermelon production in the coastal 
regions of Bangladesh.

hill-1was recorded from T 1 treatment and weight of
