Rovral 50 WP (Iprodione) @ 2 g/l, and Amistar Top 
325 SC (Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole) @ 1 ml/l, 
along with an untreated control were tested. The 
lowest disease incidence (8.87 %) was recorded in 
plots treated with Tilt 250 EC, which was statistically 
at par with Indofil M-45 (9.46) and Folicur 250 EC 
(10.48). In contrast, the highest disease incidence 
(40.74%) was observed in control plots. The highest 
seed yield (2203 kg/ha) was obtained from Tilt 250 
EC treated plots, followed closely by other fungicide 
treatments, whereas the lowest yield (1480 kg/ha) 
was recorded in the control. The maximum net 
income (Tk. 59,520/ha) was achieved with Tilt 250 
EC, followed by Tk. 55,830/ha from Indofil M-45 
and Tk. 50,160/ha from Folicur 250 EC. The results 
suggest that Tilt 250 EC, Indofil M-45, and Folicur 
250 EC are effective options for managing white 
mold in sunflower while ensuring higher economic 
returns.

Survey and Identification of summer Onion 
diseases
N. Nath, M. A. Wadud, M.M.Kamal, M. N. Yousuf 
and S. N. Mozumder
A survey was conducted at different summer onion 
growing areas of Gazipur, Faridpur, Rajbari and 
Bogura during 2024-25 to identify the diseases of 
summer onion and their causal organisms. Basal 
rot (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae) and purple 
blotch (Alternaria porri) were found predominantly 
in the surveyed areas. Black mold (Aspergillus 
niger) was seen in post-harvest storage condition. 
Basal rot was observed at growth stage (30 to 45 
days old seedlings). Purple blotch was observed as 
small, water-soaked spots on leaves that enlarge into 
purplish-brown lesions with yellow halos at the mid 
growth stage of the bulb. In storage, black mold was 
also found as a black, sooty discoloration on the 
neck and outer scales of the bulb. The causal fungi 
were identified as Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae, 
Alternaria porri and Aspergillus niger.

Detection of viruses of Chili and their vectors 
N. Nath, M. S. Rahman, M. A. Wadud, M. M. Kamal
An investigation was conducted to detect causal 
viruses of virus diseases infecting chili plant. Virus 
infected samples of chili plant were collected from 
naturally infected chili field and Double Antibody 
Sandwich Enzyme-Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay 
(DAS-ELISADAS-ELISA was performed for the 
detection of causal viruses. In this experiment, 
eight infected chilli germplasm were collected 
from 8 genotypes. An antiserum of Chilli veinal 
mottle virus (ChVMV) was used to detect the virus 
separately. Only one infected chili sample (A VPP-
1236-2) gave the positive result against the virus. 
The results suggested that Chilli veinal mottle virus 
(ChVMV) was the causal agent of the virus disease 
in chilli germplasm.

Ginger
Fungal pathogens associated with imported 
ginger rhizome
M. A. Wadud, N. Nath, Z. H. Prodhan and M. M. 
Islam 
A study was conducted to identify the fungal 
pathogens associated with imported rhizomes of 
ginger. Eight samples of ginger rhizomes were 
collected from Raja Bajar and Shwapno Super Shop, 
Police Plaza, Bogura. All the ginger were imported 
from India and Bhutan. Sclerotium rolfsii was found 
to associate with the samples. Pathogenicity test 
was done by Rhizome inoculation method. After 
pathogenicity test it was confirmed that storage rot 
of ginger was caused by Sclerotium rolfsii.
Betel Vine
Identification of causal pathogen of stem rot of 
betelvine
M. H. Rahman and R. Momotaz
An investigation was carried out to identify the 
causal pathogen of betlevine stem rot in the On-
farm Research Division, BARI, Shibpur, Narsingdi 
during December 2024 to May 2025. Bitelvine vine

pathogens are detrimental to bitelvine cultivation 
under prevailing environmental conditions in betel

Validation trial of biolife bhat-01 wp for 
controlling bacterial wilt of a bari released 
brinjalvariety 
M. T. Hossain and M S. I. Khan
An experiment was carried out to control the 
bacterial wilt in the susceptible BARI Begun 12 
using the bacterial formulated products at the 
Regional Agricultural Research Station, Hathazari 
and Chattagram. Bacterial wilt, a major threat to our 
economy, was causing their yields to decline. There 
is currently no successful remedy for bacterial wilt 
in solanaceous crops worldwide. However, probiotic 
microbial species and their formulated products had 
been used in agricultural fields around the world 
since last decade. But, in our nation, it has become 
still primitive. We have used both in vitro and in 
vivo trials using reasonable chemical pesticides 
comparing effective microbial organisms called 
BioLife BHAT-01 WP which were formulated by 
Bacillus oryzicola YC7007, Bacillus velezensis

Plant Pathology I 295
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
GL6 with some standard carrier materials against 
bacterial wilt during 2024-25. Formulated powder 
BioLife BHAT-01 WP were conducted by three-time 
sprayings to the rhizosphere till to droplet. The in 
vitro antagonistic activities by formulated product of 
BioLife BHAT-01 WP and their active inocula levels 
2.0 × 10 10 CFU/gm had been scrutinized against 
the bacterial pathogen Ralstonia solanacearum for 
controlling bacterial wilt. There were no diseases at 
2-MAT (Months after transplanting) in the treated 
plot. BioLife BHAT-01 WP powder, a formulated 
bacterial product (1 × 10 10 CFU/g) revealed 
significantly (Student's t-test, P<0.05) lower disease 
severity indices by 1.3±0.3 and 2.3 ± 0.3 than the 
control by 2.6 ± 0.3 and 3.3 ± 0.8 in the BARI 
Begun 12 respectively at 5-MAT and 6 MAT. We 
came to the conclusion that BioLife BHAT-01 are 
essential biological products to control Ralstonia 
solanacearum.

highest seedling survival rate (96.16%), greatest

Induction mechanisms for controlling bacterial 
black spot in mango
M. T. Hossain and M S. I. Khan
An experiment was conducted at the Regional 
Agricultural Research Station, Hathazari, 
Chattagram in order to ascertain the induction in the 
plant employing the bacterial formulated products at 
the farmer's field during 2024-25. Bacillus species 
have been employed for last decade in agricultural 
settings to promote plant growth, increase yields, 
and combat a variety of plant diseases. But in our 
country, it has become still infantile. However, 
we have used both in vitro and in vivo trials using 
reasonable chemical pesticides comparing effective 
microbial organisms called BioLife BHAT-04 
WP which were formulated by Bacillus oryzicola 
YC7007, Bacillus velezensis GL6, and B. subtilis 
GBO3 with some standard carrier materials against 
mango bacterial black spot, MBBS disease of exotic 
banana mango. A very clear and distinct inhibition 
zones were observed at in vitro cell bioassay, 
indicating strong antagonistic strains to Pantoea 
dispersa that had been identified by the MALDI-
TOF and 16sRNA sequencing. Formulated BioLife 
HAT-04 revealed significantly (Student's t, P<0.05) 
lower disease severity by 1.0 ± 0.6, than the control 
by 2.8 ± 0.4 in the exotic banana mangoes out of 0-4 
disease rating scales. It also revealed significantly 
induction of PR1 gene compared to control. BioLife 
BHAT-04 also revealed significantly (Student's 
t, P<0.05) higher yield (total no. of fruit/plant) 
compared to control by 35.3 ± 3.0 no/plant than the 
control by 25.0 ± 3.0. Formulated products showed 
significantly consistent disease suppression 2.8 
times to MBBS compared to control. We concluded 
that BioLife BHAT-04 is a necessary biological 
product for controlling MBBS disease.

Citrus 
Search for resistance sources of citrus sp. Against 
candidatus liberibacter asiaticus (CLAS) causing 
greening disease of citrus
R.Islam, M.S. Akhter, K. Jahan, M. Naznin, M. M. 
Islam and M. H. Hossain
Citrus, particularly sweet orange (Citrus sinensis) 
and mandarin (Citrus reticulata), is an important 
fruit crop in Bangladesh, but its production is 
increasingly threatened by huanglongbing (HLB), 
a destructive disease caused by Candidatus 
Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas) and transmitted by 
psyllid vectors. The disease leads to severe yield loss, 
fruit quality reduction, and tree decline, yet little is 
known about the interaction of CLas with commonly 
used citrus rootstocks in Bangladesh. In this study, 
four CLas isolates were collected from symptomatic 
sweet orange trees in Rajshahi, Chapainawabganj, 
Rangpur, and Moulvibazar. Molecular detection 
using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) confirmed 
the presence of CLas in all isolates. These isolates 
were subsequently graft-inoculated onto seedlings 
of three citrus species: Pummelo (Citrus grandis), 
Rangpur lime (Citrus limonia), and Trifoliate 
orange (Poncirus trifoliata). Symptom development 
was monitored and validated by PCR. Results of 
biological indexing revealed clear differences in 
host responses: Pummelo showed the highest level 
of tolerance, with minimal symptom expression 
and complete resistance to one isolate (CSCN03); 
Rangpur lime exhibited moderate and isolate-
dependent susceptibility; and Trifoliate orange was 
highly susceptible, with up to 100% infection. These 
findings demonstrate significant variability in host-
pathogen interactions and highlight Pummelo as a 
potential source of tolerance for future rootstock 
improvement. The study provides a foundation for 
resistance-based management strategies aimed at 
mitigating the threat of HLB to citrus cultivation in 
Bangladesh.

Isolation and characterization of 
entomopathogenic fungi
M. S. Rahman, M. Arifunnahar, M. M. Islam and 
M.H. Hossain
Entomopathogenic fungi (EPFs) play an important 
role for regulating insect pest populations, as they 
exist in many different ecosystems. Within these 
fungi, Beauveria, Metarhizium spp. Cordyceps 
spp. etc. genera include species that are the most 
commercially important. The aim of this study was 
to isolate and characterization of entomopathogenic 
fungi. Two entomopathogenic fungi were isolated 
and characterized. One is Cordyceps javanica from 
dead insect and another is Beauveria sp. from forest 
soil. Cordyceps javanica was characterized through 
morphological and molecular and Beauveria sp. 
through morphological technique. The ITS gene 
sequence of the Cordyceps javanica isolate was 
submitted to the NCBI database with the GenBank 
accession number PQ098453. 
Survey on disease status of various crops of 
fragile ecosystem in Bangladesh
R. Momotazm. Arifunahar, M.M.Islam, 
M.S.Rahman, I. Ahmed, R.Islam, M.S.Akhter, M. 
Monir, M. H. Rashid and M.H.Hosain
A field survey was conducted during the 
2024-25 cropping season across Khulna 
(Dumuria), Satkhira(Tala), Rajshahi (Poba), 
and Chapainawabganj (Islampur), recorded 24 
diseases affecting vegetables, spices, tubers, 
fruits, oilseeds, and pulses. Rajshahi showed the 
highest disease pressure in vegetables, especially 
cabbage (21%), brinjal (16%), and chili (15%), 
while Chapainawabganj had the lowest overall 
incidence. Khulna recorded the highest curd rot 
in cauliflower (21%), and Satkhira exhibited a 
broader range of vegetable diseases, including 
beetroot (11%) and broccoli (8%). In oilseeds 
and pulses, Rajshahi had the highest incidence of 
mustard club root (24%) and lentil Stemphylium 
blight (17%), in contrast to Chapainawabganj's 
lower levels. Among spices, Rajshahi reported 
the highest tip burn in garlic (14%) and purple 
blotch in onion (12%). Early blight of potato was 
most severe in Khulna (16%), and yam leaf spot 
occurred only in Khulna. Fruit crops in Rajshahi 
again showed high disease burdens-mango 
(24%), papaya (18%), and banana (20%)-while 
Khulna was the only district with citrus greening 
(12%). Satkhira showed milder fruit disease 
incidence. Botrytis blight of Gladiolus was highest 
in Khulna (11%) and absent in Chapainawabganj. 
The study highlights regional differences in 
disease prevalence and provides critical data for 
crop protection strategies.

Effect of seaweed extract on morpho-physiological 
response and seed yield of soybean under drought 
stress
M. S. A. Khan, A. H. M. M. R. Talukder, M. Ahmed 
and F. Ahmed
A field experiment was conducted during rabi 2024-
25 at the research field of Plant Physiology Division, 
BARI to investigate the influence of seaweed extract 
on morpho-physiological traits and seed yield of 
soybean under drought stress. BARI Soybean-6 was 
grown in field under water stress (50 - 60% FC) with 
foliar application (five levels: 0, 2.5, 5.0, 7.5 and 10 
ml/l of water) of seaweed extract at second trifoliate 
leaf to R6 stage. Seaweed extract showed significant 
effect on soybean growth characters and seed yield. 
Relative water content and chlorophyll fluorescence 
were also varied due to different levels of seaweed 
extract. Proline accumulation and reactive chemical 
compounds like H2O2 and malondealdehyde contents 
were observed maximum in water stress plant and 
the contents were decreased with increasing levels 
of seaweed extract. Antioxidant enzymes activities 
like GSTs, POD, CAT and APXs were observed 
maximum in water stress along with seaweed 
extract @ 10 ml/l of water. The lowest seed yield 
(774 kg/ha) was observed in water stress treatment 
which was 51% lower as compared to well-watered 
treatment. However, water stress along with seaweed 
extract @ 7.5 and 10 ml/l of water treatments 
produced 86.13% (1304 kg/ha) and 87.52% (1325 
kg/ha) seed yield as compared to well-watered 
treatment, respectively. Results revealed that foliar 
application of BARI Seaweed-1 extract @ 7.5 to 10 
ml/L significantly improved drought tolerance in 
soybean by enhancing physiological traits, reducing 
oxidative stress, and increasing antioxidant enzyme 
activities. These treatments resulted in substantial 
yield recovery under water-limited conditions, 
suggesting that seaweed extract is a promising 
biostimulant for sustainable soybean production in 
drought-prone areas.
Morpho-physiological and biochemical responses 
of selected sesame genotypes to waterlogging 
stress 
S. N. Mahfuza, A. F. M. S. Ahsan, A. H. M. R. 
Talukder, A. A. M. M. Mustakim and N. Mokarroma 
A pot-culture experiment was conducted at the 
pot-house of the Plant Physiology Division, BARI, 
Gazipur, from March 2025 to June 2025. The 
objective of this study was to examine and identify 
the comparatively waterlogging tolerant sesame 
genotypes. Five sesame genotypes including BARI 
Til-6 as G5 were subjected to waterlogging stress 
for 48 and 72 hours and data were measured. The 
experiment followed a randomized complete block 
design (RCB) with three replications. Ten seeds of 
each genotype were sown in each pot on March, 
2025. After emergence excess plants were thinned 
out and three plants pot-1 were maintained. Fertilizers 
were applied @100-30-55-25-3-1kg ha -1 N-P-K-S-
Zn-B. Waterlogging stress was imposed at 55 days 
after sowing (DAS) by placing the pots in a cement-
concrete tank and submerging them to maintain 
waterlogged conditions. The water level was kept 
2-3 cm above the soil surface to ensure complete 
saturation. The treatment was maintained for the 
desired stress period, with the water level monitored 
and replenished daily to prevent fluctuation. The 
present study showed that waterlogging stress 
caused severe damage to different attributes of the 
sesame genotypes compared with their control. The 
treated genotypes showed an increasing trend in lipid 
peroxidation as well as in hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) 
and Lipoxygenase (LOX) contents that corresponded 
to increased stress duration. The results also showed 
that the plants exposed to water stress presented a 
significant decline in CMSI content, yield and yield 
contributing characters, but the reduction rate was 
significantly lower in G4, which was identical with 
G5 (BARI Til- 6).

Morpho-physiological evaluation of brinjal 
genotypes at elevated temperature
S. N. Mahfuza, A. H. M. M. Rahman, N. Mokarroma, 
F. Ahmed, M. Moniruzzaman, L. Akter and A. K. M. 
Quamruzzaman 
A study was conducted to evaluate the impact of 
elevated temperature stress on the physiological 
traits and yield attributes of ten hybrid brinjal 
(Solanum melongena L.) genotypes, including 
two varieties (BARI Hybrid Begun-4 and BARI 
Hybrid Begun-6). This study was a collaboration 
program with vegetable Division, HRC, BARI. 
The experiment involved two temperature 
conditions: normal (24°C in an open field) and 
elevated, where the temperature was raised by 
5±1°C. High-temperature stress (ambient ± 5~6°C) 
was imposed at 20 days after transplanting (DAT) 
using a polythene chamber. Daily air temperature 
inside and outside the chamber was measured 
using maximum-minimum thermometers, while 
humidity was monitored with a hygrometer to 
assess atmospheric water vapor. The experiment 
followed a randomized complete block design 
with three replications. Fertilizers @ 150-50-
125-40-2 kg ha -1 N-P-K- Zn-B and Organic 
Manure 10 Kg pit -1 were applied. At 45 days after 
transplanting (DAT) samples were taken from 
both control and stressed plants to assess several 
physiological parameters, such as photosynthetic 
parameter, Cell membrane stability Index (CMSI), 
Proline content in leaves and pollen viability (%) 
of flowers. At designated time intervals, plants 
were harvested to record plant height, total dry 
matter, fruit number plant-1, and fruit yield plant -1. 
Results indicated that heat stress significantly 
reduced all measured physiological and yield 
parameters across all genotypes, reflecting damage 
to photosynthetic apparatus, membrane integrity, 
osmotic adjustment, and reproductive function. 
Notably, genotypes G4, G5, and G6 exhibited 
a comparatively lower reduction in these traits, 
performing statistically similar to the tolerant 
check variety BARI Hybrid Begun-6 (G10). Their 
ability to maintain higher CMSI, accumulate 
proline, and sustain pollen viability underscores 
their inherent thermo-tolerance. These genotypes 
were thus identified as promising, heat-tolerant 
candidates for future breeding programs aimed at 
developing climate-resilient brinjal varieties.
Exogenous application of plant growth regulators 
for mitigating heat stress and improvement of 
yield in bottle gourd
S. N. Mahfuza, A. A. M. M. Mustakim, A. H. M. 
M. Rahman, F. Ahmed, M. Moniruzzaman, L. Akter 
and A. K. M. Quamruzzaman
The present investigation was carried out with 
three plant growth regulators, namely Ethrel, 
Malic Hydrazide and GA 3, respectively were 
sprayed at 15 days after transplanting subsequently 
applied at 15-day intervals for a total of four sprays 
on bottle gourd plants to find out their response 
on bottle gourd compared to their control (water 
spray) under heat stress (ambient ± 5~6°C). The 
study was conducted at the vinyl house of Plant 
Physiology Division, BARI Gazipur during 
November, 2024-March, 2025. High temperature 
was raised by using a polythene chamber (ambient 
± 5~6°C). Pit size was top dia: 50 cm, depth: 50

were transplanted 10 December, 2024. Fertilizers 
@ 80-40-100-30-2-2 g pit -1 of N P K S Zn B 
Mn and Organic Manure (OM) 10 kg pit -1 were 
applied. Half OM, N and half of K along with full 
amount of other fertilizers were applied as basal. 
Remaining OM, N and K were top dressed in 4 
equal splits. The experiment followed a randomized 
complete block design with three replications. 
The results clearly indicated that the spraying of

and increase yield contributing characters and

Phenology, growth and yield response of rapeseed-
mustard to variable sowing environment
A.H.M. Motiur Rahman Talukder, and F. Ahmed
A field study was conducted during the 2024-2025 
rabi season at the Plant Physiology Division, BARI, 
Gazipur to observe the phenology, growth and 
yield of rapeseed-mustard varieties as influenced 
by sowing times. Two rapeseed-mustard varieties, 
namely BARI Sarisha-14 and BARI Sarisha-18 
were sown in three different time scheduling 10-
days intervals viz. 14 November, 24 November and 
04 December, respectively. The trial was laid out 
in a Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD) 
with three replications. Seeds were sown at a rate 
of 7.0 kg ha−1 with the spacing of 30 cm × 10 cm, 
in unit plots of 3.0 m × 4.0 m. To ensure healthy 
establishment, seeds were treated with Provax 200-
EC (2.5 g kg−1 seed). Crop management included 
manual weeding, light irrigation, thinning, bird 
scaring, and pest control through Malathion (2 ml 
L−1) and Rovral (0.2%). Fertilizers were applied at 
the rate of 100-30-80-20-3-1 kg ha−1 N-P-K-S-Zn-B 
in the form of urea, tripple super phosphate (TSP), 
muriate of potash (MOP), zypsum, zinc sulphate and 
boric acid, respectively. Half of the urea along with 
the full doses of tripple super phosphate, muriate of 
potash, zypsum, zinc sulphate and boric acid was 
applied as basal, while the remaining urea was top-
dressed at 20 days after sowing (DAS). Observations 
were recorded on phenological traits (emergence, 
two-leaf stages, flowering, pod initiation, seed 
setting, and maturity), growth parameters (plant 
height, leaf area index, and biomass accumulation) 
and yield-contributing characters (pods plant−1, 
pod length, seeds pod−1, 100-seed weight), and 
final grain yield. Weather data were also analyzed 
to interpret crop-environment interactions. Results 
revealed that sowing time had a significant effect 
on all growth and yield attributes. Early sowing (14 
November) promoted rapid emergence, prolonged 
vegetative growth, and timely flowering, which 
ultimately enhanced yield performance, particularly 
in BARI Sarisha-18 (1.56 t ha−1). In contrast, 
late sowing (04 December) curtailed the growth 
duration, reduced leaf area development and led to 
yield reduction, with BARI Sarisha-14 recording 
the lowest yield (0.55 t ha−1). Distinct varietal 
differences were observed, where BARI Sarisha-14 
exhibited rapid early phenological development 
and larger seed size, whereas BARI Sarisha-18 
demonstrated greater canopy expansion, higher pod 
production, and enhanced biomass accumulation, 
which collectively contributed to its superior yield 
potential. In conclusion, mid-November sowing, 
combined with appropriate nutrient management, is 
optimal for maximizing the productivity of rapeseed-
mustard in Bangladesh. The varietal performance 
data generated from this study provide a robust 
foundation for parameterization of crop simulation 
models such as DSSAT and APSIM, thereby 
supporting improved agro-climatic decision-making 
for rapeseed-mustard cultivation.

Evaluation of barley genotypes under drought and 
salinity stresses in coastal region of Bangladesh
A. H. M. Motiur Rahman Talukder, F. Ahmed and 
S. Mondal
A field experiment was carried out at the Agricultural 
Research Station (ARS), Benarpota, Satkhira during 
the Rabi season of 2024-2025 to evaluate the 
performance of selected barley varieties/genotypes 
under combined drought and salinity stresses in 
coastal Bangladesh. The study was designed using a 
Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD) with 
three replications. Four genotypes/varieties viz. 
BARI Barley-8, BARI Barley-9, BARI Barley-10, 
and the genotype T-16 were tested under two stress 
conditions: (i) salinity with irrigation and (ii)

in the trial. Fertilizers were applied following the

Barley-9, which maintained the highest 100-seed 
weight and improved resilience in grain number 
and plant yield. In conclusion, the study identified 
BARI Barley-9 and BARI Barley-10 as promising 
candidates for cultivation in drought- and salinity-
prone coastal regions, whereas genotype T-16 
proved highly susceptible. These findings highlight 
the potential of improved barley varieties for 
enhancing productivity and stability in stress-prone 
environments of Bangladesh.

Effect of gibberellic acid seed priming on soybean 
germination and quality seed production
S. A. Bagum, P.C. Sarker and M. H. Rahman
The experiment was carried out at the Seed 
Technology Division's research field in BARI, 
Gazipur, from November 2023 to April 2024 and 
November 2024 to April 2025, to determine the 
effect of seed priming with various doses of GA3 
on soybean emergence and quality seed production. 
A field and laboratory investigation evaluated four 
GA3 concentrations (0, 100, 150, 200 ppm) applied 
to three soybean varieties (BARI Soybean-5, -6, -7). 
The experiment featured a two-factor randomized 
complete block design with three replications. Seed 
priming with gibberellic acid (GA3) significantly 
improves germination performance, seedling vigor, 
and yield attributes in soybean. Priming at 100 ppm 
GA3 maximized germination percentage (up to 
95%), vigor index (up to 14,984), plant height (94.5 
cm), number of pods per plant (up to 192.7), and 
seed yield (up to 37.9 g/plant). Higher concentrations 
(150-200 ppm) produced variable results, indicating 
an optimal GA3 dose exists. These findings support 
the use of 100 ppm GA3 seed priming for enhanced 
soybean seed production and field establishment.

Enhancement of growth, seed yield and quality 
as influenced by seaweed extract, and agronomic 
bio-fortification of zinc and selenium in field pea
R. Chakma, M. Islam, Md. N. Islam, M. S. Rahman, 
P. C. Sarker and M. H. Rahman 
This experiment is conducted at Seed Technology 
Division BARI, Gazipur research field during Rabi 
season 2024-25 to find out the effect of Zn, Se and 
seaweed extract on the growth, yield, quality and 
concentration in seeds of field pea. The experiment 
design was carried out in a RCB design with three 
replications. The experiment comprises five treatments 
viz. T1= Control (RDF BARI), T 2= 16 kg/ha. ZnSO 4 
(Soil) + 2.5 ml/L (foliar), T 3 = 100g/ha Na 2SeO4 
(Foliar) T 4=2.5 ml/L Seaweed and T 5= T 2+T3+T4. 
Combined application of ZnSO4, Na2SeO4 and seaweed 
increased the grain yield by 34.62%, compared to the 
control. Application of Se, Seaweed and Zn increased 
the field pea grain yield by 33.33%, 25% and 10.26%, 
respectively, compared to the control. However, the 
combined application of Zn, Se, and seaweed, as well 
as the sole Se application, resulted in greater grain 
yield increases compared to the other treatments.

and 2.88 g), seed yield (301.50 kg/ha and 284.21 kg/
ha), seeds per umbel (325.50 and 299.40) and active 
florets per umbel (115.93 and 110.30), compared

Seed Technology I 313
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
to the control (T5) which recorded the lowest 
performance in all traits. The findings suggest that 
combining natural pollination with frequent hand 
pollination greatly improves true seed production of 
onion in Bangladesh.

2025 to evaluate the effects of different seed 
priming methods on germination and early 
growth of summer onion cultivar BARI Piaz-5.
The experiment followed a Randomized Complete 
Block Design (RCBD) with five treatments:T 1: 
Hydro-priming, T 2: Osmopriming, T 3: Hormonal

including germination (59.67%), vigor index

concludes that seed priming particularly with GA 3 
and KNO3 significantly improves germination, 
seedling vigor and early growth of summer onion 
and can be recommended for enhancing productivity 
under field conditions.

A field experiment at Spices Research Centre, 
BARI, Shibganj, Bogura (2024-2025) evaluated

Comparative study of different seed priming 
techniques on soybean 
Sabikunnahar, M. M. H. Bhuiyan and M. H. Hossain
A field experiment was conducted during the Rabi 
season of 2025 at RARS, BARI, Cumilla to evaluate 
the effects of different seed priming treatments on 
soybean (Glycine max L.) growth and yield. Seven 
treatments were tested: hydropriming for 1 hour 
(T1), hydropriming for 2 hours (T 2), osmopriming 
with 0.5% KNO3 for 1 hour (T3), osmopriming with 
1% KNO3 for 2 hours (T4), osmopriming with 0.5% 
humic acid for 1 hour (T5), osmopriming with 0.5% 
salicylic acid for 1 hour (T6), and an untreated control 
(T7). Significant differences were observed for all 
parameters. T1 produced the highest seed yield (2.79 t 
ha−1), seed yield per plant (11.14 g), 100-seed weight 
(10.6 g), harvest index (47%), early emergence (4.0 
days), and pod number (39.4 pods plant−1). The 
control had the lowest values across most traits. The 
superior performance of T1 is attributed to enhanced 
germination, improved stand establishment and 
efficient assimilate partitioning. Given its simplicity, 
no chemical cost and positive impact on yield, 
hydropriming for 1 hour is recommended as a low-
cost, eco-friendly pre-sowing treatment for soybean. 
As the experiment was conducted for only one 
season, further trials will be undertaken next year to 
validate these results.

Effect of storage material on seed quality of green 
gram 
M. Islam, M. S. Rahman, R. Chakma, P. C. Sarker 
and M.H Rahman
The present investigation was carried out 
in laboratory of Seed Technology Division, 
Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute, Gazipur 
from August, 2024 to February, 2025, wherein 
freshly harvested quality seed of mungbean cv. 
BARI Mug 6 having high germination percentage 
and low moisture content (5.83%) was stored in 
different packages in ambient storage condition. 
There were five packaging materials i.e. i) Plastic 
container with air-tight lid, ii) PET bottle, iii) Gunny 
bag inside laminated with polybag, iv) Plastic bag 
inside laminated with polybag and v) Tin container 
used for storage of mug bean seed. The experiment 
was carried out using completely randomized design 
(CRD) with four replications. Observations were 
recorded at bimonthly interval on seed moisture 
content (%), germination (%), root length (cm), 
shoot length (cm), seedling dry weight (g) and 
seedling vigor index. The results indicated that all 
the treatments exhibited significant difference for 
all the traits studied after two, four and six months 
of storage. Maximum germination (87 %), seedling 
length, seedling dry weight, vigor index and low 
moisture content (5.93%) was found in seed stored 
in air tight PET bottle after six months of storage. 
Therefore, mung bean would be stored up to six 
months in air tight PET bottle or plastic container 
maintaining low moisture content and good seed 
quality.

Effect of bait station design on bait uptake and 
control efficacy of rodent in wet crop field
A T M Hasanuzzaman and M S Alam 
The experiment was conducted in outdoor rat 
enclosure at vertebrate pest division, BARI, 
Joydebpur, Gazipur during 2024-25 to increase the 
consumption of poison bait by rat through providing 
bait with suitable bait station and to increase the 
control efficacy of Zn3P2 poison bait in wet crop field. 
Plain bait was offered to rats with six newly designed 
bait stations and their consumption was recorded. 
The different bait stations were bamboo pipe bait 
station type 1 (BPB1), bamboo pipe bait station type 
2 (BPB2), banana leaf sheath bait stations (BLB), 
cork sheet bait stations (CSB), plastic bottle bait 
station (PBB) and Polythene sheet bait station (PSB. 
Rat consumed significantly higher amount of plain 
bait from BLB bait station which was statistically 
similar with BPB2 and BPB1 bait station whereas 
CSB bait station was least preferred by rat which was 
statistically similar with PSB and PBB bait station. 
Similarly, in poison bait consumption, BLB (0.56 g/
rat/day) bait station was highly preferred by rat that 
was followed by BPB1 (0.43g/rat/day) bait station 
which was statistically similar with BPB2 (0.37g/rat/
day) bait station. On the other hand, Highest success 
in rodent control was observed in BLB bait station 
(59.76%) that was followed by BPB2 (44.05%) and 
BPB1 (41.67%) bait station. The lowest success was 
observed in PBB bait station (26.67%).

Effect of edible wax coating and storage 
temperature for improving quality and enhancing 
shelf life of Mango fruit
M.G.F. Chowdhury, M. M. Rahman, M.M. Molla
This study evaluated the effects of edible surface 
coating (Endura FreshTM 9000) and storage 
temperature (9±1°C) on postharvest quality 
and shelf life of mango (BARI Aam-3). BARI 
Aam-3 was collected from farmers' orchard of 
Chapainawabganj and then washed with 1000 ppm 
thiabendazole, 0.1% calcinated calcium and treated 
with hot water at 55oC for 5 mins and wax coating 
(Endura fresh TM9000) were applied and then stored 
at 9±1°C and 80±5% RH. For uniform surface 
coating a hand sprayer was used to apply wax 
@500 fruit/L on the fruit peel. The study revealed 
significant variations in colorimetric parameters, 
β-carotene content, and total soluble solids (TSS) 
of BARI Aam-3 mangoes during 05 weeks storage 
(9±1°C) under different treatments. At the initial 
stage, fruits exhibited moderate lightness (45.48), 
high chroma (112.75), hue angle (85.91), and a low 
β-carotene content (13.77 mg/100 g), with TSS 
recorded at 7.27° Brix. During 05 weeks storage, 
the control fruits exhibited a rapid decline in L* 
and h° values, accompanied by a sharp increase in 
β-carotene (114.58 mg/100 g at 14 DAS), indicating 
fast ripening and color changes. However, fruits 
treated with hot water treatment (HWT) and edible 
surface coating retained higher lightness and hue 
angle values throughout storage, reflecting delayed 
ripening and better color preservation compared to 
control. Chroma values were significantly reduced 
in treated samples, particularly in treatment HWT 
and treatment HWT and edible surface coating, 
suggesting a slower degradation of green pigments. 
Beta carotene increased progressively in all 
treatments, with the highest accumulation in HWT 
and treatment HWT and edible surface coating at 
later storage periods (30.92 mg/100 g and 30.81 
mg/100 g after 04 weeks storage, respectively). 
TSS also increased gradually across treatments, 
reaching 21.64 °Brix in treatment HWT and edible 
surface coating after 02 weeks storage indicating 
enhanced sweetness with storage period. HWT and 
edible coating effectively maintained peel color 
and controlled ripening, while untreated fruits 
exhibited rapid senescence. It can be concluded 
that hot water and edible surface wax coating may 
extend storage life upto 5 weeks at 9±1°C with 
80±5% RH and maintain the physico-chemical 
quality of mangoes.

decreased drastically (42.85), whereas sajeeb soya

soybean: wheat (50:50) (0.73 ± 0.01), followed by 
soybean: wheat (25:75) (0.85 ± 0.01) and treatment 
soybean: wheat (75:25) (0.85 ± 0.01). That means 
it is less prone to microbial growth and is likely the 
best for shelf stability. Formulated sauces maintained 
stable pH (≈5.1-5.5), moderate fat content (2.5-
2.7%), and higher protein (6.89-6.93%) compared

soya sauce retained more favorable color attributes

consistent pH stability, higher protein, and fat

Physicochemical and nutritional quality of 
freeze-dried Mango chips
M.G.F. Chowdhury, M.M. Molla, P.Sen
This study aimed to standardize the processing 
protocol for freeze-dried green mango chips using 
starch, citric acid, and maltodextrin (MD). Fresh 
mango slices (2-3 mm thick) were treated with 2.5% 
starch, 0.3% citric acid, and varying MD levels 
(10%, 15%, 20%), then packed in high-density 
polyethylene packets (~60 μm) and frozen at-18oC 
for 24-36 hours. The frozen slices were freeze-
dried at -55oC for 24 hours followed by -45oC 
for 48 hr. and packaged in foil packets (~50 μm). 
Freeze-drying was performed using a laboratory-
scale freeze dryer under controlled vacuum pressure 
(0.001 mBar). The drying process was carried out at 
-55oC for 24 hours followed by-45oC for 24 hours to 
achieve optimal dehydration. After drying, the chips 
were packed in laminated aluminum foil packets 
(~50 μm) and stored at room temperature (26±2oC, 
75±5% RH). Results revealed that the lightness 
values of control treatment, 2.5% starch, 0.3% citric 
acid and 10% MD treatment, and 2.5% starch, 0.3% 
citric acid and 15% maltodextrin (MD) treatment 
were statistically similar, ranging from 58.07 to 
58.74, signifying that the application of starch and 
citric acid coatings with 10-15% MD effectively 
preserved brightness comparable to untreated 
samples. However, treatments 2.5% starch, 0.3% 
citric acid and 20% MD exhibited a significantly 
lower lightness value (48.27±0.01), indicating a 
darker appearance at higher MD concentrations. 
Chroma value indicates color intensity, was highest 
in the control (41.60±0.01), and followed by 
treatments (39.87±0.06). In contrast, 2.5% starch, 
0.3% citric acid and 10% MD treatment and 2.5% 
starch, 0.3% citric acid and 20% MD treatment 
revealed relatively lower values (34.05±0.06 and 
31.06±0.06), indicating that excessive MD reduced 
the vividness of chip color, while moderate levels-
maintained intensity close to the control. Hue angle 
values (79-81) reflected a typical yellowish-orange 
tone of mango. Treatment 2.5% starch, 0.3% citric 
acid and 10% MD treatment (81.08±0.01) and 
treatment 2.5% starch, 0.3% citric acid and 20% MD 
(80.12±0.07) exhibited slightly higher hue angles, 
shifting toward a lighter yellow, whereas 2.5% starch, 
0.3% citric acid and 15% MD treatment (79.78±0.01) 
indicated a deeper orange tone. Moisture content 
was highest in the control (10.06±0.87%) and the 
lowest in 2.5% starch, 0.3% citric acid and 15% MD 
treatment (6.42±0.02%), highlighting the role of MD 
in reducing moisture retention. Titratable acidity 
was maximum in control treatment (2.41±0.05%) 
and the lowest in 2.5% starch, 0.3% citric acid 
and 20% MD treatment (1.47±0.05%). Phenolic 
content increased with coating, the highest in 2.5% 
starch, 0.3% citric acid and 20% MD (8.32±0.03 mg 
GAE/g), while antioxidant activity peaked in 2.5% 
starch, 0.3% citric acid and 10% MD treatment 
(29.09±0.57%), confirming improved nutritional 
and functional quality. Freeze-dried mango chips 
treated with moderate MD levels (10-15%) 
preserved brightness and intensity, while excessive 
MD (20%) led to reduced lightness and chroma, 
negatively influencing visual quality. On the other 
hand, mango chips treated with 2.5% starch, 0.3% 
citric acid and 10% MD and 2.5% starch, 0.3% 
citric acid and 20% MD enhanced phenolic content 
and antioxidant properties while maintaining lower 
acidity and moisture levels.

Study on the heat stress and edible surface

M.G.F. Chowdhury, M. M. Rahman, M. A. Hossain,

A study was conducted on mango fruits treated

days for peel color, total soluble solids (TSS) and

1). This indicated a characteristic fresh greenish

(11.91 N) and color stability. Physiological weight 
loss increased, ranging 1.85-8.31% that indicate 
faster moisture loss and metabolic activity. Similar 
trends were almost observed at 12 days of storage. 
By the end of storage (20 DAS), control treatment 
and edible surface coating treatments fruits were 
fully rotten. HWT treatment and HWT with surface 
coating exhibited residual lightness (52.07 and 
50.37), while hue angle decreased further (76.74-
73.29), reflecting senescence-related discoloration. 
Edible coating alone reduced brightness after 8 days 
of storage and firmness consistently decreased with 
complete softening after 16 and 20 days of storage. 
Among them, hot water treatment and edible coating 
exhibited delayed senescence and higher carotenoid 
accumulation suggesting better storability and 
nutritional quality retention.

Development and validation of low-cost semi-
commercial ripening chamber at entrepreneurs' 
level for uniform ripening of fruits
M.G.F. Chowdhury, M.H.H.Khan, M. M. Rahman
Low-cost semi-commercial ripening chamber was 
established and validated in entrepreneurs' level at 
Godagari, Rajshahi and Monohardi, Narsingdi for 
uniform ripening of mango, tomato and banana. 
The fruits were exposed to different doses of 
concentrated liquid ethylene such as 0, 50, 100, 
150 and 200 ppm for overnight at PHTD Low-cost 
Ripening Chamber (3.5m L×2m W×2m H), BARI, 
Gazipur. After that, the fruits were kept at 20±2°C 
with 80±5% RH and at ambient temperature for 12 
days for the shelf life and physico-chemical quality. 
For validation similar type of ripening chamber 
was fabricated and trial experiment was conducted. 
In Noadia, Monohardi, Narsingdi, bananas (BARI 
Kola-1) were ripened using approximately 100-150 
ppm of ethylene gas overnight. The results were 
highly satisfactory, with bananas ripening uniformly 
within 72 hrs. After 48 hrs fruits were partially 
ripen and 72 hrs, bananas were marketable and fully 
edible, exhibiting consistent color, texture, and taste. 
This process not only accelerated ripening but also 
improved the quality and appearance of the bananas, 
making them more appealing to consumers and 
suitable for sale. In Sona Dighi, Godagari, Rajshahi, 
tomatoes were placed in the ripening chamber to 
ensure uniform ripening. The results were equally 
promising, with color development starting after 24 
hrs of exposure to the controlled conditions in the 
chamber. Green matured tomatoes (local variety) 
developed attractive red color and fully ripen within 
08 days but within 06 days tomatoes were marketable 
as per the observation trial and farmers comment. 
This accelerated process ensured that the tomatoes 
reached the desired ripeness while maintaining high 
quality, with the right color, firmness, and taste to 
meet consumer expectations. Those demonstration 
findings exhibit the effectiveness of the ripening 
chambers in providing controlled, uniform ripening 
conditions for both bananas and tomatoes. The 
results indicate that exogenous ethylene treatments, 
particularly at higher concentrations of ethylene gas 
(100-150 ppm), significantly enhance the ripening 
process in bananas by increasing TSS and reducing 
weight loss. The findings also highlight that 100-
150 ppm ethylene treated mangoes may provide 
an optimal balance, enhancing sweetness and 
preserving nutrients while minimizing weight loss, 
making it suitable for managing postharvest quality. 
This ripening chamber is convenient for semi-
commercial purpose to ripen matured fruits safe and 
maintaining uniformity for large amount at a time. 
At least 290 tons of fruits need to ripe to return back 
money within 16 months.

Shelf-life study of Foxtail Millet fortified 
Sourdough bread at different storage 
temperatures
P. Sen, M. H. H. Khan, M. M. Rahman, M.G.F. 
Chowdhury, M.M. Molla, S. Pervin And B.C. Dey
This study evaluated the shelf-life stability of 
foxtail millet fortified sourdough bread stored under 
different temperature conditions: ambient, freezing 
(-5±2°C), refrigeration (4±2°C), (26±2°C) winter-
considering, and (37±2°C) summer-considering. 
Foxtail millet sourdough bread was prepared and 
packaged in parchment paper to prevent direct 
moisture exchange with the environment. It was 
observed that the acidity of foxtail millet sourdough 
bread increased during storage, while pH declined. At 
ambient conditions, pH dropped from 5.44 ± 0.03 on 
Day 0 to 4.65 ± 0.03 on Day 4. Similarly, at summer-
simulated conditions (37 ± 2 °C), pH decreased 
from 5.37 ± 0.04 to 4.70 ± 0.06. Freezing (−5±2°C) 
and refrigeration (4±2°C) slowed acidification, 
maintaining higher pH values. The outcome 
aligns with studies on sourdough fermentation, 
which indicate that higher temperatures generally 
favor faster microbial growth, resulting in higher 
acidification. The moisture content also increased 
at both ambient and winter temperatures, with a 
notable increase from 23.72±0.191 to 27.13±0.347 
at ambient temperature on day 4. Conversely, there 
was a decrease in the moisture content in the freezing 
(-5±2°C) and refrigerated (4±2°C) conditions. This 
suggests that both higher temperatures accelerated 
moisture retention as well as low temperatures acted 
to facilitate water loss due to the inactive status of 
microbes and enzymes at low temperatures. The 
texture also increased significantly from 92.89 at Day 
0 to 127.70 at Day 4 (-5±2°C). Freezing may form 
ice crystals, causing physical changes and firmer 
bread. Storage temperature exerted a significant 
influence on the physicochemical stability of foxtail 
millet fortified sourdough bread. Ambient and 
summer conditions promoted rapid acidification, pH 
decline, softening of texture, and color deterioration. 
Refrigeration provided partial preservation, whereas 
freezing at -5±2°C most effectively maintained 
acidity, pH, texture, and color stability. Therefore, 
freezing represents the optimal storage condition for 
extending the shelf life of foxtail millet sourdough 
bread.
Effect of coatings on the physicochemical 
properties of air fried Jackfruit chips
P. Sen, M. H. H. Khan, M. M. Rahman, M.G.F. 
Chowdhury, M.M. Molla, S. Pervin, B.C. Dey
This study investigated the impact of different 
coatings: rice flour, corn flour, maltodextrin, 
and sugar flour; on various physicochemical 
properties of air fried jackfruit chips. In this study, 
physiologically matured khaja-type jackfruits 
(BARI Kathal-2) were procured, peeled, decored, 
and sliced into 5 mm strips, then frozen at -18°C 
for 24-48 h. The slices were coated by dipping in 
10% solutions of rice flour, corn flour, maltodextrin, 
and sugar flour for 30 min, followed by blanching 
and then drying to reduce initial moisture. Moisture 
content was observed to be higher in the coated 
treatments compared to the raw jackfruit. The raw 
jackfruit had a moisture content of 2.99%, while the 
maltodextrin-coated jackfruit exhibited the highest 
moisture retention at 6.77%. Air frying is known 
to remove less moisture than traditional frying, 
thereby better preserving moisture and reducing oil 
absorption-this combination keeps chips less dry 
and potentially softer in texture. Coating with corn 
flour yielded higher TSS (4.4°Brix), most likely 
due to the concentration of soluble solids in the 
retained moisture fraction. maltodextrin was lowest 
(2.13°Brix), possibly because maltodextrin itself 
does not contribute appreciable soluble sugars and 
may dilute extractable fruit solids. Air-fried jackfruit 
chips showed significantly reduced fat content with 
sugar flour (5.48%), followed by corn flour coating 
(7.70%), compared to the control (9.54%). This 
indicates that flour-based coatings, can effectively

Postharvest Technology I 323
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
lower oil absorption during air frying. The greatest 
breaking force (24.55 N) for the most complex 
structure (rice flour) may result from a crusted 
and structured uniform crust of gelatinized paste 
during hot air frying. Corn flour provided for a 
softer (11.75 N). Air frying-with high-velocity hot 
air-encourages rapid crust formation, and coatings 
like corn flour can enhance crispness. Corn flour's 
higher starch content leads to decreased moisture 
retention within the chip's coating, which results in 
a crispier texture after frying. The control appears 
as the lightest sample (highest L*), which is to be 
expected since the sample of non-coated jackfruit 
was used. The rice flour and corn flour coatings 
cause a moderate lightness reduction, probably 
due to the pacification (rice starch-based) or the 
color of the corn flour. Matter of corn flour coatings 
is beneficial in retention of these constituents, 
primarily because of the protective matrix and 
pigment sources in the corn. Maltodextrin alone as 
a coating may lower the extraction and retention 
values, unless combined with other substances, such 
as gum arabic, for improved encapsulation. Rice and 
sugar flour-coatings have lower retention caused by 
their surface characteristics and composition 
The edible coatings significantly changed the 
physicochemical and nutritional characteristics of 
air-fried jackfruit chips. Corn flour was the most 
effective, providing crisp texture and better retention 
of bioactive compounds, while maltodextrin 
enhanced moisture retention and crispy texture but 
lowered antioxidant extractability. In contrast, rice 
flour and sugar flour coatings resulted in inferior 
texture and lower nutrient retention and higher fat 
reduction.
Standardizations of mixed foxtail millet-Jackfruit 
sourdough bread
P. Sen, M. H. H. Khan, M. M. Rahman, M.G.F. 
Chowdhury, M.M. Molla, S. Pervin, B.C. Dey
This study evaluated the impact of incorporating 
jackfruit and foxtail millet flour on the 
physicochemical, functional, and nutritional 
qualities of sourdough bread. 
BARI Kaun-4 was collected and de-husked to 
prepare flour. BARI Kathal-2 jackfruits were 
peeled, decored, and dried at 65°C to make flour. 
Six treatments were prepared: T 0: Wheat flour 
(100); T 1: Millet Flour : Jackfruit Flour (0:100); 
T2: Millet Flour : Jackfruit Flour (25:75); T 3: Millet 
Flour : Jackfruit Flour (50:50); T 4: Millet Flour : 
Jackfruit Flour (75:25); T 5: Millet Flour : Jackfruit 
Flour (100:0). Moisture content of the prepared 
bread samples ranged from 18.45% to 27.31%, with 
the highest value observed in the jackfruit-based 
formulation (T1) and the lowest in the 100% wheat 
bread (T0). Similarly, total soluble solids (TSS) were 
highest in jackfruit formulations. The higher MC 
and TSS in jackfruit-rich breads can be attributed 
to their soluble fibre and sugar content, which 
increases water retention. In contrast, millet-rich 
blends showed lower MC due to the lower solubility 
of millet proteins. The pH values remained stable 
across treatments (5.41-5.49), confirming a slightly 
acidic nature, while titratable acidity was higher 
in millet-rich blends (T 4, T5). The acidic nature of 
millet can be attributed to the phenolic acids and 
fermentable carbohydrates naturally present in the 
grain. Texture analysis showed hardness ranging 
from 84.93 N (T 0) to 133.79 N (T 3). Composite 
flour blends (T1- T3) showed firmer textures than the 
control, likely due to gluten dilution and restricted 
gas retention for jackfruit flour. Moreover, higher 
levels of millet flour (T 4 and T 5) reduced hardness 
slightly compared to T 2 and T 3, likely due to 
improvements in water retention and the softening 
of the crumb resulting from the increased fibre 
and soluble sugars. Colour analysis indicated that 
lightness decreased in millet-rich blends (T3 = 74.39 
vs. T0 = 87.52), while jackfruit contributed to higher 
yellowness due to carotenoids and slightly elevated 
redness. Specific volume ranged 1110 to 1200 cm3 
and inversely tracked loaf density (8.29 to 11.86 g/
in3). The lowest volume and highest density were 
observed with 100% jackfruit within the blend 
(T1), indicating weaker gas retention due to gluten 
dilution and interference with the gluten network 
by fibre and pectin. By contrast, 100% millet within 
the blend (T 5) restored volume to the control level 
(1200 cm3) and yielded a low density (8.39 g in−3), 
suggesting better gas cell stabilization than jackfruit 
and a less disruptive interaction with the gluten 
matrix. Higher jackfruit ratios resulted in the lowest 
baking loss, at 8.85%. Millet-rich loaves (T 4- T 5) 
exhibited greater baking loss (~20-21%) along 
with higher specific volume, as grater expansion is 
accompanied by higher moisture loss during baking. 
This study showed that millet flour contributed more 
favorably to the physical and functional quality of

324 I Postharvest Technology
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
composite breads compared to jackfruit flour. Millet-
rich formulations exhibited higher specific volume, 
lower loaf density, and improved phenolic content, 
enhancing both texture and bioactive properties. 
In contrast, jackfruit flour increased carotenoid 
levels but compromised loaf structure due to gluten 
dilution and reduced gas retention. Overall, millet 
flour proved to be a more effective ingredient for 
improving bread quality.

Effect of blanching on the quality and shelf life of 
green chili
S. PERVIN, M.M. Molla. M. A. Hossain, M.G.F. 
Chowdhury, M. M. Rahman
This study investigated the effects of blanching 
(0, 20, 40, and 60 seconds) and low-temperature 
preservation on the quality and shelf life of Jamalpur 
and BARI Morich-4 varieties. Those chilies were 
then blanched in hot water for 60 0C, according to 
different treatments and immediately cooled. After 
blanching and cooling, the chilies were packed in 
high-density polyethylene (HDPE) bags and stored 
at refrigerator for a duration of 8 months. Six 
treatment groups, T 1 = No blanching of Jamalpur 
Chili; T2 = No blanching of BARI Morich-4; T 3 = 
Blanching @ 20 S of Jamalpur Chili; T4 = Blanching 
@ 20 S of BARI Morich-4; T 5 = Blanching @ 40 S 
of Jamalpur Chili; T6 = Blanching @ 40 S of BARI 
Morich-4; T7 = Blanching @ 60 S of Jamalpur Chili; 
and T8 = Blanching @ 60 S of BARI Morich-4 were 
conducted. Vitamin C content declined steadily in 
all treatments during storage. Fresh Jamalpur and 
BARI Morich-4 initially contained 83.0 and 90.0 
mg/100g, but decreased to 12.5 and 13.0 mg/100g 
after 8 months. Blanching for 20 seconds was 
most effective, with BARI Morich-4 retaining 16.0 
mg/100g. Longer blanching times (40-60 s) caused 
greater losses, though still better than unblanched 
samples. Overall, short-time blanching combined 
with low-temperature storage minimized nutrient 
degradation. The decline in vitamin C is linked to 
oxidation, enzymatic activity, and thermal damage, 
with brief blanching reducing enzymatic losses 
while excessive heating accelerates degradation. 
Total phenol content declined during storage 
across all treatments. Unblanched Jamalpur BARI 
Morich-4 decreased from 9.8 to 4.0 and 8.4 to 3.6 
mg GAE/100g, respectively. Blanching for 20 
seconds showed better retention, with Jamalpur Chili 
maintaining 5.1 mg/100g after 8 months, compared 
to 3.4 mg/100g in BARI Morich-4 blanched for 60 
seconds. Lycopene content decreased over storage 
but was better preserved with blanching. Unblanched 
Jamalpur and BARI Morich-4 declined from 67 to 
18 and 84 to 32 μg/100g, respectively. Blanching 
for 20 seconds gave the best retention, with BARI 
Morich-4 maintaining 41 μg/100g after 8 months. 
Declines result from oxidation and isomerization, 
while blanching reduces enzyme-driven degradation. 
On the other hand, β-carotene declined in all 
treatments during storage. Fresh BARI Morich-4 
dropped from 88.93 to 31.20 μg/100g unblanched, 
while 20-second blanching best preserved content 
(28.87 μg/100g). Longer blanching caused greater 
losses but remained superior to unblanched 
samples. Investigated enzyme inactivation time of 
chili (blanching temperature 60±1°C and time 60 
sec) with six months storage was found suitable. 
Therefore, chili can be stored at home refrigerator 
using the above blanching condition for six months.
Drying kinetics and rehydration behavior of 
BARI Tomato-14
S. Pervin, M. A. Hossain, M.M. Molla. M.G.F. 
Chowdhury, M. M. Rahman, B.C. Dey
This study evaluated the drying kinetics and 
rehydration behavior of BARI Tomato-14 using a 
cabinet dryer at three temperatures such as 55°C, 
65°C, and 75°C. Moisture ratio (MR) decreased with 
time at all temperatures, with higher temperatures 
accelerating drying rates. Fresh BARI tomato-14 
were collected and then blanched in hot water at 
800C for 2 min. After blanching, the tomatoes were 
sliced and ground into fine powder and packed 
in high-density polyethylene bags and stored at 
ambient temperature for a duration of 6 months. 
The experiment involved three treatment groups: 
T1=blanched tomato dried at 55°C, T 2=blanched 
tomato dried at 65°C, and T3=blanched tomato dried 
at 75°C. The tomatoes were dried in a Mummert 
dryer at three different temperatures (55°C, 65°C 
and 75°C) with single layer of material. It was 
observed that the moisture ratio (MR) decreased 
with time and the time to dry at a specific moisture 
ratio decreased with increasing temperature. At very 
high temperature and low humidity drying rate may 
initially increase, but the resulting case hardening 
would reduce the drying rate significantly and the 
product quality would be degraded by boiling 
instead of drying. The tomato dried very quickly at

326 I Postharvest Technology
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
a temperature of 75oC. It was observed that for dried 
BARI tomato-14 (5 g samples), rehydration after 
30 min varied slightly with temperature treatments. 
Blanched tomato reached 20.45 g (rehydration 
ratio, RR = 4.00), T 2 gave 19.87 g (RR = 3.97), 
and T3 yielded 19.59 g (RR = 3.92). Corresponding 
dehydration ratios (DR) were 0.36, 0.35, and 0.34, 
yielding coefficients of reconstitution (RR/DR) 
of 11.11, 11.34, and 11.53, respectively. Drying 
temperature strongly affected BARI Tomato-14. 
Higher temperatures (75°C) reduced drying time 
but slightly lowered rehydration due to structural 
damage. 
Processing and preservation of fermented miso 
soup
S. Pervin, M.M. Molla , A. Shimizu, M. Afroz, P. 
Sen
The study aimed to prepare fermented miso soup 
using different cereal-legume combinations. 
The BARI Barley-9 and BARI Soyabean-6 rice 
were collected and rice, mash dal and Mung dal 
were purchased. Six treatments such as T 1 (50% 
Barley+50% Soybean); T2 (50% Barley+50% Mash 
dal); T 3 (50% Barley+50% Mug dal); T 4 (50% 
Rice+50% Soybean); T5 (50% Rice+50% Mash dal); 
and T6 (50% Rice+50% Mug dal). In preparing the 
miso paste (fermented base), soybeans, Mung dal, 
and mash dal (black gram) were soaked overnight, 
while barley was soaked for 6-8 hours. The soybeans 
were then boiled until soft (about 2-3 hours), and the 
Mung dal, mash dal, and barley were lightly boiled 
until tender but not mushy. The cooked barley was 
mixed with Aspergillus oryzae spores (koji mold) and 
incubated for up to 48 hours at 30 °C until fragrant. 
Afterwards, the boiled soybeans and cooked Mung 
dal were mashed and combined with the koji barley. 
Salt (12-15%) was added, and the mixture was 
packed tightly into sterilized containers, pressed to 
remove air, and covered. Fermentation was carried 
out at room temperature for 3-6 months, with 
longer fermentation resulting in deeper flavor. pH of 
fermented miso soup declined during six months of 
storage. At the start, pH ranged from 6.33 (T4) to 6.57 
(T3). By the sixth month, it dropped to 5.08-5.46. 
Barley-soybean (T 1) showed the sharpest decline, 
while rice-mug dal (T6) retained slightly higher pH 
values. Overall, soybean-based treatments exhibited 
faster acidification compared to dal-based ones. 
Variations depend on raw material composition, 
as soybeans promote stronger acid formation than 
dals, and barley enhances fermentation more than 
rice. Moisture content increased progressively 
throughout storage. Initially, values ranged from 
63.67% (T 4) to 74.66% (T 3). By six months, they 
rose to 67.76%-78.35%. Barley-based treatments 
(T2, T 3) maintained higher moisture compared to 
rice-based ones, while soybean mixtures had lower 
moisture levels than dal mixtures. Moisture rise 
occurs due to enzymatic breakdown of starches 
and proteins, releasing bound water. Water activity 
(aw) increased steadily over storage. At start of the 
experiment, water activity values ranged between 
0.45 (T 6) and 0.50 (T 1). By the sixth month, they 
reached 0.68-0.73. Barley-soybean (T 1) showed 
the highest a w, while rice-Mung dal (T 6) remained 
the lowest. Barley-based treatments consistently 
maintained higher a w compared to rice-based 
ones. Variations among treatments are due to raw 
material differences; barley and soy promote higher 
solubilization, while rice and dal mixtures release 
relatively less free water. Fermented miso soup 
showed decreasing pH and increasing moisture 
and a w during storage, influenced by ingredient 
composition. Barley-soybean combinations 
promoted greater acidification and higher water 
activity, suggesting better fermentation activity, 
while rice-based mixtures maintained relatively 
higher stability.

Storability of watermelon pulp for retaining 
bioactive compounds during ambient storage
M. M. Rahman, M.G.F. Chowdhury, M.M. Molla, 
M. A. Hossain, M. H. H. Khan
The objective of this study was to evaluate the 
storage stability of watermelon pulp, rich in 
lycopene and β-carotene, for its potential diversified 
applications. Red flesh watermelon (Citrullus 
lanatus) was purchased and peeled off by stainless 
steel knife. Seed-free watermelon slices were 
blended to obtain fresh pulp and treatments were: 
10% sugar, 15% sugar, 20% sugar, 25% sugar, 30% 
sugar and 35% sugar. The pulp was slowly heated 
at 80-90 °C and concentrated to approximately 
15°Brix. Xanthan gum powder, pre-mixed with 
an equal quantity of sugar, was added gradually 
and homogenized. The pulp was heated to reach 
23-27 °Brix. Color measurements of the pulp 
showed no significant variation among treatments 
or compared to the fresh pulp, suggesting that 
color was stable during storage. The pH of the 
fresh watermelon pulp was 6.95, reflecting its 
low acidity. The addition of citric acid (0.5%) 
successfully reduced the pH to around 4.5, ensuring 
a moderately acidic environment that is more 
suitable for preservation. The pH values remained 
relatively stable across treatments with only minor 
variations throughout the storage period. Similarly, 
the total soluble solids remained consistent 
between treatments, with no marked differences 
observed between 10% sugar supplementation and 
20% sugar supplementation. This indicates that 
no significant sugar conversion occurred during 
storage. In contrast, the phytochemical compounds 
lycopene and β-carotene showed a gradual decline 
compared to the fresh pulp. However, among the 
treatments, 10% sugar supplementation exhibited 
the best retention of both lycopene and β-carotene, 
suggesting that lower sugar concentration favored 
the preservation of these bioactive compounds. 
Watermelon pulp supplemented with 10% sugar, 
along with the required stabilizing ingredients, can 
be safely preserved under ambient conditions (29-
38 °C, 75-92% RH) for up to six months.
Efficacy of clove essential oil and carnauba wax 
in extending shelf life of Mango
M. M. Rahman, M.G.F. Chowdhury, M. A. Hossain, 
M.H. H. Khan
The study evaluated the effectiveness of clove 
essential oil and carnauba wax coating in controlling 
stem-end rot and anthracnose of mango, caused by 
Botryodiplodia theobromae and Colletotrichum 
gloeosporioides, respectively, with the aim of 
extending fruit shelf life. Mango cv. BARI Aam-3 
(Amrapali) was collected. Clove essential oil (EO) 
was extracted using a steam distillation apparatus. 
Ethanol (Absolute GR, Merck), Triton X-100, 
Thiabendazole fungicide, and calcinated calcium 
(EcoWashTM) were obtained. Surface-sterilized 
fruits were placed in a rotating wax-coating 
machine. Clove EO (1 mL L−1), premixed with 
ethanol (1 mL L−1) as a stabilizer and Triton X-100 
(40 mg L−1) as a surfactant, was applied by hand 
spraying. Immediately after, carnauba wax coating 
was sprayed onto the fruits. Treated mangoes were 
placed in plastic foam cup liners, dried under a fan 
for 1-1.5 hours, and then transferred to a constant 
temperature and humidity chamber. Clove essential 
oil (EO) extracted by steam distillation yielded 
approximately 5% oil. Mangoes treated with the 
combination of clove EO and carnauba wax showed 
the highest shelf life, with no rotting observed 
after 30 days of storage at 10 ± 2 °C and 85-95% 
RH. In comparison, control fruits exhibited 83.7% 
rotting, while fungicide-treated fruits had 53.3% 
rotting. Firmness of EO + carnauba-treated mangoes 
remained significantly higher (51.29 N) at 30 days, 
compared to control (22.73 N) and fungicide-treated 
fruits (25.87 N), indicating better textural retention. 
Total soluble solids in EO-treated fruits were lower 
(18.35 °Brix) than in control and fungicide-treated 
fruits, suggesting slower sugar conversion and 
delayed ripening. Bioactive compounds were also 
better retained in EO + carnauba-treated mangoes. 
β-Carotene content remained higher (93.20 μg/100 
g) compared to control (120.68 μg/100 g) and 
fungicide-treated fruits (30.54 μg/100 g), while 
antioxidant activity (38.09 μg/100 g) was maintained 
more effectively than in controls (34.63 μg/100 g). 
In the sensory triangle test, only 7 of 35 panelists 
correctly identified treated fruits, below the 16 
required for significance (p = 0.05), indicating that 
EO and wax coating did not adversely affect taste.

Postharvest Technology I 331
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
These findings suggest that clove EO combined 
with carnauba wax is effective in extending shelf 
life, maintaining quality, and preserving bioactive 
compounds in mangoes during cold storage. Clove 
EO in combination with carnauba wax coating 
effectively reduced postharvest fungal infestation 
and extended the shelf life of mangoes for 30 days 
at 10±2 °C, followed by 7 days of acclimatization 
at 25±3°C for marketing. The in vitro pathogenicity 
test of the stem end rot and anthracnose will be 
evaluated next year.
Shelf-life extension of fresh Guava fruits through 
postharvest treatments 
M. M. Rahman, M. A. Hossain, M. H. H. Khan
The study evaluated the effects of gibberellic acid 
(GA3) and cling wrap packaging on the quality and 
shelf life of guava. Commercially mature guava 
(Psidium guajava L.) 'BARI Peyara-2' commonly 
known as "Thai Peyara" was obtained and were 
dipped in gibberellic acid (GA3) solutions at 400, 
600, and 800 ppm for 10 minutes. After dipping, 
fruits were air-dried for 30 minutes and then 
wrapped with cling film (cellophane). All fruits 
were placed in plastic foam cup liners and stored 
at 6±2°C and 80-90% relative humidity. Treatment 
with gibberellic acid (GA3) combined with cling 
wrap significantly slowed firmness loss. After 21 
days, firmness of treated fruits ranged 103.0-108.1 
N, whereas control fruits reached 64.5 N by 14 days. 
No significant differences were observed among 
GA3 concentrations, indicating effective softening 
inhibition across tested doses. TSS, ascorbic acid, 
and β-carotene were better maintained in treated 
fruits. TSS remained 9-9.5% compared to 11.4% 
in controls, indicating slower sugar accumulation. 
Vitamin C retention ranged 101-106 mg/100 g vs 
89.7 mg/100 g in controls, while total carotenoids 
were 6.59-7.14 μg/100 g compared to 5.34 μg/100 
g, demonstrating preservation of nutritional quality. 
Overall, GA3 combined with cling wrap effectively 
extends guava shelf life while preserving firmness, 
nutritional content, and overall quality, providing 
a practical postharvest strategy for this climacteric 
fruit. Gibberellic acid treatment combined with cling 
wrap effectively extended the shelf life of guava at 
6±2°C and 80-90% relative humidity for 21 days 
with maintaining firmness, nutritional quality, and 
bioactive compounds.

Varietal improvement of oyster mushroom 
(Pleurotus sp.) through induced variation
S. Yesmin, K. Nahar and M. M. Khatun
The study examined the effects of gamma radiation 
on dikaryotic and monokaryotic mycelia, as well as 
spore suspension, of oyster mushroom (Pleurotus 
ostreatus, PO2). In all cases, the treatments 
produced thick white cottony mycelia. In 
dikaryotic cultures, the control condition showed 
the highest growth (2.54 cm) after 7 days, whereas 
irradiated treatments (100-1000 Gy) resulted in 
reduced growth (1.35-0.34 cm). Mycelial growth 
decreased progressively with increasing radiation 
dose, with complete mycelial coverage achieved 
within 9-11 days at 100-1000 Gy. No growth was 
observed at higher doses (1500-3000 Gy), even 
after 11 days. Similar trends were observed in 
monokaryotic mycelia, where the control exhibited 
the highest growth (4.61 cm) after 7 days, while 
treatment at 100 Gy also supported considerable 
growth (4.18 cm). Growth was progressively 
reduced (3.64-2.33 cm) at doses of 200-1000 Gy. 
In spore suspension experiments, germination was 
observed only at 200 Gy, while other treatments 
were contaminated when spread on PDA medium; 
therefore, the experiment needs to be repeated for 
confirmation. Overall, the findings suggest that 
lower gamma doses (100-1000 Gy) permit limited 
growth, whereas higher doses (1500-3000 Gy) 
completely inhibit the mycelial development of 
Pleurotus ostreatus (PO2).
In vitro conservation of mycelia of oyster 
mushroom (Pleurotus sp.) 
S. Yesmin, M. K. Hasan and M. M. Khatun
This study evaluated the effectiveness of three 
preservation methods-periodical subculture (PS), 
sterile distilled water (SDW), and sterile paraffin 
oil (PO)-on the long-term viability of three oyster 
mushroom (Pleurotus sp.) species OS, POP, WS 
respectively. Mycelial growth was measured on 
potato dextrose agar (PDA) plates after 3, 6, 12, 
15, 18, and 24 months of storage. Results showed 
that the WS variety preserved in SDW exhibited 
the highest regrowth (~4.0 cm), followed by WS 
and OS preserved by PS and PO, which maintained 
moderate growth (~2.5-3.5 cm). In contrast, POP 
culture lost viability rapidly under all preservation 
conditions, showing negligible regrowth beyond 6 
months. These findings highlight varietal differences 
in preservation response and suggest that SDW 
is a highly effective method for the long-term 
maintenance of WS, while alternative strategies are 
needed for POP.

Morpho-molecular characterization of 
blackgram germplasm
K. Nahar, Kamrun Nahar (Ph.D Student), M. N. 
Amin, M. A. Y . Akhond
Characterization of crop diversity panels enables the 
identification of genetic variation and markers linked 
to target traits relevant for breeding. Bangladesh 
harbors a wide range of blackgram (Vigna 
mungo L.) germplasm, much of which remains 
uncharacterized at the molecular level. In this study, 
DArTseq technology was employed to evaluate 
the genetic diversity of 92 blackgram accessions 
collected from diverse regions of Bangladesh. The 
objectives were to screen germplasm for drought 
tolerance at the seedling stage under PEG-induced 
stress and to identify genetic markers associated 
with drought tolerance through genome-wide 
association study (GWAS). Population structure 
analysis revealed five major groups, consistent with 
the clustering pattern obtained from dendrogram 
analysis. DArTseq genotyping identified 278,618 
single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) aligned to 
the blackgram reference genome. These SNPs were 
utilized in GWAS, which detected 25 novel SNP 
markers significantly associated with 4 drought-
related traits. The findings contribute to the growing 
pool of phenotypic and genotypic data on blackgram, 
providing a valuable foundation for conservation, 
management, and genetic improvement strategies, 
as well as for the development of efficient breeding 
programs aimed at expanding crop cultivation.

Susceptibility of Leucinodes orbonalis Guenee 
populations to the cry1 ac protein 
M. Z. H. Prodhan, M. K. Hasan and N. Z. Bristy
Studies were carried out to determine the 
susceptibility of the brinjal fruit and shoot borer, 
Leucinodes orbonalis (Guenée) to Cry1Ac protein 
of Bacillus thuringiensis by a diet incorporation 
method for the populations collected from ten 
different brinjal growing areas of Bangladesh during 
2024. Leucinodes orbonalis larvae were reared to 
adults on a semi-synthetic diet and were allowed 
to mate using standardized rearing techniques in 
the laboratory at Agricultural Research Station, 
BARI, Pabna, Bangladesh. Eggs were collected 
from the mating cages were allowed to hatch and 
neonates emerged from these eggs were used for 
bioassay. The bioassay was performed with different 
concentration as of the Cry1Ac protein along with 
an untreated control to determine their susceptibility 
level. Median lethal concentrations (LC 50) ranged 
between 0.02 and 0.09 ppm and Moult inhibitory 
concentration (MIC50) values for L. orbonalis ranged 
from 0.01 to 0.03 ppm. Variation in susceptibility 
amongst field populations was 4.5-fold for LC50 and 
3.00 -fold for MIC 50. These values can be used for 
resistance monitoring.

Nanoscale zinc oxide particles for improving 
yield and quality of tomato
h. M. Naser, S. Sultana, M. Akter, M. B. Banu and 
M. R. Khatun
A field experiment was carried out to study the 
effectiveness of soil and foliar application of Zn on 
the yield of tomato. The micronutrients - zinc (Zn) 
in the form of zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoparticles (NPs) 
and zinc sulphate heptahydrates (ZnSO4.7H2O) were 
applied as foliar and basal on the yield of tomato. 
Zinc supplied to the soil boosted yields, however 
they were lower than Zn nutrients foliar applied 
either ZnO nanoparticles or ZnSO 4, 7H 2O. The 
increments of yield were 9.47 to 56.0; 12.8 to 36.0 
and 9.43 to 23.7%, respectively over control, foliar 
application of ZnO nanoparticles and soil application 
of ZnSO 4, 7H 2O. The treatment with 15 ppm of 
ZnO nanoparticles produced the highest levels of 
TSS (5.10 °Brix), vitamin C (32.3 mg 100g -1) and 
β carotene (22.3 mg 100g -1). Nanotechnology has 
provided better results than conventional method.

This study evaluates unmanned aerial vehicle

imagery was acquired from bare soil plots over 
two seasons. Twenty-four spectral indices were 
calculated and used to cluster plot data, which

342 I Soil Management

most nutrients except OM, N, S, and B. The best-

Effect of microbial amended organic fertilizers 
on yield and quality of broccoli
Marufa Sultana, M M Masud, M S Islam and H M 
Naser
Excessive use of synthetic fertilizers degrades soil 
and increases nitrate accumulation in vegetables like 
broccoli, posing health risks. This study, conducted at 
SSD, BARI, Gazipur, evaluated microbial-amended 
organic fertilizers on broccoli (var. Hybrid EARLY 
YOU). Six nutrient packages were tested: 100% 
chemical fertilizer, 80% chemical fertilizer, 80%

Effect of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and 
phosphorus on onion
M. M. E. Ali, A. Barman, M. Rahman, M.B. Banu 
and H.M Naser
A field experiment was conducted at Central Farm, 
Soil Science Division, Bangladesh Agricultural 
Research Institute, Gazipur during Rabi season of 
2024-2025 with the objectives to study the effect 
of combined use of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi 
and phosphorus on growth and yield of onion, 
and to reduce to the use of P-fertilizer under field 
condition. The experiment was designed in factorial 
RCBD with eight treatments and four replications. 
The onion variety was BARI Piaj-4 as test crop. Soil 
based arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) inoculum and 
infected root pieces of the host plant were used at 
the rate of 1 kg soil m -2 in seedbed for producing 
onionseedlings. The treatment combinations were: 
T1P1U: 0% P × without AM, T2P2U: 50% P × without 
AM, T3P3U: 100% P × without AM, T4P1AM: 0% P × 
with AM, T5P2AM: 50% P × with AM and T6P3AM: 
100% P × with AM. Mycorrhizal inoculation 
significantly increased plant height (cm), bulb 
height (cm) and bulb yield (t ha-1). Root length (cm), 
and curd circumferences (cm) were non-significant. 
The plant that received AM in nursery bed produced 
higher bulb yield than without AM in all phosphorus 
levels of onion. The highest onion bulb yield 14.84 t 
ha-1 was recorded in 50% P with AM (AM was used 
in nursery bed) in Madhupur Tract soil (AEZ 28). 
The result indicates that inoculation of AM used in 
nursery bed can save 50% P in the field. The plant 
which did not receive AM in nursery bed produced 
lower yield in all phosphorus levels in the field.

Strategic tillage options and integrated nutrient 
inputs on soil enzyme activity and nutrient 
bioavailability in field pea-okra-t. Aman cropping 
systems
M.S. Islam, S. Brahma, R.S. Smriti, and H.M. Naser
Conventional tillage practices and prolonged 
reliance on chemical fertilizers often disrupt 
microbial communities, enzymatic activity, and 
nutrient bioavailability, which can hinder soil health 
and crop productivity. While conservation tillage 
combined with integrated nutrient management 
has shown potential in addressing these challenges 
globally, its application in the grey terrace soils of 
Bangladesh remains largely underexplored. This 
study investigates the effects of two tillage methods 
conventional and conservation and four Integrated 
Plant Nutrition System (IPNS) treatments: (i) 100% 
chemical fertilizers, (ii) 20% RDCF + 80% compost, 
(iii) 40% RDCF + 60% compost, and (iv) 60% RDCF 
+ 40% compost, on microbial indices, enzymatic 
activity, nutrient bioavailability, and the productivity 
of a pea-okra T. aman cropping sequence. A split-
plot design was used to evaluate these variables. 
The results revealed significant improvements in 
microbial indices, with 11% higher dehydrogenase 
activity (DH), 4% greater organic carbon, and 15% 
more total nitrogen in strip tillage compared to 
conventional tillage, contributing to a higher field 
pea yield by 9.18%, 16.4%, and 16.9% in the F 2, 
F3, and F 4 nutrient inputs, respectively, compared 
to those receiving only chemical fertilizers. Off 
the treatment, strip tillage with F 4 showed superior 
result at par to F3 over chemical fertilizer. However, 
after the fourth cropping, the higher soil density 
in strip tillage resulted in a 14% reduction in okra 
yield, highlighting the need for careful management 
of soil compaction over time. The findings suggest 
that conservation tillage, combined with appropriate 
nutrient management, is essential for sustainable 
soil health and crop yield. 
Role of organic amendment on improvement 
of nitrogen use efficiency in grey terrace soil in 
spinach
R.S. Smriti, S. Bramah, A.T.M.A.I. Mondol, M.S. 
Islam and H.M. NASER
A pot experiment was conducted at the net house of 
SSD, BARI, Gazipur, under AEZ-28 during the rabi 
seasons of 2023-24 & 2024-25 to observe the impact 
of organic amendments on soil physico-chemical 
properties and nitrogen (N) use efficiency in spinach 
cultivation. Six treatments were applied: T 1-80% 
Recommended Dose of Chemical Fertilizer (RDCF) 
+20% RDCF from cowdung (CD); T 2- 60% RDCF 
+ 40% RDCF from CD; T 3- 40% RDCF + 60% 
RDCF from CD; T4- 20% RDCF + 80% RDCF from 
CD; T5- 100% CD; and T6- 100% RDCF as control, 
with three replications in a CRD. Results showed 
that organic amendments substantially improved 
soil properties and crop performance. Among the

yield (19.53 t ha−1) and nitrogen use efficiency 
(45.6%). Conversely, T5 (100% cowdung) improved 
soil properties but recorded the lowest yield (7.39 
t ha−1). These findings suggest that combination of 
organic and inorganic fertilizers, particularly at a 
60:40 ratio, enhances soil fertility, crop yield, and 
nitrogen efficiency in spinach cultivation.

greater than conventional tillage), while WHM

increased yield by 24.1% compared to no mulch.

productivity in terrace soils.

Requirement of potassium fertilizer under 
conservation agriculture practice in wheat-
mungbean-T. Aman cropping system
N Salahin, Nu Mahmud and Ku Ahammad
A four-year field experiment, spanning from 2021-
2022 to 2024-2025, at RARS, Jashore, evaluated 
potassium (K) fertilizer rates under two crop 
establishment methods: T 1 (conventional tillage, 
residue removal) and T 2 (conservation agriculture 
with minimal tillage and residue retention). Four K
