5.23 t ha-1 for wheat, raising system productivity to 
17.8 t ha-1year-1. After four years, CA improved soil 
organic matter, total nitrogen, and available K. 
Effect of long-term fertilization on crop 
productivity, soil properties and nutrient use 
efficiency under conservation agriculture practice 
with mustard-boro-t. Aman cropping pattern
N Salahin, Nu Mahmud and Ku Ahammad
A four-year study (from 2021-2022 to 2024-
2025) assessed chemical fertilizer impacts on 
crop yield, soil health, and nutrient use efficiency 
under conservation agriculture (CA) in a Mustard-
Boro-T. Aman rotation. Two methods were 
compared: T1 (conventional) and T2 (CA), with four 
fertilizer levels (N 1: 75%, N 2: 100%, N 3: 125% of

methods produced more rice, while CA enhanced 
mustard yield due to better soil moisture retention.

increased mustard yield, rice equivalent yield, and 
nutrient use efficiency. After four years, CA plots 
showed improved soil organic matter, total nitrogen, 
and potassium over conventional plots.

The experiment was carried out at the research

spinosad (Success 2.5 SC) @ 1.2 ml/L of water; 
T5= Farmers' practice: Spraying of chlorpyrifos + 
cypermethrin (Nitro 505 EC) @ 1.0 ml/L of water; 
T6= Untreated control.
The results indicated that T 3 i.e. spraying of 
Spinetoram (Delegate 11.7 SC) @ 1 ml/l of water 
offered significantly the highest reduction (86.35 
%) of larval population of DBM over control and

angulatus (Bio Chamak 1.0% EW) @ 2.0 ml/L of 
water (78.25%). The highest marketable yield (54.72 
t/ha) was also obtained from spraying of spinetoram 
followed by spraying Celastrus angulatus (51.24 
t/ ha).

Survey on the abundance of natural enemies 
of rugose spiralling whitefly, aleurodicus 
rugioperculatus attacking coconut in Bangladesh
K. Begum, N. K. Dutta, A. K. M. R. H. Ferdous, M. 
K. Uddin, M. A. Sarkar and F. Yasmin
Field surveys were conducted in Manikganj, 
Kishoreganj, Pabna, Khulna, Sylhet, Cumilla and 
Chapainawabganj districts to identify and assess the 
abundance of natural enemies of rugose spiralling 
whitefly attacking coconut crop during June 2024 
to April 2025. In each location, five infested plants 
were selected for collecting natural enemies. Each 
plant was considered as a treatment replicate. 
From each plant, 20 severely infested leaflets were 
collected with different life stages of parasitoids 
and predators kept in polythene bags, brought to 
IPM lab, BARI, Gazipur, and observed under stereo 
zoom microscope. Collected bio-control agents 
were identified taxonomically and a few are yet to be 
identified. Parasitism (%) and adult emergence (%) 
of nymphal parasitoids were also recorded.
Through the survey, five species of parasitoids of the 
rugose spiralling whitefly viz. Encarsia guadeloupae, 
Encarsia dispersa, Comperiella bifasciata and two 
unidentified species were documented. Among 
them, Comperiella bifasciata is a new record in 
Bangladesh. Additionally, four predatory beetle 
species (Nephaspis oculata, Scymnus interruptus, 
Nephus quadrimaculatus, Jauravia pallidula) were 
also documented. Among them Scymnus interruptus, 
Nephus quadrimaculatus, Jauravia pallidula are 
newly recorded in Bangladesh. One species of 
predatory mite (unidentified) was also documented 
from the survey work. 
It revealed that, parasitization (%) and adult 
emergence (%) of nymphal parasitoids of rugose 
spiraling whitefly varied significantly among 
different locations. Natural parasitism by these 
parasitoids ranged 11.43 to 18.17% across different 
locations with highest parasitism recorded in 
Kishoreganj and lowest in Chapainawabganj, while 
parasitoid adult emergence ranged 8.05 to 11.65 
%, with highest emergence recorded in Pabna and 
lowest in Chapainawabganj.

M.D.H. Prodhan, M. Afroze, A. Begum, S. Jahan

The study was carried out in Pesticide Analytical

Research Institute during 2024-25. Pesticide standard

lufenuron were prepared separately in acetonitrile 
(MeCN) at a concentration of 1000 mg/L and stored 
at -20°C until use. A mixed standard solution of 50 
mg/L in MeCN containing all the aforementioned 
pesticides was prepared by adding the appropriate 
volume of each individual stock solution in a 50 ml 
volumetric flask and made to volume by addition of 
acetone. An intermediate mixed standard solution 
of 10 mg/L in MeCN was prepared from the 
mixed standard solution of 50 mg/L. Then working 
standard solutions of 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, and 
5.0 mg/L in MeCN were prepared by transferring 
the appropriate amount from 10 mg/L intermediate 
mixed standard solution into seven separate 10-mL 
volumetric flasks. All the standard solutions were 
kept in a freezer at -20 °C until use. In this study, 
the modified QuEChERS extraction technique was 
used for the extraction and clean-up of samples. 
The concentrated extracts of the selected matrices 
were analyzed by GC-2010 (Shimadzu) coupled 
with Electron Capture Detector (ECD). The present 
study was conducted to analyze multiple pesticide 
residues in eggplant, bitter gourd, yard long bean, 
apple and date fruits collected from Dhaka, Jashore 
and Gazipur district of Bangladesh.
A total of 210 samples were analyzed. Out of 210 
samples, 40 (19.0 % of the total number of samples) 
contained detectable residues and 170 samples 
(81.0 % of the total number of samples) contained 
no detectable residues of the sought pesticides. Out 
of 20 apple samples, 1 had chlorpyrifos residue 
with a level above the EU-MRL. In case of 20 
dates fruit samples, 1 had acetamiprid residue with

352 I Entomology
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
a level above the EU-MRL. Out of 50 eggplant 
samples, 3 had residues of chlorpyrifos with a 
level above the EU-MRL. In case of 60 yard long 
bean samples, 17 had residues with a level above 
the EU-MRL. In case of 60 bitter gourd samples, 
7 had residues of chlorpyrifos with a level above 
the EU-MRL.

The study was carried out in Pesticide Analytical

kg. Overall, 10% (6/60) of the analyzed samples

accessions. The findings indicate that CA Kha-

germplasm lines for future breeding and cultivation 
in the hilly region.

An experiment was conducted during November

Khagrachari hill district to evaluate the productivity 
and profitability of intercropping cabbage with 
sweet gourd under different planting systems. The 
trial was laid out in a Randomized Complete Block 
Design (RCBD) with three treatments Results 
revealed that sweet gourd yield alone was highest 
in T3 (31.50 t/ha) compared to T1 (29.56 t/ha) and 
T2 (29.63 t/ha). Cabbage yield varied significantly 
with the highest yield (38.12 t/ha) under T3. 
In terms of sweet gourd equivalent yield, T3 
outperformed all treatments (50.56 t/ha) followed 
by T2 (41.09 t/ha) and T1 (29.56 t/ha). Economic 
analysis showed that T3 achieved the highest 
gross return (Tk. 15,16,800), gross margin (Tk. 
10,66,800) and benefit-cost ratio (3.37). Farmers 
expressed positive feedback, highlighting better 
land use efficiency, higher income and improved 
soil fertility. Therefore, intercropping cabbage 
with sweet gourd (T3) can be recommended for 
sustainable intensification in the hill district of 
Bangladesh.
Piloting of BARI mustard varieties in the eastern 
part of Bangladesh
J.A. Chowdhury, M. R. Karim and M.A.A. Malek
A field trial was conducted at Khagrachari in 
the eastern region of Bangladesh to evaluate the 
performance of two mustard varieties BARI 
Sarisha-14 and BARI Sarisha-20 under local 
agro-ecological conditions. The primary objective 
was to increase mustard productivity and identify 
the most suitable variety for expansion in hilly 
regions. The experiment was carried out on 1.0 
ha land during November 2024 with proper 
fertilizer application, irrigation and spacing. Data 
on yield and agronomic traits were collected and 
statistically analyzed. Results showed that BARI 
Sarisha-14 had a significantly higher seed yield 
(1411.6 kg/ha) compared to BARI Sarisha-20 
(1363.7 kg/ha), with better seed weight and earlier 
maturity. Farmer opinions also favored BARI 
Sarisha-14 due to its earlier harvest and higher 
economic return. The findings suggest BARI 
Sarisha-14 is more suitable for mustard expansion 
in the region.

vegetative growth, reaching up to 170.9 cm in height 
(Alikadam) and achieving yields as high as 1807.33 
g per plant (BandarbanSadar). Arabica showed 
consistent growth, with a peak height of 126.3 cm 
(Alikadam) and maximum yield of 1234.67 g per 
plant (BandarbanSadar). Tree volume increments 
averaged 424% for Robusta and 554% for Arabica 
in favorable locations, reflecting strong adaptation. 
These results demonstrate Robusta's broader 
adaptability and higher yield potential, while 
Arabica thrives in specific microclimates, offering 
strategic insights for expanding coffee cultivation 
sustainably in Bangladesh's hill regions. Continued 
monitoring will refine varietal recommendations to 
enhance farmer livelihoods and support national 
agricultural diversification.

Detection of differences in vegetation and 
chlorophyll content in agricultural field using 
unmanned aerial vehicles
M. Mukhlesur Rahman, Nur Mohammad, Istiak 
Ahmed, Md. Monirul Islam 
This reports a field-scale study to detect differences 
in the amount of vegetation and chlorophyll content 
of crops using an unmanned aerial vehicle (UA V) 
fitted with a multispectral camera. The purpose 
of this study, on the experimental farm of TCRC, 
Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute. The 
normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) 
and normalized difference red edge (NDRE) were 
obtained from five spectral band images (red, green, 
blue, infrared (NIR), and red edge (REDGE)) that 
were processed by software into a full image map. 
We used the image map obtained to analyze the 
farmland and identify variations in the greenness 
of plants. We compared three layers with different 
indices and indicated differences in vegetation 
activity for NDVI and NDRE. NDVI showed a 
visible green color wherever vegetation was present. 
With NDRE and NDCI we observed crops with low 
chlorophyll content, indicating nitrogen limitation 
in the leaves. These observations demonstrate 
the efficacy of using NDRE and NDCI as a 
sensitive index for monitoring chlorophyll content. 
Therefore, we suggest from our study that NDRE 
and NDCI may be most useful index chlorophyll 
deficiency detection. Nutrient application will 
be implemented exclusively where chlorophyll 
deficiency is present.
Yield prediction of mustard crop by using satellite 
based remote sensing technique in Bangladesh
M. Mukhlesur Rahman, Nur Mohammad, Istiak 
Ahmed, M. A. Monayem Miah and Suman Biswas
Mustard (Brassica spp.) is one of the important 
oilseed crops which has potential demand as the 
preferred edible oil for the majority of people 
of Bangladesh. The accurate estimation of both 
harvested area and yield of mustard are equally 
important in ensuring the accurate determination of 
their product. The traditional measurement of these 
statistics is time-consuming, tedious, and costly. 
Whereas remote sensing techniques are being used 
to easily measure these statistics at high spatial 
and temporal resolutions. Therefore, an attempt 
was made to predict the mustard yield through 
satellite-based remote sensing techniques before 
its harvesting. To get this done, the high spatial-
temporal resolution Satellite imageries of Sentinel 
2A (~10m) and Landsat 8 (~30m) were acquired for 
the three study locations after setting the experiment 
in a farmer's field for three consecutive mustard 
growing seasons of 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25. 
The mean Normalized Difference Vegetation Index 
(NDVI) was extracted from the maximum NDVI-
produced temporal satellite imageries within the 
growing season from 20 farmer's mustard fields of 
each study location. The first year's results revealed 
that in most cases the yield was maximum for the 
field where the NDVI values were not maximum 
and vice-versa. However, the relationships of the 
extracted mean NDVI and yields were established 
using the classical linear regression model where 
the model was developed using the first two years' 
data and was validated using the data of the last 
study period. These equations were validated by 
using data from 2023 to 2025 seasons and found 
that an average error of estimation is about 8 to 
12% for the three study region. It can be concluded 
that NDVI derived from remote sensing can be 
an effective tool for early estimation of mustard 
yield. The study developed a remotely sensed yield 
prediction model using high-resolution satellite 
imagery to predict mustard yields 15 days before 
harvest.

Crop-type mapping acreage and yield estimation 
of major crop in dry seasons using remote sensing 
and machine learning algorithms
Nur Mohammad, Mohammad Mukhlesur Rahman, 
Istiak Ahmed, Mohammad Rasel, and Kaushik 
Kumar Saha
Crop acreage analysis and yield estimation are prime 
importance in field-level agricultural monitoring and 
management. This enables prudent decision making 
during any crop failure event and for ensuing 
crop insurance. The free availability of the high-
resolution Sentinel-2 satellite datasets has created 
new possibilities for mapping and monitoring 
agricultural lands in this regard. The present study 
conducted on the Tatibandha and Vaina unions/
blocks at Sujanagar upazila in Pabna district, 
Bangladesh during 2024-2025. The heterogeneous 
crop area was mapped according to the respective 
crop type, using Sentinel-2 multi-spectral images 
and two machine learning algorithms- Suport Vector 
Machine (SVM) and Random Forest (RF). Plot-
level field information was collected from different 
cropland types to frame the training and testing 
datasets (comprising 70% and 30% of the total 
dataset, respectively) for cropland classification and 
accuracy assessment. The major dryseason (winter) 
crop acreage was identified based on three major 
crops like Boro rice, onion and mustard in the study 
area through this classification. The extracted maps 
had an overall accuracy of 74.24% and 77.27% 
respectively, in the SVM and RF classifications, 
with respective Kappa index values of 64.22% and 
67.83%, along with F1-score 74% and 77% and 
showed that RF method proved to be more accurate. 
The methods used in this paper can be readily applied 
elsewhere for accurately enumerating the respective 
crop acreages. Effective estimation of crop yields 
at a regional scale holds significant importance in 
facilitating decision-making within the agricultural 
sector, thereby ensuring grain security. However, 
traditional ground-based measurement techniques 
suffer from inefficiencies, and there exists a need 
for a reliable, precise, and effective method for 
estimating onion yields. In this study, we employed 
five machine-learning algorithms: partial least 
squares regression (PLS), support vector machine 
(SVM), random forest (RF), and extreme graidient 
boosting (XGBoost) and decision tress (DT). We 
combined these methods with multi-temporal 
indicies like NDVI, GNDVI, EVI, CGVI and 
NDRE data for onion yield estimation. Following an 
accuracy evaluation, the RF model emerged as the 
most accurate for onion yield estimation, achieving 
an R2 of 0.26, an RMSE of 3.57, and followed by the 
XGBoost (R2=0.15, and RMSE=4.13). We concluded 
that the efficacy of combining multi-temporal remote 
sensing data with machine-learning techniques for 
accurate onion yield estimation, thereby aiding 
agricultural authorities and production enterprises in 
the timely formulation and refinement of cropping 
strategies and management policies for the ongoing 
season.
Forecasting onion yield by using satellite-based 
remote sensing technique in Bangladesh
Nur Mohammad, Mohammad Mukhlesur Rahman, 
Istiak Ahmed, Mohammad Rasel, and Md. Abdul 
Monayem Miah
Onion is one of the major vegetables as well as 
spices crops with the largest production worldwide. 
Onion plays as a major contribution as spices crop 
which is used in daily meal in Bangladesh. This 
study used remote sensing (RS) techniques for 
forecasting pre-harvest onion yield to improve 
the management system and accurate strategies 
regarding food security. Remote sensing can be 
used for yield estimation prior to harvest at the field 
level to provide helpful information for agricultural 
decision making. The Normalized Difference 
Vegetation Index (NDVI) calculated from remotely 
sensed data has been widely used to predict crop 
yield. The study used Landsat 8/9 (~ 30 m) high 
resolution data for 2022-2023 and 2023-2024 
to predict onion yield based on the year 2024-
2025 at Sujanagar, Pabna; Baliakandi, Rajbari 
and Durgapur, Rajshahi district respectively. The 
single cloud free image acquisition date based on 
maximum NDVI for Landsat 8/9 satellite image 
was used for each onion growing period to develop 
the yield prediction model. A regression model was 
performed between NDVI values and 35 farmers 
field-level onion yields based on model accuracy 
criterion like R 2, RMSE, MAPE and NRMSE for 
selected locations. The mean yield gap of onion 
was found 5.97%, 4.83% and 5.30% for the study 
area. It can be concluded that NDVI data extracted 
from Landsat 8/9 high resolution satellite images 
can be successfully used to predict the onion

yield with appreciable accuracy. This research 
recommends the implementation of satellite 
multispectral imagery for accurate onion yield 
forecasting to enhance agricultural planning and

Calibration and performance evaluation of 
IOT-based sensors for precision monitoring of 
horticultural crops
Kowshik Kumar Saha, Istiak Ahmed, Dilip Kumar 
Roy, Md. Abdur Rab Gazi, Md. Ashrafuzzaman 
Gulandaz
Soil moisture sensor performance is strongly 
influenced by the type of growing media. This 
study evaluated Teros 12 and Rod sensors in 
100% garden soil, 100% cocodust, and a 50:50 
garden soil and cocodust mix. Teros 12 showed 
high accuracy in garden soil, while the Rod 
sensor was highly sensitive but overestimated at 
low moisture levels. In cocodust, only the Rod 
sensor responded significantly, though nonlinearly. 
Findings underscore the need for substrate-specific 
calibration to ensure reliable moisture monitoring 
across different media.
Genome-wide identification, characterization, 
and bioinformatics analysis of the major 
functional regulatory elements of the Rnai genes 
in Bnassica napus L.
Zobaer Akond, Sheikh Hasna Habib, Md. Shakil 
Hossain, Nurul Haque Mollah
Dicer-like (DCL), Argonaute (AGO), and RNA-
dependent RNA polymerase (RDR) are known 
as RNAi genes in eukaryotes, which control 
gene expression at the transcriptional or post-
transcriptional level and are often involved in 
maintaining plant growth and development. These 
genes also control expression in response to 
various biotic and abiotic stressors. This molecular 
mechanism is, however, maintained by the 19-
24 nucleotide non-coding small RNA molecules 
(miRNA/siRNA). The identification and analysis of 
the motif structure, chromosomal mapping, major 
functional regulatory components, synonymous 
and non-synonymous substitution ratios (Ka/Ks), 
duplication and divergence periods of the genes, 
and expression at various organs/tissues have not 
yet been studied in detail for these gene groups. This 
study finally identified 8 DCL, 27 AGO, and 17 RDR 
RNAi-related genes in Brassica napus. The motif 
analysis revealed that most of the proteins conserved 
a similar motif sequence to those of the RNAi genes 
in Arabidopsis. Furthermore, sequence logo and 
relative frequency analysis showed that Alanine 
(A), Glutamic acid (E), Lysine (K), Serine (S), Valin 
e(V), Glycine (G), Leucine (L), Proline (P), Arginine 
(R), Aspartic acid (D) were the leading amino 
acids in the predicted motifs. Genomic distribution 
showed that 52 genes were distributed among the 19 
chromosomes. Segmental distribution of the genes 
was observed in high, and some tandem duplication 
was observed in the BnAGO and BnRDR genes. The 
trans-regulatory analysis revealed that the top six TF 
families were Dof, ERF, C2H2, bZIP, TCP, and HD-
ZIP. The BnRNAi genes-TFs network analysis also 
showed that three (Dof, ERF and C2H2) TF families 
of the BnDCL group were highly connected to the 
identified RNAi genes, whereas 5 (Dof, C2H2, ERF, 
bZIP and TCP) TF families of the BnAGO group 
were largely linked to the identified genes, and four 
(bZIP, ERF, TCP and HD-ZIP) TFs were highly 
connected to the BnRDRs. The findings of this work 
would be valuable for further in-depth investigation 
of their molecular mechanisms to utilize the RNAi 
pathway technique to improve a sustainable climate-
smart-ready rapeseed-mustard variety from the B. 
napus species at BARI.

Foreseeing the field emergence of bt brinjal seed 
lots unifying with the vigor test 
M. Rasel, M. S. Rahman and I. Ahmed
An experiment measuring the viability, vigor and 
germination of BARI Bt Begun-1 (brinjal) seed lots 
with tetrazolium test, Electrical conductivity (EC) 
test and standard germination method respectively 
was conducted to predict the field emergence (FE)

germination ratio (GR) it can be predicted that EC

Efficiency of agricultural practices for food 
security in Barind region of Bangladesh: an 
exploratory survey
M. Rasel, K. S. Rahman and S. M. A. Shiblee
This exploratory study investigates the efficiency 
of agricultural practices and their impact on food 
security in the Barind region of Bangladesh, one 
of the country's most climate-vulnerable and 
agriculturally significant areas. Data were collected 
from 100 farming households across five blocks 
in Raninagar Upazila of Naogaon district using 
structured questionnaires and field observations. 
Key areas examined included crop cultivation, 
irrigation, input use, post-harvest management, and 
socio-economic conditions. Findings reveal that 
while most households achieve basic food self-
sufficiency for 8-10 months per year, the efficiency 
of their practices is hampered by groundwater-
dependent irrigation, overuse of chemical inputs, 
limited mechanization, and poor access to markets 
and storage facilities. Statistical analysis using 
Exploratory Descriptive Statistics (EDS) in 
R-Studio shows a strong association between farm 
size, education, training access, and food security 
outcomes. Households with institutional support 
performed better in terms of yield and resource use 
efficiency. Despite moderate staple crop sufficiency, 
nutritional security remains inadequate due to low 
dietary diversity. The study underscores the need 
for integrated interventions-such as sustainable 
water use, capacity building, improved extension 
services, and inclusive market access-to enhance 
the resilience and productivity of agriculture in the 
Barind region, thereby contributing to long-term 
food and nutrition security
A statistical investigation of climate parameters 
on the mango yield of Rajshahi district
Jamila Khatun Prioty, Istiak Ahmed and Mohammad 
Rasel
This study investigates the statistical relationship 
between climate parameters and mango production 
in Rajshahi District, Bangladesh, using annual data 
from 1993 to 2023. Climate variables considered 
include maximum, minimum, and average 
temperature, total precipitation, and solar radiation. 
Two time-series approaches were applied: ARIMAX 
with external regressors (climate variables and 
cultivated area) and Prophet (models) with climate 
regressors. The baseline ARIMA(0,1,0)+drift model 
produced RMSE ≈ 42,087 and MAPE ≈ 21.14%. 
Incorporating cultivated area provided the greatest 
improvement (RMSE ≈ 39,512; MAPE ≈ 14.46%). 
Among climate-only regressors, precipitation and 
solar radiation modestly improved accuracy (RMSE 
≈ 41,511-41,523; MAPE ≈ 20.7-21.5%), while 
temperature regressors had limited effect. Prophet 
models performed best when minimum temperature 
was included, supporting short-term forecasts. 
Overall, cultivated area dominates yield variation, 
with precipitation, solar radiation, and minimum 
temperature emerging as consistent climatic drivers.
Efficiency of agricultural practices for food 
security in Charland region of Bangladesh: an 
exploratory survey
J. K. Prioty, K. S. Rahman and S. M. A. Shiblee
This study investigates the efficiency of agricultural

366 I Agricultural Statistics and ICT
BARI Annual Report 2024-25
floods. While traditional methods dominate,

Bioinformatics analysis of the dicer-like (DCL), 
argonaute (AGO), and RNA-dependent RNA 
polymerase (RDR) gene families in Lens culinaris 
L.
M. S. Hossain, Z. Akond and M. Z. A. Talukder
RNA silencing is mediated through RNA 
interference (RNAi) pathway gene families, i.e., 
Dicer-Like (DCL), Argonaute (AGO), and RNA-
dependent RNA polymerase (RDR) and their cis-
acting regulatory elements. The RNAi pathway is 
also directly connected with the post-transcriptional 
gene silencing mechanism, and the pathway 
controls eukaryotic gene regulation during growth, 
development, and stress response. Nevertheless, 
genome-wide identification of RNAi pathway gene 
families such as DCL, AGO, and RDR and their 
regulatory network analyses related to transcription 
factors have not been studied in many pulse 
crop species, including lentil (Lens Culinaris). 
In this study, we studied In-silico genome-wide 
identification and characterization of DCL, AGO, 
and RDR genes in lentil thoroughly via integrated 
bioinformatics approaches. A genome-wide analysis 
identified 4 LcDCL, 12 LcAGO, and 5 LcRDR 
candidate genes based on multiple sequence 
alignment and phylogenetic tree related to the RNAi 
pathway in lentil genomes. These genes correspond 
to the Arabidopsis thaliana RNAi silencing genes. 
The analysis of the conserved domain, motif, and 
gene structure (exon-intron numbers) for LcDCL, 
LcAGO, and LcRDR genes showed higher 
homogeneity within each group of their Arabidopsis 
counterpart. These genome wide analyses of these 
RNAi gene families provide valuable information 
related to RNA silencing, which can be useful to 
lentil breeding programs as well as those in closely 
related species such as pea, grass pea or faba bean, 
providing more data to increase the knowledge of 
this interesting gene family.
Potential use of remote sensing platforms for 
garlic yield prediction
M. A. Mottalib, M. A. Alam, A. H. F. Fahim, M. A. 
Rahman, M. A. Islam, M. M. Hasan, M. M. Alam, 
M. Z. Hasan, M. A. Hoque, M. A. Rahman, K. 
Hassan, and Z. H. Prodhan
This study evaluated the suitability of various 
vegetation indices from Sentinel-2 imagery for 
predicting garlic yield across different growth 
stages. The indices analyzed included NDVI, 
SA VI, GESA VI, GCVI, EVI2, NDRE, and 
MCARI. NDRE consistently showed the strongest 
correlation with yield, achieving the highest R2 
value (0.6798) on 09 March 2024 coinciding with 
garlic's bulb development and maturity stage. GCVI 
(R2 = 0.5573) and GESA VI (R2 = 0.5281) also 
performed well, while MCARI showed poor results 
throughout. NDRE's sensitivity to chlorophyll and 
canopy structure under high biomass makes it highly 
effective in dense garlic fields. GCVI provided the 
best model fit (R2 = 0.6063), while NDRE had the 
lowest prediction error (RMSE = 194.80 kg/ha; 
MBE = 160.62 kg/ha). GESA VI, despite weaker 
statistical performance, aligned most closely with 
BBS yield estimates, highlighting the importance 
of ground validation. Yield mapping revealed that 
68% of the area produced 9.3-10.1 t/ha, confirming 
NDRE as the most reliable index during late growth 
stages.
Land suitability assessment for spices crop 
production through remote sensing and GIS in 
southern saline region of Bangladesh
M. A. Mottalib, KK Saha, M. A. Rahman, M. A. 
Alam, A. H. F. Fahim, M. Z. Hasan, M. A. Hoque,

This study aims to identify suitable land for spices 
crop production in the southern saline region of 
Bangladesh, considering topography, climate, and 
soil properties. The Analytical Hierarchy Process

was applied using GIS. Key criteria included

BARI Annual Report 2024-25
soil texture, depth, salinity, land type, surface

organized at BARI during the year 2024-25 on 
different aspect of agricultural Knowledge share to 
achieve the goal of Annual Performance Agreement 
(APA). A total of 560 participants of BARI and

Photography Section
Pankaj Sikder and Naznin Akter
Photography Section of BARI is one of the big 
service provider in research and technology transfer 
events. The photography section is involve in 
processing photographs and video clips to ensure 
effective use of its parent institute and is assigned 
to support the researchers in print, soft images and 
electronic form of the important images at the right 
time.
Major functions of photography section:
 To expose, collect, preserve and display 
photographs of different research activities and 
events held in BARI.
 To display photographs of visitors, research 
activities, agricultural fairs, BARI technology 
village activities, publications and other 
activities on the central display board.
 To ensure all kind of photographic equipment's 
information.
 Make video documentary for broadcasting 
technology based on the scientists demand.
 To arrange and supply the photography news 
of different programmes for publishing in the 
newspapers, magazine, journal, TV etc.
 To supply the photographs and news info to the 
editorial and publication section for newsletter.
 To supply the photographs and news info to the 
ICT for BARI Facebook and website. 
 Coverage the Director General and Directors 
visit at different stations of BARI.

activities were performed by this section during

photograph, 20,000 were photo editing and 22 were

Planning &
Evaluation Wing
Introduction
The Planning and Evaluation Wing of the 
Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute 
(BARI) plays a pivotal role in steering the nation's 
agricultural development towards sustainable and 
innovative pathways. As the foundation upon which 
BARI's strategic initiatives are built, this wing 
serves as the compass for agricultural research and 
policy formulation in Bangladesh. Its multifaceted 
responsibilities encompass meticulous planning, 
rigorous evaluation, and the alignment of research 
activities with the ever-evolving needs of the 
agricultural sector.
Activities of the Planning and Evaluation Wing
Planning and Evaluation Wing is playing a pivotal 
role for BARI. Planning is a process of deciding in 
advance what we want to get (goal) and how we will 
get it. Evaluation enables us to assess how well we 
are doing and to learn from this. The activities of 
planning & evaluation wing of BARI are:
• Preparation and processing of Project Proposal 
(DPP/RDPP/TAPP)
• Preparation of new scheme (Karmasuchi) under 
revenue budget.
• Preparation of monthly report (IMED-05) and 
quarterly report (IMED 02 and 03)
• Preparation of project director`s profile (IMED-01)
• Preparation of procurement plan (works, goods 
& services), work plan of projects and their 
subsequent approval by the authority.
• Monitoring and evaluation of development 
projects including procurement status (tender 
related activities).
• Preparation of Project Completion Report (PCR) 
(IMED-04).
• Preparation of financial and physical progress 
report of the project and send to the Ministry of 
Agriculture
• Co-ordination of planning and development of 
co-ordination committee (P&DC) meetings of 
BARI
• Liaison with IMED, planning commission and 
different ministries as and when necessary.
• Performing other activities as directed by the 
Director General, BARI.
• Participate in the monthly ADP review meeting 
in Ministry of Agriculture.
• Preparation of budget and report for "Sustainable 
Development Goals target, 2030".
• Preparation of ADP and RADP for on-going & 
proposed development projects.
• Preparation of monthly progress report on work 
plan for prime minister's office and Ministry of 
Agriculture.
• Participate in Budget Working Group Meeting in 
Ministry of Agriculture.
• Participation in Mid-term budget framework 
meeting.
• Preparation of Five Year Plan (FYP).
• Preparation of research activities according to 
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) which 
was instructed by cabinet division as well as 
collaborated with United Nations (UN) and Food 
and Agricultural Organization (FAO).
• Preparation of Projects for Delta Plan-2100.
• Participation in different meetings conducted by 
Ministry of Agriculture (MoA).

INFORMATION REPORT
(As per Information Commission Requirements)
Institutional information:
BARI (Bangladesh Agricultural research Institute) is 
the largest multi-crop research institute conducting 
research on a wide variety of crops such as tubers, 
pulses, oilseeds, vegetables, fruits, spices, flowers, 
cereals, etc. Besides variety development, this 
institute carries out research on such areas as soil and 
crop management, disease and insect management, 
water management and irrigation, development 
of farm machinery, improvement of cropping and 
farming system management, post-harvest handling 
and processing, and socio-economic studies related to 
production, processing, marketing and consumption. 
The institute functions with the Director General as 
the chief executive along with four directors of its 
four major wings such as Research Wing, Support 
Services Wing, Training & Communication Wing 
and Planning & Evaluation Wing.
BARI has a long historical background of its 
own. The emergence of the Institute in its present 
status has occurred through a number of changes 
starting from simply a sub-ordinate status under 
the Department of Land Records in the then 
Bengal. On the recommendation of the famine 
commission in 1880, the Bengal Department of 
Agriculture was established as a sub-ordinate part 
of the Department of Land Records in the then 
Bengal. In 1906, Lord Curzon, the then Vice Roy 
of India had granted separate status to the Bengal 
Department of Agriculture and in the same year, a 
Nuclear Agriculture Research Laboratory under 
this department was established at Tajgaon, Dhaka. 
In 1908, an experimental station what has become 
known as Dhaka Farm was established on an area 
of 161.20 hectares of land. This Dhaka Farm was 
the predecessor of BARI and some other research 
institutes. Establishment of Dhaka Farm offered a 
good scope for conducting research in the field level 
in 1947, Bengal Department of Agriculture was 
renamed as East Pakistan Department of Agriculture. 
The two constituent divisions of the department 
were Research and Extension. In 1962, there was 
a severe blow to agriculture research when the 
land of Dhaka Farm was acquired for establishing 
Second Capital (today called Sher-e-Bangla Nagar). 
In 1968 two separate directorates were established 
- one was Directorate of Agriculture (Extension 
and Management) and the other was Directorate 
of Agriculture (Research and Education). The 
Directorate of Agriculture (Research and Education) 
was mostly concerned with research. This 
directorate was also responsible for the management 
of Bangladesh Agriculture Institute (BAI) at Sher-
e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka. Later in 1980s and 1990s, 
two other agriculture colleges, one in Patuakhali 
and the other in Dinajpur, were established. These 
two agriculture colleges were also administered 
by BARI until these became universities, the 
former provincial organization took on national 
responsibilities. Like many other sectors, agriculture 
sector inherited poor manpower and insufficient 
administrative set ups as well. Therefore, it was 
rightly thought to have established a coordinated 
and comprehensive research and some major 
decisions were taken up in 1973. Another important 
development in the year was the presidential Order 
No. XXXII that helps strengthen and reconstitute 
agricultural research organizations and system in 
the country. Upon subsequent developments of 
research institutions led to further restructuring in 
1976, through the presidential Order No. LXII, the 
Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) 
emerged as an autonomous and effective research 
organization following the dissolution of the 
Directorate of Agriculture (Research and Education) 
with sufficient operational flexibility, structural 
modification and improvement of regional and sub-
stations.

BARI Annual Report 2024-25

INFORMATION REPORT
(As per Information Commission Requirements)
Operational information:
Director General who is the Chief Executive of the 
institute has overall responsibility for administration, 
finance, development and execution of program 
related to research, manpower development, 
dissemination of information, transfer of technology 
and other extension activities. The Director General 
is assisted by four directors: Director (Research), 
Director (Support & Service), Director (Training 
& Communication) and Director (Planning & 
Evaluation).
Director (Research) is responsible for program 
planning, monitoring and evaluation of the research 
activities as performed by the research centers, 
divisions and the regional and sub-stations. 
Director (Support & Service) is responsible 
for personal management, finance & accounts, 
procurement, infrastructure development, security, 
transportation and repair & maintenance.
Director (Training & Communication), on the other 
hand, is responsible for the transfer of technologies 
to the users through trainings, seminars, workshop, 
print & electronic media. Human resource 
development through training and arrangement 
scholarships for higher studies at home and aboard 
also fall within his responsibilities.
Director (Planning & Evaluation) is responsible for 
developing, executing, monitoring, evaluation of 
different projects under development budgets and 
Programmes (Karmosuchi) under revenue budget 
of GoB with the help of crop centers, sub-centers, 
divisions, Regional Agricultural Research Station 
(RARS) and Agricultural Research Station (ARS). 
Also involves in financial management, procurement 
activities, infrastructure development and arrange 
meetings like Project Implementation Committee 
(PIC), Project Evaluation Committee (PEC) of 
different projects and Planning & Development 
Committee (P&DC) meeting of the institute.
Each research division is headed by a Chief 
Scientific Officer (CSO) who is also designated as 
divisional head whereas a research center is headed 
by a Director/CSO. Each divisional head is assisted 
by the concerned scientists starting from Scientific 
Officer (SO) to Principal Scientific Officer (PSO). 
On the other hand, each research center is comprised 
of scientists from various disciplines in the rank of 
Scientific Officer (SO) to Chief Scientific Officer 
(CSO).
